ASRS:1824647.n: I flew from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. I landed just over the number at ZZZ. Halfway down the runway I notice that I did not have any brakes. The airplane continued over the end of the runway and came to a stop.
ASRS:1824647.s: The pilot landed an aircraft at ZZZ and discovered a total brake failure halfway down the runway. The airplane overran the runway end and came to a stop.

ASRS:1824672.n: The hold short markings at the approach end of Runway 27 are blacked almost all the way out due to dirt or other material (actually look as though they have blanked out).Applicant wasn't sure if it was the actual hold short line. Looking at the lines I wasn't sure those were the hold short lines, due to the lack of distinction, I looked to see if there were any closer to runway and didn't see any so knew these should be them.Applicant turned aircraft around quickly once he figured it out and the wing may have crossed the line. There were no communications from the Tower or Ground controllers about the aircraft position.Recommend that the hold short lines be cleaned or repainted as needed so as to prevent confusion as to the distinction of the lines.
ASRS:1824672.s: A pilot reported that faded hold short markings at the approach end of Runway 27 caused uncertainty about the line's location, potentially resulting in a wing crossing the boundary. The pilot turned the aircraft around without controller intervention and recommended cleaning or repainting the markings to prevent confusion.

ASRS:1824677.n: Did not check airspace prior to take off. Flew drone over dwelling for roof inspection without prior authorization from AZO. Management discovered airspace incursion during monthly flight reviews. I shall always include airspace checks prior to every flight.
ASRS:1824677.s: A pilot flew a drone over a dwelling for roof inspection without checking airspace or obtaining authorization from AZO. Management discovered the airspace incursion during monthly flight reviews, prompting the pilot to commit to checking airspace before every future flight.

ASRS:1824679.n: Please be advised that on Date and Date 1, I was flying 1,500 feet MSL the exact same track, although on Date 1 I was flying the opposite direction, south-eastbound in the Los Angeles basin. In the exact same place Southwest of the Disneyland TFR, and 4 NM on the [073]° radial from [SLI VOR], I lost the GPS signal on both my Garmin GPS 650 and 750 units and my Apple iPad for about 3 minutes. I was just about to advise the SNA tower when they all three came on. All these are new Garmin radios less than a year old. I have never had that happen anywhere before or since. As you can imagine that's quite unnerving down in that airspace.
ASRS:1824679.s: A pilot flying 1,500 feet MSL southeastbound in the Los Angeles basin lost GPS signals on Garmin 650/750 units and an iPad for three minutes near the SLI VOR. The signals returned before the pilot could contact SNA tower, with no cause identified for the isolated incident.

ASRS:1824682.n: I was making a normal approach to Runway XXR on a solo flight. Winds were about 220 @ 6 mph at the time. After I had turned to base, ATC inquired if I had turned to base. I informed ATC that I had turned to base and at that point immediately needed to turn to final. ATC asked the plane at taxiway to hold position. Glide slope was normal. I was on centerline and airspeed was 85 mph. Final approach continued normally and as I crossed threshold, I reduced throttle to idle. The airplane landed firmly but did not bounce. When the nose wheel came down, I perceived a violent shaking of the nose wheel. The airplane began heading to the right side of the runway and I attempted to correct as normal. However, my corrections started a series of oscillations that grew in amplitude. The airplane was now headed in to the grass safety area after taxiway and I let the plane continue on its track for fear of flipping the plane. The airplane went into and out of the drainage ditch and came to a stop about 2-3 yards from taxiway X. I believe that one of the contributing factors to the event was task overload. This was my second solo flight and the additional load of ATC's inquiry, the follow on instructions to the other plane near my intended runway, and my focus toward the other aircraft may have used more attention than intended. I believe also that a greater emphasis overall on safe after landing roll would be good. In the FAA 'Airplane Flying Handbook', after landing roll safety is addressed but does not receive the emphasis it deserves.
ASRS:1824682.s: A solo pilot on final approach to Runway XXR experienced violent nose wheel shaking and directional oscillations upon landing, causing the aircraft to veer off into a drainage ditch. The pilot attributed the incident to task overload from ATC communications and a lack of focus on the landing roll.

ASRS:1824710.n: After landing at MDW around XA:30L, we were taxiing from Taxiway Y to T. At the end of Concourse XX, a 737 was being pushed back. Ground did not warn us of this aircraft. The First Officer (F/O) was calling Company Ops (Ground Ops) at that moment to verify the gate assignment. Ground Ops gave us the gate assignment and proceeded to give details that I needed to call Crew Scheduling upon parking. Meanwhile, I could see that the other 737 had been pushed back farther than it should have, causing me to hit the brakes to avoid a collision. At the same time, monitoring the Company frequency and the First officer's communication to Ground Ops, I was also suddenly distracted with the thought that Crew Scheduling had an unscheduled assignment for me and that I was on the hook to call them upon parking. To me, this was a clear violation of FAR 121.542, which outlines sterile cockpit requirements, it wasn't a violation on our part, rather the Company violated this regulation. I told the F/O that I was deviating to the right of the taxiway centerline, which leaves little room to the right, to avoid the pushed 737 off my left. I slowly and carefully taxied past, ensuring we had distance. I estimate we had only 15' distance from our wingtip to theirs. Thereafter, I taxied to the gate, still distracted and frustrated that I had been tagged to call Crew Scheduling. This distracted me from the primary task of safely taxiing the aircraft. Notification to contact Crew Scheduling has no place in the sterile cockpit environment. FAR 121.152 says, 'No certificate holder shall require, nor may any Flight Crew Member perform any duties during a critical phase of flight except those duties required for the safe operation of the aircraft. Duties such as Company required calls made for non-safety related purposes as ordering galley supplies and confirming Passenger connections, announcements made to Passengers promoting the air carrier or pointing out sights of interest and filling out Company payroll and related records are not required for the safe operation of the aircraft. Ground Ops generally has no idea what Crew Scheduling is doing or needs, they're not involved in the function of who flies what and where. In this case, I believe Crew Scheduling must have deliberately contacted MDW Ground Ops ahead of time and specifically instructed them to notify us during taxi-in. If they did this, this was willful on their part, it is beyond egregious, and it cannot be tolerated. Highly recommend that the FAA issue a notice to Air Carriers and their Ground Ops and Crew Scheduling departments, explaining what sterile cockpit rules are and when Crew Scheduling assignments cannot be allowed (i.e., during aircraft taxi). I also recommend that the FAA review our FOM and Ground Ops Manual, and specifically include verbiage prohibiting messages from Crew Scheduling during critical phases of flight and sterile cockpit.
ASRS:1824710.s: During taxi-in at MDW, the flight crew avoided a collision with a pushing 737 after Ground Ops distracted them with a Crew Scheduling call. The pilot attributed the near-miss and subsequent distraction to a violation of sterile cockpit rules caused by non-safety related duties during a critical phase of flight.

ASRS:1824729.n: Stock item X, ice release labeled flammable and stickered Hazmat was found on the jetbridge at gate X
ASRS:1824729.s: A ground handler found a flammable, Hazmat-labeled ice release item on the jetbridge at Gate X. The report does not specify the aircraft, phase of flight, or the outcome of the discovery.

ASRS:1824764.n: I, the CA (Captain), was PM (Pilot Monitoring), the FO (First Officer) was PF (Pilot Flying). During the climb-out phase in level flight in mildly hazy VMC at 17,000 MSL at 290 KIAS with Autopilot B engaged the Master Caution, the 'FLT CONT' item on the CA-side SAP ('6-pack'), and the right half only of the 'STAB OUT OF TRIM' light illuminated. Press-to-test of the 'Stab out of trim' light showed both bulbs operable. After establishing that FO was actively remaining the PF, I performed 'Stabilizer Out of Trim' QRH procedure with the result that the autopilot electric trim and both pilot yokes trim switches were inoperative in both directions. I notified ATC that we had a mechanical problem that would eventually result in [requesting priority] and landing at a nearby airport, probably ZZZ, but for now we were content to remain at 17,000 slowly outbound from ZZZ while we worked the problem. Knowing we were also over landing weight, nicely under control, and still had a lot of checklists to run, I had no desire to rush into diving towards some final approach fix before we were ready to land. I performed the 'Stabilizer Trim Inoperative' QRH procedure with the result that manual hand-cranked trimming was possible in either direction, albeit against unusually high resistance and with a 'cogging' feel as if pushing against a powered but stalled electric motor. This was true even when the aircraft was in-trim. One pilot could move the trim using one arm, but two pilots using one arm each worked much better for anything more than a couple turns of the trim wheel. We found that one pilot could both hand-fly and crank the trim, but tended to make unwanted aileron inputs while doing so. So it was doable in a pinch but not smooth. The forces required to turn the trim wheel did not appreciably reduce as we later slowed & configured. In the course of reading & discussing or doing the 'deferred items' section of the 'Stabilizer Trim Inoperative' QRH I started to activate the GPWS Flap inhibit switch. The FO stopped me saying we were above the 250 KIAS speed limit at that time. That sounded familiar to me, but no such limitation is stated at that point in the QRH. Nevertheless, we chose to delay activating the GPWS flap inhibit until we had slowed to first configuration speed around 220KIAS. Discussed with [the] FO whether ZZZ was the best divert option and which runway to use. ZZZ & longer Runway XXL was the unanimous choice. By that time we were a few miles south of [the] VOR on a south-southwesterly course for ZZZZZ, roughly 100nm from ZZZ.I then performed the 'Non-routine Landing' QRH procedure, alerting ATC for a return to ZZZ XXL with ARFF (Airport Rescue Firefighting) standing by. Coordinated with ATC for return via direct arrival for ILS XXL. Asked Company explicitly to alert ZZZ Approach & Tower of the intended non-standard XXL landing. Notified Dispatch via ACARS report. Briefed FAs via intercom, and passengers via PA on the situation, my expectations, and their roles. We selected the non-standard landing Runway XXL based on that runway being much longer than the more typical landing Runway XXR. That was a minor miscue, because I/we had not considered the effect of the large displaced threshold. Which I now consider insignificant. For landings eastbound the difference is 2500 feet and would be significant. Lesson learned: the big runway length number on the 10-9 page can be significantly misleading, take the time to dig into the 10-9A details page. The fact that was our takeoff runway and within Jepp FDPro I'd used the green highlighter to extend the highlighting all the way to the takeoff threshold didn't help. What had been useful to help direct my taxi to the correct threshold for takeoff became mildly misleading when evaluating which runway to land on. Which was not a side effect I noticed at the time or had considered previously. Still working as PM I performed normal divert preparations and top-of-descentprocedures: Reconfigured FMS & ACARS for ZZZ arrival, obtained ATIS, set up radios and performed approach brief, landing assessment, etc. Notified ZZZ Ops of our return by direct radio call to obtain a gate assignment.We discussed that we'd be a little above the normal max landing weight, but the already requested priority covers for that administrative requirement, and the runway available was nearly double what the QRH procedure's performance chart said was required. Performed descent checklist and before landing checklists and flows as normal. Throughout the evolution the FO kept us neatly in control, tight on the FD despite sometimes having to hand-crank the trim himself, caught a few radio calls I missed, and demonstrated overall high situational awareness and excellent systems knowledge. This is especially impressive for someone fairly new to the airplane who is just back from 6 months of furlough. During descent below 10,000 ft approaching downwind we changed control to CA as PF w FO as PM. We sighted the field while on base. During the turn-on to final I was using visual lookout primary, backed up by the LNAV purple line and the ILS. There was a moment of confusion as the ILS and LNAV came together before I was aligned with what I had thought was the landing runway. Having landed on XXR dozens (hundreds?) of times over the decades, that habit was unhelpful for a few seconds before we got fully established pointing at the correct runway. We then realized that Runway XXR is concrete and very easy to see in mildly hazy conditions while Runway XXL is asphalt and much harder to see. In fact XXL was invisible until we got closer in following the LNAV & LOC. My general habit on any landing involving parallel runways is to verbalize seeing all the relevant runways by name and explicitly saying which one I'm aligning / aligned with. E.g. 'I see XXL and XXR. I'm aligning with XXL.' For whatever reason that verbalization didn't occur, with sorta predictable results.Intercepted final outside intermediate fix in level flight at 3,000 ft. Configured to flaps 15 early and slowed gradually to Vapp of approximately 160KIAS before glideslope intercept at final approach fix. FO kept the airplane nicely in trim on my requests.Made a flaps 15 slightly overweight (approx. 148K#) approach and landing to a smooth touchdown on ZZZ Runway XXL just shy of the 2000ft marker. Upon stopping made a PA to reassure the passengers & remind them the safety vehicles would be seen around the airplane. ATC gave us an alternate frequency to contact ARFF on. Which surprised both of us a bit. Once we were communicating with ARFF I requested they inspect us for hot brakes or damaged tires. ARFF found normal brake temps and no tire damage. At ARFF's request I released them at that point and we taxied normally to [the] gate.Following shutdown the FO attempted to manually crank the trim to the usual post-shutdown 5 units from the 8-9 units we'd used at touchdown. At zero airspeed the trim was still 'cogging' and almost as difficult to move as it had been in flight. So we left the trim at the landing setting for Maintenance's edification. Which point we discussed with the Chief Pilot who met the flight and again later with the maintenance folks who also met the flight. I made appropriate aircraft maintenance log book entries for the stab trim failure and for the overweight landing. Spoke with Dispatch by phone before leaving aircraft per FOM. The next morning I filed the required report. In all I think this event worked out pretty close to textbook, minus the small glitches identified above.The main electric trim failing was the causal factor. Everything else is just details.1. Subsequent research on the ground shows that activating the GPWS Flap Inhibit switch is called for in 11 different QRH procedures, and in the Flaps 15 landing procedure. Only the 'One Engine Inoperative' QRH procedure and the 'Flaps 15 Landing' procedures mention that limit, the other 10 QRH procedures do not.I do not know whether those differences are deliberate or an oversight. Suggest someone on the 737 fleet team look into this. If the difference is deliberate there probably ought to some verbiage available in QRH or [procedures] to explain the rationale so others don't mistakenly apply a remembered restriction where it's not intended. 2. We were both surprised to see that only half of the 'Stab out of trim' annunciator illuminated. Which left us wondering at first if we had a warning system malfunction or a trim malfunction. I surmise now that the right bulb is connected to FCC (Flight Control Computer) B and the left is connected to FCC A. And that had the Captain been PF, we'd have seen the left half illuminate instead.However it works, the details of left & right are not documented in [manual] where the annunciator is described. At a minimum there should be a statement like 'Only half of the annunciator may illuminate. That is still a valid indication of an out-of-trim condition.'3. Overall, from the 'Stab out of trim' annunciator illuminating to touchdown was about 30 minutes. From reviewing the ACARS logs I know it was at least 28 minutes and less than 35. As the CA / PM / QRH operator I was working quickly and diligently almost the entire time to accomplish all the non-routine and normal procedures in full without hurrying. Had we turned back even a couple minutes earlier the airplane would have been approaching the airport before we were fully caught up and mentally transitioned from handling an [urgent inflight situation] to performing a normal low-stress, albeit flaps 15, landing.Given the reality that following all the procedures fully takes nearly 30 minutes, I believe we do a disservice to pilots in the sim, rushing around the traffic pattern with an engine out. That encourages hurrying, doing QRH steps without really thinking them and their implications through, etc. We fight how we train, and we're training to hurry. I question the wisdom of that.Further I question the wisdom of planned arrival fuels that only allow for approximately 30 minutes to flameout at traffic pattern altitudes. The so-called FAR '45 minute reserve' is 45 minutes at cruise, not 45 minutes at traffic pattern altitude with e.g. flaps stuck partly extended. I now conclude that performing a major QRH evolution discovered in the arrival traffic pattern while down near Company planned arrival fuels would necessitate skipping a lot of steps or giving them at best a lick and a promise.I believe it is unwise to plan arrival fuels that tightly. Yes, we commonly have additional hold and / or Dispatch fuels. But each of those may legitimately be burned in delays encountered before the [urgent situation] appears. This saves Company a lot of money on the many flights that don't turn out worst-case. But it really sucks to be the pilot who draws that short straw, and is faced with either doing a rushed job of handling the [situation] or running out of fuel.That's planning, in extremis, to fail. An industry-leading FAR 121 carrier should not be planning to fail. In extremis or otherwise. At a level off of 17,000 ft we noticed stab out of trim light. I was the PF so it was my aircraft. The Captain ran the stab out of trim QRH checklist which lead to the QRH stab trim inoperative checklist. We did not regain electric trim. Manual trim was what we were left with. Then the non-routine QRH checklist was performed. The manual trim wheel was difficult to work for both us even when the plane was near an in trim condition. Speed was slowed to about 270kts from about 290kts then. [ATC was advised] and we planned and set up for an arrival back to ZZZ. I flew the aircraft and worked the manual trim while the CA performed checklists, set up for the arrival and approach, and the briefings. Manual trim did not become much easier until on approach when aircraft was slowed to approach speed, however even then it was difficult. The CA took the aircraft and I became the PM. The landing was nice and smooth. Once on the ground using the manual trim wheel to reset the stab trim to 5 units was still very difficult.
ASRS:1824764.s: The Captain and First Officer experienced a stabilizer trim failure during climb at 17,000 feet, causing inoperative electric trim and requiring manual hand-cranking. They diverted to ZZZ for a safe, slightly overweight landing on Runway XXL after coordinating with ATC and ARFF.

ASRS:1824766.n: We [were] on the Vanze 2 Arrival into MEM and I was flying. After reviewing the arrival and expecting a south landing, we got a new ATIS with the airport now landing to the north. This required a change of FASOP Intersection to 10,000 and 230 knots. I put this in the FMS. I also read the North arrival on the RNAV approach to the FO. When we got to the top of descent, we had not been given a descent yet, so we requested lower. The FMS showed us high as we continued to ask for lower altitudes to make the crossing restriction. Eventually the controller gave us direct to FASOP Intersection. I told the FO we were already going there. Then the FO realized that we were not going to FASOP Intersection, but were going to FASON Intersection. We realized that I had put the crossing restriction in the FMS at FASON Intersection, and not FASOP Intersection!! This was the reason the FMS showed us high. This error was because there are two almost identically named intersections on the arrival, With the change of runway from South to North and having already verified the points, the names being so close in spelling make the error one that could easily be repeated by other crews. Once we corrected the crossing restrictions to the correct FASOP Intersection, we were very low and we slowed our rate of descent.Because we had already verified the points on the arrival, when we got the runway change, we verbally reviewed the changes and the need to insert the crossing restriction in the FASOP Intersection. It was night and when I looked at the FMS, the first point that came up was FASON, which I mistook for FASOP. Both the FO and I did not catch it. We did not realize the mistake until we were given direct FASOP because we were requesting a descent because we thought we were high and were not going to make the crossing restriction. I did mention the two intersection name similarities to the Controller, and told him it was a potential problem. He said he agreed, but the fix was above his pay grade.The names of FASOP and FASON need to be changed, especially when there is a crossing restriction that needs to be entered in to the FMS. With both names so similar, it is easily to put the crossing restriction at the wrong point like we did. The runway change was the key here, as we were already set up to land to the South. Then the runway changed to land North, prompting the change to put the crossing restriction in the FMS.
ASRS:1824766.s: The pilot flying a Vanze 2 Arrival into MEM entered a crossing restriction at FASON instead of FASOP in the FMS after a runway change, causing the aircraft to appear high. The error resulted from similar intersection names and was only corrected after ATC issued a direct routing, leaving the crew low and requiring a reduced descent rate.

ASRS:1824805.n: During preflight W&B Preliminary report 1 and 2 and Final W&B all showed FOM XYZ Sup Proc [Supplementary Procedures] in effect. It was not on the [Final] release. Received ACARS message that FOM XYZ Dry Ice Sup Proc in effect but failed to adequately QA the ACARS message for Time and Dispatcher Initials. Enroute checked reviewed ACARS log confirming no T&I [time & Initial] to amended [Flight] release. Called Dispatch on arrival to verify that we hadn't just missed the T&I. [Cause was reporter's] Inattention to detail... just missed it.
ASRS:1824805.s: The flight crew failed to verify time and dispatcher initials on an ACARS message regarding Dry Ice Supplementary Procedures during preflight and enroute phases. The reporter attributed the oversight of the amended release to their own inattention to detail.

ASRS:1824819.n: When departing Runway XXR in ZZZ, the left throttle was difficult to set for takeoff power, but by the time the problem was identified the aircraft was already at V1. Departure commenced and climb continued. The left engine APR (Automatic Performance Reserve) fired and the left engine was non-responsive to the movement of the throttle. When reaching 10,000 ft the aircraft was under control, the Captain transferred the controls to me and told me to get delayed vectors. The Captain started the QRH checklist for Uncommanded acceleration/ENG OVERSPEED after completion of the emergency checklist. The single engine in-flight engine shutdown checklist was commenced on Abnormal. After completing Abnormal the problem still continued. The Captain [advised] ATC and commenced the Severe Engine Damage In-flight QRH procedure. After selecting LH ENG FIRE PUSH switch light, the problem resolved and all associated emergency, abnormal, and normal checklists were completed. The captain and I briefed the approach and landing to Runway XXR at ZZZ. The Flight Attendant was notified that the aircraft would be returning to ZZZ for a precautionary landing. The passenger announcement was made in flight advising passengers of a maintenance issue that required the aircraft to return to landing at ZZZ. The Captain had me transfer the controls back to him and landed the aircraft. Upon landing we taxied off Runway XXR and [airport] crews did a post flight walk around of the aircraft. During crew walk around another passenger announcement was made advising passengers to remain seated with seat belts fastened and that the aircraft would be parking at [the] gate. After the aircraft was given all clear, the aircraft taxied to the gate and parked without further issue. After gate arrival passenger announcement was made advising passengers of the reason we returned to field. After parking at the gate, Maintenance write up was made by the Captain and associated phone calls were made to document the incident. [A] defective thrust lever on the left engine [could be solved by] possible checks more often on engine thrust levers. When departing Runway XXR in ZZZ, the left throttle was difficult to set for takeoff power as reported by the First Officer, but by the time the problem was identified the aircraft was already at V1. Departure commenced and climb ensued. Left Engine APR (Automatic Performance Reserve) fired and Left Engine was non-responsive to throttle lever movement. Upon reaching 10,000 ft and aircraft under control. Captain transferred controls to the First Officer and told FO to get delay vectors. Captain started QRH checklist for Uncommanded Acceleration/ENG OVERSPEED after completion of emergency checklist. Commenced Single Engine Inflight Engine Shutdown checklist on Abnormal. After completing Abnormal problem was still ongoing. Captain then [advised] ATC and commenced Severe Engine Damage in Flight QRH procedure. Upon selecting LH ENG FIRE PUSH switch light problem resolved and all associated emergency, abnormal, and normal checklists were completed. Flight crew briefed approach and landing to Runway XXR at ZZZ. Flight attendant was notified that we would be returning to ZZZ for a precautionary landing. Passenger announcement was made in flight advising passengers of a maintenance issue that required return to landing at ZZZ. Captain then commenced transfer of controls back to Captain and landed aircraft. Upon landing aircraft taxied off Runway XXR and [airport] crews did a post flight walk around of the aircraft. During crew walk around another passenger announcement was made advising passengers to remain seated with seat belt fastened and that aircraft would be parking at [the] gate. After aircraft was given all clear we taxied to the gate and parked without further issue. After gate arrival passenger announcement was made advising passengers of reason we needed to return to field. After parking at gate maintenance write-up was made and associated phone calls were made to document incident.
ASRS:1824819.s: During takeoff from Runway XXR at ZZZ, the left throttle was difficult to set, causing the left engine APR to fire and become non-responsive to throttle movement. The crew returned to ZZZ for a precautionary landing after resolving the issue by selecting the left engine fire push switch, attributing the event to a defective thrust lever.

ASRS:1824947.n: My student and I were practicing commercial pilot maneuvers in the South Practice Area of the ZZZ terminal area. We were .5 NM SE of [the lake] doing a steep spiral from 4,500 feet down. We made multiple radio calls and this was our second maneuver. After the first turn and a half, we were alerted to a traffic conflict on my iPad, which was supplied by a Sentry Mini ADS-B receiver. We looked for the traffic and spotted them on a collision course. We immediately terminated the maneuver and I took controls from the student to execute an emergency climb, as our paths were roughly perpendicular and I did not believe a turn would be enough to clear us. The other aircraft (C172) passed directly under us without making a control input or diverting course. We did some more maneuvers, also with thorough radio calls but had no further conflicts.
ASRS:1824947.s: A commercial pilot and student practicing steep spirals in a ZZZ terminal area aircraft detected a C172 on a collision course via ADS-B. The pilot executed an emergency climb to avoid the conflict, while the C172 passed directly underneath without altering course.

ASRS:1824957.n: Shortly after capturing the VNAV for descent into ZZZZ from FL450, when the auto throttles reached idle power, there was a loud bang followed by intense airframe vibration and noise. When I looked at the engine instruments the left Turbine Gas Temperature (TGT) was indicating in the amber arc and bouncing into the red. Based on the fact that the vibration and noise was increasing in intensity I made the decision to shut down the left engine with the fuel cock. After shutting down the engine the noise and vibration stopped, and everything was normal. We ran all pertinent check lists and after [advising ATC] continued on to an uneventful landing in ZZZZ. I feel that I may have acted prematurely in shutting down the engine so quickly but based on the intense noise and vibration, along with elevated TGT I was worried that the engine was going to come apart. I still have no information on the engine as mechanics have not been able to make it here yet.
ASRS:1824957.s: The pilot reported a loud bang, intense vibration, and elevated left engine TGT shortly after initiating descent from FL450. The pilot shut down the left engine, which stopped the symptoms, allowing for an uneventful landing at ZZZZ, though the specific cause remains unknown.

ASRS:1824959.n: I was cleared for taxi to Runway 28R at MYF. The clearance was, 'Taxi H, A, 28R' I taxied straight ahead for Hotel taxi way and accidentally continued onto Delta and onto Runway 28L. The Controller informed me of my mistake and I immediately exited runway 28L. There were no other aircraft in the pattern and this mistake did not impede traffic flow for another aircraft.The Controller did not seem concerned and did not ask me to copy a phone number.This was an early morning flight with the sun just coming up. As I taxied out, the sun was in my eyes and with 28L being such a narrow runway, I did not notice that I had crossed onto a runway.Although I am in no way placing blame, I do feel it would be helpful for ground control to remind pilots to take an immediate RIGHT onto taxi way Hotel. I feel this would been a great help to me and would also help other pilots in the future.
ASRS:1824959.s: The pilot taxied at MYF and accidentally entered Runway 28L instead of following the clearance for Taxiway H to Runway 28R due to sun glare obscuring the narrow runway. The controller notified the pilot, who immediately exited the runway with no traffic impact.

ASRS:1824970.n: Chain of Events: During taxi out for a formation flight I was #2 of 6. Taxi was single file with a standard spacing. As we taxied I added a slight amount of power to adjust my spacing from the lead aircraft. The flight lead gave a frequency change while we were in route to the runway. Due to frequency congestion I was not sure I had entered the correct frequency and glanced down to check it. When I looked up the leader had stopped and I immediately cut the power and applied brakes. As I was still closing on the lead aircraft I attempted additional braking which caused the tail to rise and the prop caught the rudder of the lead aircraft. I immediately shut down my engine and advised the lead aircraft to shut down.The lead aircraft had damage to the rudder, vertical stabilizer and elevators.My aircraft had gouges in the propeller and paint on the nose cone and engine cowling.Contributing Factors: Frequency congestion, Momentary distraction, Unbriefed/Called stop by lead aircraft.Corrective Action: Review and modify formation taxi procedures to prevent reocurrance.
ASRS:1824970.s: The #2 pilot in a six-aircraft formation taxi collided with the lead aircraft's rudder after a momentary distraction from frequency congestion caused a delayed stop. The incident resulted in damage to both aircraft's propellers and control surfaces due to the unbriefed stop and closing speed.

ASRS:1824978.n: Near miss with a T-38 during a right downwind at ZZZ Runway XX. The T-38 did a go around for Runway XY and started a climb while we were turning crosswind to downwind, upon intersecting Runway XY the T-38 had leveled off co-altitude and was headed at us from the arrival end of Runway XY. IP (Instructor Pilot) had them in sight and was about to take controls to make evasive action when the T-38 aggressively pitched up as if they spotted us as well. Ultimately, the T-38 passed over and behind us within 500 ft. The T-38 was on a military frequency however we overheard Tower respond to their call with something along the lines of 'He was in a right downwind for [Runway] XX, no factor'. ATC cleared me for right traffic out of Runway XX and I was staying in the pattern. ATC had cleared a T-38 for landing on Runway XY. The T-38 performed a go around and my instructor point out that he was headed directly for us. I saw him aggressively pitch up and climb above our wing.
ASRS:1824978.s: A pilot and instructor in a right downwind for Runway XX at ZZZ experienced a near miss with a T-38 that executed a go-around for Runway XY. The T-38 leveled co-altitude and headed toward the aircraft before aggressively pitching up to pass 500 feet above and behind, despite conflicting ATC clearances.

ASRS:1824985.n: I was proceeding northbound on a VFR flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 with flight following (ZZZ2 or ZZZ3- I can't recall which). I had observed an aircraft on my ADS-B traffic that appeared as if it would be slightly to the right of my flight path but presented no conflict (blue vs red indication). It was very hazy and as I was concerned with the varying cloud layer conditions ahead, I scrolled my flight display forward, located the AWOS for ZZZ1 and had just dialed it into my #2 comm (monitoring flight following on comm 1). Before I could scroll the ADS-B driven display back to my immediate area and so that I could re-acquire the ADS-B traffic target I heard the beginning of an urgent alert for traffic conflict from ATC. I heard the traffic alert warning and the words 'Immediate turn...'. Simultaneously I had a traffic alert alarm flash with audible warning on my ADS-B flight display (but no display of the target itself, just to have the AWOS I had dialed in come blasting in over comm 2, completely blocking comm 1 ATC instructions beyond the words 'immediate turn'. The volume had been set too high on comm 2. Since my last view of the oncoming target I had on ADS-B seemed to indicate that it would pass on my right, I immediately and automatically turned left and visually scanned as it was no time to have my head in the cockpit or fiddle with radios. The Controller repeated the warning and that time I heard his instructions to 'turn right' (his second warning) during the AWOS lull. I heard the 'turn right' about the same time I visually acquired the oncoming aircraft. I saw it at my approximately 10 to 11 O'clock at about a mile or so, opposite direction at what appeared to be 200 feet lower than me (very rough, estimate) about 5,300 feet MSL, I think. I immediately turned hard right. The target was a Cessna (C152 I think) flying on a roughly parallel course by then on my left wing at the incorrect altitude for their direction of flight. I was flying at about 5,500 feet MSL on a north-northeast heading. After shutting down the background noise from Comm 2, and resuming course, ATC asked me if they had clearly communicated the instructions to 'turn right' which they had transmitted twice. I replied, Yes" as this as the Controller certainly had transmitted clearly, but due to the audible interference from comm 2 and the ADS-B traffic alert, I could not hear the communication clearly until the second warning, after I had already initiated a left turn. Given the last known position of the other aircraft and hearing only a partial warning from ATC, and the need to immediately react, I initially turned into (left) instead of away from (right) the traffic conflict as per ATC transmission."
ASRS:1824985.s: A VFR pilot flying northbound at 5,500 feet MSL initially turned left into a Cessna 152 conflict after AWOS audio on Comm 2 blocked the first ATC "turn right" instruction. The pilot corrected to a right turn upon hearing the second warning and visually acquiring the aircraft at approximately 5,300 feet MSL.

ASRS:1825015.n: I was working and had just arrived to start my shift. I had been working the sector less than 10 minutes when I cleared Aircraft X to cross ZZZ at or above 14,000 ft. and issued an approach clearance for the ILS approach. The pilot read back a crossing restriction of 11,000 ft., which I did not catch. I was relieved from the position for a break, and after leaving the control room I was told that [the flight] had descended below the MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) prior to reaching ZZZ and was issued a low altitude alert. I do not have any recommendations.
ASRS:1825015.s: An air traffic controller cleared Aircraft X to cross ZZZ at or above 14,000 ft, but the pilot read back 11,000 ft, which the controller missed. The aircraft subsequently descended below the Minimum IFR Altitude before reaching ZZZ, triggering a low altitude alert.

ASRS:1825023.n: While cruising at FL370, approximately 40 miles south of SAV, we experienced a severe updraft, causing the aircraft to rapidly climb to approximately 37,300 ft and then rapidly descend to approximately 36,500 ft. There was no weather displayed on our weather radar in our area of flight. The fluctuations lasted for about one minute. The rest of the flight continued as normal. In cruise at FL370, encountered clear air turbulence. No radar echoes, must have been convective activity building below our altitude. Updraft produced rain from below, lifted aircraft 300 ft above our cruise altitude. First Officer applied upset recovery controls which required descent 600 ft below our cruise altitude. Reported the event to Jacksonville Center. No other traffic in the area, no evasive action required. Flight continued normally without further incident.
ASRS:1825023.s: While cruising at FL370 south of SAV, the crew encountered clear air turbulence with no radar echoes, causing a rapid climb to 37,300 ft and descent to 36,500 ft. The First Officer applied upset recovery controls to stabilize the aircraft, and the flight continued normally after reporting the event to Jacksonville Center.

ASRS:1825156.n: Dirty sock odor descending into ZZZ. [Suggest] aircraft filtered bleed air.
ASRS:1825156.s: A pilot reported a dirty sock odor while descending into ZZZ. The reporter suggested the cause was filtered bleed air.

ASRS:1825171.n: GPS Jamming causing ADS-B OUT L and R alerts with loss of GPS position. GPS jamming.
ASRS:1825171.s: The crew experienced GPS jamming that caused ADS-B OUT L and R alerts and a loss of GPS position. The incident was attributed to GPS jamming.

ASRS:1825174.n: GPS Jamming in Russian Airspace 36,000 feet from LOGMU to ROKUB. [Cause was] Russian Jamming.
ASRS:1825174.s: The pilot reported GPS jamming while flying at 36,000 feet from LOGMU to ROKUB in Russian airspace. The reporter attributed the loss of GPS signal to Russian jamming.

ASRS:1825187.n: ATC advised we would be following a heavy aircraft on approach into ORD. While on short final, I observed the aircraft we were following on Taxiway P, headed eastbound. We continued on the approach and did not experience any effects of wake turbulence. I heard ATC instruct the aircraft to turn left onto Taxiway EE and taxi onto Runway 28R, which requires a turn of more than 90 degrees to complete. As the heavy aircraft negotiated the turn, I was just beginning to flare for the landing. I suddenly experienced what seemed to be a heavy crosswind from the right (much heavier that what was being reported), associated with a higher than normal pitch attitude to arrest the descent rate just before touchdown. Approximately 1-2 seconds before touchdown, the stick-shaker activated until the main landing gear made contact with the runway. A normal touchdown and roll-out was performed and we taxied to the gate without incident. The First Officer and I both agreed during the debrief that the approach and landing was stable and on proper speed throughout.I believe the cause of this event was a result of ATC giving the instruction to the heavy aircraft to make the left turn, causing its jet blast to cross directly over the approach end of Runway 28C. It appeared to create a crosswind/tailwind from the 5 o'clock position of our aircraft. I believe this is what contributed to the higher than expected crosswind from the right and the stick-shaker to activate just before touchdown. If ATC would have had the heavy aircraft hold short until the turn could be made in between arrivals, I believe this situation could have been avoided.
ASRS:1825187.s: The pilot reported that while landing at ORD, a heavy aircraft turning onto Runway 28R generated jet blast that caused a sudden crosswind and stick-shaker activation just before touchdown. The pilot attributed the event to ATC instructing the heavy aircraft to turn while the reporting aircraft was on final approach.

ASRS:1825212.n: Crew was nearing the bottom of the Hawks 7 Arrival in to Seattle and had descended to 5,000 ft. per ATC instruction. Shortly after leveling at 5,000 ft., crew experienced multiple wake turbulence events from a preceding B737. The pilot turned off the autopilot. Roll rates were roughly 15-20 degrees with about 5-10 degrees of bank. We did not deviate from course or have any exceedance. At the time of the event, the pilot flying (Captain) had auto-throttles off for practice.On the STAR, we were made to slow down early due to the close proximity of the airplane ahead of us. And for metering. We also had tailwinds and were only about 5 miles behind the airplane in front of us. We suspect the tailwinds made it take longer for the wake vortices to dissipate leading to our situation. In the future, I will be more vigilant when encountering this type of threat and talk about it with the Captain. If needed, we can ask for a delayed descent or vectors to mitigate this.
ASRS:1825212.s: The crew encountered wake turbulence from a preceding B737 while descending to 5,000 ft on the Hawks 7 Arrival into Seattle. The pilot attributed the event to tailwinds delaying vortex dissipation and close spacing, resulting in 15-20 degree roll rates without course deviation.

ASRS:1825221.n: Leaving ZZZ1 I was in the right seat training [the pilot flying]. We had received a clearance to make a right turn after departure to follow our given flight plan. I was handling the radios and [the pilot flying] was performing all other duties in a simulated single pilot operation. During the climb out I noticed that he was not cleaning up the airplane or turning at the prescribed times. I was in contact with ATC so it was a few seconds before I was able to ask him what the problem was. He told me that the trim was not working on his side while he was attempting to trim nose down. I did a quick verification that all circuit breakers where pushed in on my side in case it was an indication problem. We then switched the trim control over to the co-pilot side to see if it was an issue with just his trim control. Neither my trim control or the auxiliary trim switch was working. While he was holding the control yoke and manually controlling the pitch I tried the trim to see if the nose up trim would work. When it did I once again tried the nose down trim on my side. It worked but at a severely reduced rate. I then transferred trim control back to him and he was able to use it at the reduced rate. We began discussing how we would write up the trim system upon return to ZZZ1. [The pilot flying] then informed me that the trim had stopped working in the nose down direction completely. After once again trying to get the trim moving we referenced the QRH and ran the Trim Failure in Flight (Both Sides) checklist. We also [advised ATC] and opted to remain heading to ZZZ. There were several factors in the decision. The airplane was stable and controllable during cruise, we had Maintenance in ZZZ, the weather was VFR, ZZZ has a tower and emergency services and it would give us time to run the problem and formulate a plan for landing. We briefed and complied with the Landing with Flaps not Down Do-list. Since this was an unusual situation we opted to run the rest of the flight as two crew operations. We flew the ILS into ZZZ to help with altitude control and to give us a path to follow. We were able to land without further incident and taxied to the ramp and had an uneventful shutdown. [The pilot flying] became aware of the issue shortly after takeoff in the climb. I became aware shortly after when asking about the delayed response in the climb out. The trim system on the aircraft was failing to trim nose down. We checked the aircraft to verify no breakers or equipment was turned off. We then ran the appropriate emergency checklist and informed ATC of the situation along with [advised ATC]. We also reverted to two crew operations for the remainder of the flight to lessen the workload of the pilot flying. We also wrote up the problem upon landing in ZZZ. We had written up this problem the previous time we flew the airplane, thankfully with not as drastic results, and Maintenance had signed it off as fixed. We gave as accurate description as possible that this was a problem that would happen in flight but would be normal on the ground. The subsequent corrective action was just to test it on the ground and sign it off as unable to duplicate. When flight control issues are written up they can become serious very quickly. If they had dived deeper into the issue it might have been resolved the first time and we wouldn't have had to lose our ability to fully control the airplane and [advised ATC].
ASRS:1825221.s: During a training climb after departure from ZZZ1, the crew experienced a complete nose-down trim failure that reduced to a slow rate before stopping entirely. They executed the Trim Failure checklist, reverted to two-crew operations, and landed safely at ZZZ1, noting the issue had been previously reported but not resolved.

ASRS:1825261.n: This event involved a Crew Rest Module (CRM) change from Aircraft X to Aircraft Y. This is a common maintenance task that occurs when 767s are flown internationally. The process is controlled and documented by EO (Engineering Order) XXXXXX Part 1 CRM loaded ON aircraft and EO XXXXXXX Part 2 CRM removal. The EO affects the weight and balance and requires the BOW (Basic Operating Weight) to be changed before flight when the CRMs are installed or removed. The AMT is responsible for all maintenance actions. Once the changes are made he has to bring the paperwork to QC so that we can initiate the BOW change through [Flight Info]. [Flight Info] in turn contacts systems Engineering who makes the required BOW change in the computer weight and balance system. Once the BOW has been changed an e-mail is sent to [Flight Info] and QC (Quality Control) so that the paperwork can be stamped by QC indicating this step has been complied with. The paperwork is then returned to Maintenance and the EO and associated [Maintenance Release] can be signed off by the AMT. Engineering often takes several hours to make these changes so the paperwork often gets stamped by an inspector who did not initiate the BOW. On this event the AMT brought the paperwork to QC at approx XA:50 am. I started the scanning procedure and e-mail notice was sent to [Flight Info] at XB:12. I received the confirmation notice from [Flight Info] at XB:23. I notified the other Inspectors in the office of the BOW change requirements and that the paperwork was my desk. At some point I was called out to another aircraft for an inspection that I thought would take extended time to comply with. I gave the EO work cards to another inspector on duty. After I returned from the Inspection, the time was close to XC:30 which is clock out time for QC day shift. Just before I left for the day a swing shift Inspector asked about the CRM change paperwork. I was somewhat surprised that it had not been completed at this point. The paperwork was still on the inspectors desk that I had given it to nearly 3 hours earlier. Swing shift came in to a very busy day with many inspections, and several complex jobs to take care of so I checked and saw that an e-mail had just been sent notifying that the BOW had been changed. I stayed and tried to help out by taking care of the BOW weight issue. The e-mail was sent at XC:27 that the BOW Change was completed. I thought the e-mail addressed the BOW change for both Aircraft X and Y. I stamped the paperwork for both aircraft and notified the AMT that he could pick up the paperwork in the QC office. The mistake in this event is that I did not read the e-mail closely enough to insure that the BOW change included both aircraft. The original e-mail I sent to [Flight Info] initiating the process included info for both Aircraft X and Y. So I thought the reply was for both Aircraft. If I had noticed this I would have only stamped the E.O. for Aircraft X and not Y. Although the BOW was changed in the computer before the aircraft departed for flight, the mistake could have resulted in an improper BOW listed for the weight and balance computation. I have to slow down, read and understand the e-mail notification. Also it would be nice if we could get timely updates from Systems Engineers on the BOW changes. This one took in excess of 5 hours.
ASRS:1825261.s: A Quality Control inspector incorrectly stamped maintenance paperwork for two aircraft after misreading an email confirming a Basic Operating Weight change for only one. Although the weight data was updated before departure, the error could have resulted in an improper weight and balance computation due to the inspector's oversight.

ASRS:1825275.n: I was leading a flight of two [warbirds] to land at ZZZ on Runway XX right which is the north runway. Runway XX left is the south parallel runway. Tower cleared us to land. I was a straight in and Aircraft Y was a go-around. Aircraft Y announced that he was breaking to land from the overhead. Tower instructed him to break left which is non-standard when landing on the right runway since it would be across the left runway and we are always instructed to break right when landing on the right runway. As I touched down I heard tower instruct Aircraft Y to break left and immediately heard tower repeat break left as the tower operator noticed that Aircraft Y was breaking right. I looked straight up through my bubble canopy and saw Aircraft Y make an immediate correction and enter the left break as instructed. At no time did Aircraft Y make more than a 10-20 degree turn before correcting. The following day I was notified that there was a CFI with a student in a Cessna 172 in the right downwind to Runway XX right who was startled and was claiming that there was a near miss between herself and Aircraft Y although it is hard to imagine how that would be possible given that the Cessna would have been in downwind offset from the runway by quite a distance. Since I was leading the flight of 2 aircraft and was carrying the squawk and ADS-B for the flight, I am concerned that a complaint may be incorrectly filed against me even though I had landed at the time the incident occurred.
ASRS:1825275.s: The pilot leading two warbirds landing on Runway XX right reported that a trailing aircraft received a non-standard "break left" clearance, causing a brief deviation before correction. A Cessna 172 pilot later claimed a near miss, though the warbird pilot believes this is impossible given the Cessna's downwind position.

ASRS:1825280.n: After arriving at ZZZ, I requested 50 gallon of a gas, 25 per side. On initial departure climb CHTs (Cylinder Head Temperature) on both engines spiked to red line. I verified mixtures rich, airspeed and deck angle. Immediately decided to make a left 180 and land. After landing queried lineman about fueling. He verified that aircraft had been misfueled with Jet A.
ASRS:1825280.s: The pilot reported that after departing ZZZ with 50 gallons of fuel, both engine CHTs spiked to red line during climb. The pilot executed a 180-degree turn to land, discovering the aircraft had been misfueled with Jet A.

ASRS:1825284.n: Student pilot went for second solo in ZZZ Delta Airspace. During the second lap in the pattern, the student pilot was told to extend upwind followed by instructions to make left traffic. In the left downwind, ATC told the student pilot to make right 360's and after two right 360s he was required to extend downwind as well. At this time the student pilot may have become disoriented and misheard a communication from ATC where he began to turn left base where the near miss happened with a Lear Jet on Final for Runway XX. ATC told the Learjet to go around and evasive action was taken to avoid a collision. After the Learjet passed over head ATC gave the student pilot a right base to final for Runway XX and that was to a full stop. I believe ATC didn't really treat my student as a priority when the number of aircraft on the ground and in the airspace increased. I would have liked ATC to have taken more consideration for a student pilot. Having a student pilot extend upwind to almost outside the Delta followed by asking him to make multiple right 360s on downwind, followed by the making him to extend downwind all in one traffic pattern could throw a seasoned pilot off and cause a problem to stir. Aircraft Y Was Cleared to land on Runway XX. Aircraft X student pilot solo was making 360s abeam the numbers for Runway XX. Aircraft X was instructed out of the 360 to rejoin the downwind for Runway XX. I noticed that Aircraft X was heading towards the final. For Runway XX. I questioned Aircraft X to verify that he was remaining south of the center line for Runway XX. I then sent Aircraft X Around to stop his descent. With ground construction there are very complex taxi instructions. With a growing level of traffic. Student pilot solo should have be made a full stop (to come back [at] a less busy time). Additional positions should have been opened up to reduce workload and complexity.
ASRS:1825284.s: A student pilot soloing in ZZZ Delta Airspace became disoriented after complex ATC instructions, misheard a clearance, and turned left base toward a Learjet on final for Runway XX. The Learjet executed a go-around to avoid a collision, while the student was vectored for a full stop landing.

ASRS:1825294.n: I was on an IFR flight plan from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 after having transitioned from [Victor airway] to direct VOR. As I did not hear any hand off from ZZZ Approach to the next sector, I attempted to communicate with the last assigned frequency at ZZZ, but I was unsuccessful as I was most likely out of range. I then called Center on and was advised that they we're looking for me and to immediately climb from 7000 to 8000 ft which I complied with. While on that frequency I was advised to call ATC when I landed which I did. I was informed that I had flown for a period of time at 7000 ft. While the minimum vectoring altitude was 7,200 ft, but had not yet arrived at the point where it was 8,000 ft. During the period of deviation where I was 200 ft. Below the MVA I had visual contact with the terrain below as conditions were VMC with clear weather the entire time. I also advised ATC of that fact after they ordered me to climb to 8,000 ft. I believe that it would have been helpful and possibly avoided the situation had I attempted to check in with ATC sooner after not hearing a hand-off.
ASRS:1825294.s: The pilot flew 200 feet below the 7,200-foot minimum vectoring altitude while transitioning from Victor airway to direct VOR due to a missed hand-off and communication failure. The pilot climbed to 8,000 feet after Center advised the deviation, noting visual contact with terrain in VMC conditions.

ASRS:1825301.n: ZZZ ATC handed me off about 12nm north of the airport. I got the ASOS/AWOS info indicating 9kts at 230 degrees, no gusts. I used Runway XX.I applied 20 degrees of flaps, slowed to 80MPH, and transitioned into a forward slip. Had a smooth landing initially. The plane suddenly jumped back into the air with a dangerously slow airspeed and when I got it back on the ground it was pointed towards the left and I felt as if I was going to clip the nose of a parked Cessna 172 at the edge of the runway.It didn't seem to matter how much right rudder was applied, so I decided to go further left since that is what the plane wanted to do anyway to go around the back of the 172 in the grass. That was successful but I hit a taxi light with my left wing in the process.No property damage save my own wing and the taxi marker light. Student was cleared to Solo at ZZZ. During his Landing at ZZZ, The student described a wind shear event in which his aircraft clipped a runway light. The damage was assess less than $XXXX. No bodily harm nor personnel property damage had occurred. A dent into the leading wing was the result.
ASRS:1825301.s: A student pilot soloing at ZZZ experienced a wind shear event during landing that caused the aircraft to bounce and drift left. The pilot veered off the runway to avoid a parked Cessna 172, striking a taxi light and denting the wing, resulting in minor damage with no injuries.

ASRS:1825339.n: Our originating aircraft was towed from remote parking to the gate. I observed no pitot covers on the aircraft, but the probe heat switch streamers were attached to probe heat switches on the overhead panel. This led me to consider that the pitot tube covers had possibly been removed prior to the aircraft being towed from remote parking, which would require further inquiry. About ten minutes prior to push, Ground Ops personnel tapped on the side of aircraft to notify us that the pitot tube covers were removed. I inquired if they were removed prior to towing the aircraft from remote parking. I was advised that no pitot tube covers had been installed overnight due to a shortage of pitot tube covers in ZZZ. I called Dispatch/Maintenance to discuss this in reference to [document]. Chief Pilot was also advised. We decided to have contract maintenance inspect the pitot tubes to ensure no wasps had built any nests overnight. We pushed 29 minutes late due to the lack of probe covers in ZZZ to enable compliance with [document].From a Safety perspective, if wasps are still a concern in ZZZ, why were pitot heat covers not installed in accordance with [document]? If we had not made careful inquiry, we would have never known that pitot tube covers had not been installed and the first indication of wasp nests would have been with an IAS DISAGREE alert on takeoff, which would have required either a reject over 80 knots (possibility of aircraft being unsafe to fly) or flight with Airspeed Unreliable with an overweight landing or burning off approximately 25,000 lbs. of fuel to allow for landing within landing weight. It seemed to me that Ground Personnel in ZZZ were not clear on the requirements of the [document], not only because the pitot tube covers were not installed, but also because the Ops Agent seemed to be confused on whether or not the probe heat switch streamers were to stay on the aircraft or with Station Personnel.
ASRS:1825339.s: The flight crew discovered pitot covers were missing overnight at ZZZ due to a shortage, causing a 29-minute delay for maintenance inspection. The reporter noted that without this inquiry, undetected wasp nests could have caused unreliable airspeed alerts during takeoff, potentially requiring a rejected takeoff or overweight landing.

ASRS:1825372.n: APU fire return to field. Boarding and pre-flight normal. Once the packs were turned on the cabin cooled down easily, but we were not able to get the flight deck under 80 degrees until after engine start. Taxi was also normal, from [the gate] onto Taxiway 1, Taxiway 2, and to RWY XXL. To fly the departure up to and maintain 3,000 ft. Takeoff normal (full thrust takeoff per Maintenance request on maintenance release). On the climb out approaching 3,000 ft, in LNAV, we hit ALT CAP (Altitude Capture), and PNF (myself) rolled the speed to 230 knots. Right at this moment the APU FIRE EICAS message displayed, and the Fire bell alert sounded. Captain took both flight controls and radios, put the auto pilot on and addressed ATC. [Advised ATC] and requested an immediate return to the field for landing. I ran the APU QRC paper checklist. Which reads, Pull the APU Fire handle and rotate to the stop for 1 second. I completed the QRC items, and then turned to the electronic checklist to complete the full APU FIRE checklist. Which stated 'Choose one: APU Fire warning light stays illuminated (which it did), land at nearest suitable airport'. Captain then handed flight controls and radios to me, so that he could consult with the Flight Attendants and the Company. After doing so he took back over the role of PF (Pilot Flying). Captain then made a turn with ATC instruction back toward field for a downwind to RWY XXL. Still level at 3,000 ft. ATC requested where the fire indication was. We set up for an ILS approach, with appropriate frequency and FMS arrival selection for XXL. We were then given a descent to 2,000 ft. by ATC as well as a turn to base leg. Captain began to slow to configure for landing. Using speedbrakes to slow the aircraft. On this turn in the descent with Flaps 1, while retracting speedbrakes, and the MCP (Mode Control Panel) speed in the window set to minimum flaps 1 speed, we had a momentary shaker activation, less than 1 second, and I immediately put out Flaps 5 and we continued to slow and configure from there. We were cleared to maintain 2,000 ft. until established, and cleared for the ILS approach. We continued to add flaps to 15, then 20. Gear down, flaps 25 and 30 without event. Landing data was requested for landing on XXL, overweight 235k lbs, Auto brakes 2 was set for sufficient stopping distance. Also performed a small dip low on GS for touchdown to use full runway length. We touched down with 200 fpm descent. Rolled to Taxiway 3. Exited runway at 60 kts. Continued onto Taxiway 2 to hold short of Taxiway 4. At this time the [it was] assessed that no heat was found in the tail or any other part of the aircraft. The flight attendants also assessed no smoke or heat in the cabin. The decision was then made to taxi to a gate expeditiously to deplane passengers and get maintenance on board. Taxied to the gate, shut down the left engine to allow the jet bridge to be attached to the airplane, then shut down the right engine once ground power was established. APU Fire Indication after takeoff. Flight was the first segment on day one from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I was the flying pilot for this leg. Loading and boarding were normal with a mostly full flight. The cabin of the aircraft had been cooled nicely, but we were having a bit of a challenge cooling down the flight deck, with temperatures hovering in the high 80's. The ZZZ weather was 340/10, 10SM FEW 040 SCT080 BKN250 28/18 29.86. We pushed off the gate on time. [We taxied] to Runway XXL and contacted Tower. We accomplished the before takeoff checklist items and were cleared to takeoff Runway XXL on the ZZZ Departure. The maintenance release noted that a Max power takeoff was due, so we did so, at a TOG weight of 238,192 lbs and the flaps 5. During takeoff roll as we accelerated, water dripped out of the overhead panels which was interesting, we took off, cleaned up the gear and flaps as scheduled. Somewhere between 2,000 ft and 3,000 ft. in the climb in a left hand turn to heading 290, we had a Master Warning and an EICAS annunciation APU Fire. I continued to fly the aircraft, took the radios, and while the First Officer accomplished the APU Fire QRC. It is important to note that the fire light remained on and did not go out after running the QRC with no other indications of a fire. Also, it is important to note that the APU was shut down on the ground after engine start during the after-start checklist, and had been off for approximately 20 minutes. We ran the appropriate checklists, notified Dispatch and spoke with the flight attendants. The Purser was informed that we had an APU Fire indication and was asked if there were any fire indications in the aft cabin? They said they did not have smoke but noted a slight odor (possibly the fire extinguishing agent that was fired into the APU during the QRC). I told them to prepare the cabin quickly as we would be on the ground in 8 minutes. My FO (First Officer) and I spoke about the overweight landing, briefed the approach, and identified the ILS. We planned a flaps 30 ILS to Runway XXL at a weight of 235,000 lbs. as 235,000 lbs. was below our performance limit weight of 259.9, so a 30-flap landing was appropriate. Fortunately, we discussed the possibility of an overweight landing prior to takeoff, so we were already familiar with the requirements. Although we suspected an erroneous APU Fire warning, time was still a driving factor as the fire indication never went away. We maintained 250 kts for as long as possible then configured using flaps and speed brakes to slow the aircraft. We were configured with flaps 1 and were decelerating with the flaps tracking to 5 and the speed brakes out. We decelerated to flaps 5 maneuvering speed, and just as I started to retract the speed brakes for literally a split-second I heard a sound that was so brief I could not tell what it was. The FO told me that it was a split second of the shaker due to the boards being out at the flaps 5 maneuvering speed. We continued configuring with gear and flaps 30, accomplished the landing checklist. We flew the ILS to Runway XXL with the autopilot and auto throttles engaged until 500 ft when I disconnected the autopilot. I disengaged the auto throttles around 100 ft. I briefed that I would slightly duck under the glideslope with a planned touched down early in the landing zone.We touched down approximately 1,200 ft. down the runway with auto brakes 2 selected. The touchdown was extremely smooth with a VVI (Vertical Velocity Indicator) of less than 200 fpm. During the landing roll, we queried the Tower to see if they could see any smoke trailing the aircraft, and they said all looked normal. We rolled clear of the runway on Taxiway 3 and stopped on Taxiway 4 where the ground personnel looked us over. The ground personnel informed us that they could see no indications of a fire and that their thermal imaging scan showed no heat in the APU area. We ran through our after-landing flows and taxied to the gate. We shut downthe left engine so they could start deplaning the passengers. When ground power became available we secured the right engine and secured the aircraft. I proceeded into the cabin to chat with maintenance, passengers etc. Maintenance opened the APU area and said that they suspected a faulty fire loop, as there was no evidence of a fire. Maintenance later found that a faulty APU fire control panel was the cause of the warning. Also, the total flight time from wheels up to wheels down was 11 minutes. That is extremely fast when considering all the factors to evaluate. All in all, I feel that this was a well-executed event, and resulted in the safe return for passengers and crew.
ASRS:1825372.s: The flight crew experienced an APU fire warning at 3,000 feet during climb-out and returned for an overweight landing. Maintenance later determined the cause was a faulty APU fire control panel, as no actual fire or heat was found.

ASRS:1825419.n: On taxi to runway XX, holding short of runway, turned on cabin heat to use defrost (ram air and defrost fully open) for windshield and visible smoke and smoke smell was in the cockpit, turned off heater, and opened crew door, and promptly returned to gate, smoke dissipated and did not continue. At the gate, promptly deplaned passengers, and wrote up airplane.Caused by heater [malfunctioning].
ASRS:1825419.s: During taxi to runway XX, the crew detected smoke and odor in the cockpit after activating the cabin heat for defrost. The aircraft returned to the gate, passengers deplaned, and the incident was attributed to a malfunctioning heater.

ASRS:1825426.n: While preparing for departure we noticed we would not make the departure crossing restrictions on the ZZZZZ1 departure. Our plan was to bring this to the attention of ground so departure could be made aware. They seemed unwilling to help as did clearance and our overworked dispatcher. We went back and forth and finally were given a 'modified' ZZZZZ2 departure and proceed to ZZZZZ. While doing this departure we stayed in NAV and the plane turned east towards ZZZZZ. ATC gave us headings and informed us that it was not correct. Had we reviewed the departure closer we would have noted the headings and briefed better. Also, that departure is not in the FMS database.[The causes are] a long list. First cause is [the company] operating an airplane under conditions that it should not. An Airbus 321 weighing 192,000 lbs. in 38 Celsius temperature should not be allowed. The plane barely makes it off the ground and we have to climb out in unfamiliar configurations to get climb performance. I do not believe we will have an acceptable outcome if we ever lose an engine. 90+ Fahrenheit cockpit temps doesn't help and cabin temps of mid 80's are a distraction. Constant interruptions by FA's (flight attendants) due to pax getting up is a threat while attempting to find an acceptable departure. Uncooperative ground and clearance controllers who seemed irritated to even interact with us. Overloaded dispatcher which seemed to be the norm lately and was confirmed to me by 2 dispatchers riding the jump seat. Incorrect verbiage in the performance manual regarding the IAE (International Aero Engine) bump feature which was unfamiliar procedure to me. That was a distraction because it was a green B next to the EPR gauge, not a blue B next to the N1. Missing SID from our database (that would have prevented this event). Operating an aircraft under conditions that are borderline unsafe and expected to do so. The climb was so poor the aircraft started a 1,000 - 1,200 RPM descent upon flap retraction because of the temps and lack of power. Good CRM and PIC experience was our biggest asset managing the aircraft. Of course weather close to the airport was yet another factor. Make sure bump description is correct in the performance manual. Use of A321 under heavy and hot situations need to be reviewed out of ZZZ. Continue training emphasis for CRM because it made ATC and aircraft management seem minor.
ASRS:1825426.s: The A321 crew and ATC faced departure issues due to high weight, heat, and a missing SID, resulting in poor climb performance and incorrect routing. The pilot attributed the event to unsafe operating conditions, uncooperative controllers, manual errors, and distractions, noting that CRM prevented a worse outcome.

ASRS:1825483.n: I was on a solo time-building flight to ZZZ1. While climbing to 4,000 ft, I noticed the oil pressure was low on yellow and oil temp was high on the red arc. I leveled off and requested ATC to return to ZZZ and did not declare an emergency. Following ATC instruction, I descended to 3,000 ft, oil temps were still 250 on red and the pressure was 45. As I began my descent into the airspace the temperature was around 245, still on red, and would raise with any power over 1,700 rpm. As I reduced my throttle oil pressure went to 35. So I presumed the engine might fail and requested ATC to land immediately on Runway XXR (XXL was the active runway, So ATC called in Level 1 alert). After landing safely I taxied back to the ramp while the oil temp remained on red. The airplane was squawked.
ASRS:1825483.s: A solo pilot flying to ZZZ1 experienced low oil pressure and high oil temperature while climbing to 4,000 ft. The pilot returned to ZZZ, landed safely on Runway XXR after requesting immediate landing due to suspected engine failure, triggering a Level 1 alert.

ASRS:1825484.n: As we were in the flare on Runway 29 at EWR with power at idle or being reduced towards idle, maybe 10-20 ft off the ground, we were hit by jet blast from a departing heavy aircraft on the intersecting Runway, 22R. EWR was landing 29 and departing aircraft from [Runway] 22R at intersection [Taxiway] W or Y. The aircraft weather vane into the jet blast, the aircraft was pushed right of center line, we experienced moderate turbulence, and the aircraft rolled slightly to the right. I was able to control the aircraft as if [it was] landing in a crosswind and land safely. The aircraft never got into an unsafe situation. Needless to say, this caught us completely off guard. Maybe EWR needs to reevaluate this practice when heavy aircraft are departing. In the landing flare is not a great time to get hit with jet blast. Crews should also be aware of this hazard. As we were in the flare on Runway 29 at EWR with power at idle or being reduced towards idle, maybe 10-20 ft off the ground, we were hit by jet blast from a departing heavy aircraft on the intersecting runway, 22R. EWR was landing [Runway] 29 and departing aircraft from [Runway] 22R at intersection [Taxiway] W or Y. The aircraft weather vane into the jet blast, the aircraft was pushed right of center line, we experienced moderate turbulence, and the aircraft rolled slightly to the right. I was able to control the aircraft as if landing in a crosswind and land safely. The aircraft never got into an unsafe situation. Needless to say, this caught us completely off guard. Maybe EWR needs to reevaluate this practice when heavy aircraft are departing. in the landing flare is not a great time to get hit with jet blast. Crews should also be aware of this hazard.
ASRS:1825484.s: Pilots landing on Runway 29 at EWR encountered jet blast from a departing heavy aircraft on intersecting Runway 22R during the flare at 10-20 feet. The aircraft weather vaned right of centerline with moderate turbulence, but the crew maintained control and landed safely.

ASRS:1825488.n: Descending through 4,300 feet on arrival vectors for visual approach, rwy 28R PDX, heading 030 magnetic, 210KIAS, approximately 2-4 nm SSE of town of Damascus, OR. Captain PF, First Officer PM, Clear and vis greater than 10sm. Drone came into view, spotted only by First Officer for less than 1 second, left side, 11 o'clock to 9 o'clock passed between 50 ft and 100 ft off left wing. Unable to perceive drone movement due to fast, brief pass. Drone was same altitude as aircraft when spotted. Drone was roughly size of larger DJI drone, but type/style of drone could not be determined. Appeared symmetrical laterally and longitudinally. It was bright white and highly reflective on top. No avoidance maneuvers made due to how quickly we passed it (otherwise maneuvers likely would've been made). Immediately reported to Portland approach. Flight continued without further incident. Seeing as we could not have done anything different ourselves, only suggestion is to implement TCAS on all drones, provide drone-finding radar, and/or equip aircraft with anti-drone lasers.
ASRS:1825488.s: During a visual approach to PDX runway 28R at 4,300 feet, a First Officer spotted a drone passing 50 to 100 feet off the left wing at the same altitude. No avoidance maneuvers were made due to the brief encounter, and the flight continued without incident after reporting to Portland Approach.

ASRS:1825540.n: Training flight with student pilot training for initial solo. Student used improper control input during takeoff, and caused the aircraft to veer off the runway. Instructor onboard was not able to keep the airplane from rolling into the grass, even with immediate control input in attempt to maintain proper takeoff attitude. Instructor was able to taxi the airplane back onto the runway safely, once control was regained. There were no injuries, and no damage to the aircraft or airport property.
ASRS:1825540.s: During a student pilot's initial solo training takeoff, improper control inputs caused the aircraft to veer off the runway into grass despite the instructor's immediate corrective actions. The instructor safely taxied the aircraft back onto the runway with no injuries or damage reported.

ASRS:1825554.n: Inbound on the ILS [Runway] 03 practice approach into OGD. Tower had departing traffic off of [runway]17. Departing traffic told to fly runway heading and get us (ILS traffic) in sight. Departure aircraft reported us in sight. Tower then requested the traffic pass behind us to continue on their course to the northwest. Departing traffic then turned in front of us on the ILS with myself as the instructor having to take control from my student who was under the foggles and break off the approach to the south in order to avoid a closer occurrence.
ASRS:1825554.s: An instructor and student practicing an ILS approach to Runway 03 at OGD broke off when a departing aircraft turned in front of them instead of passing behind as cleared. The instructor took control to avoid a closer occurrence after the departing pilot failed to maintain the requested separation.

ASRS:1825558.n: I was taxiing for takeoff and announced back taxi to runup pad on Runway 26. I did not hear any other aircraft on the radio, but noticed I was getting a traffic alert of 0.3 nm on my ADS-B in cockpit display. I stopped and held short of the runway and noticed [another aircraft] departing on Runway 08. At this airport, the hold short line is really close to the runway.
