Aircraft Y is at this point 100-200 ft. above Aircraft X, and enters Aircraft X's field of view high and crossing to the left.ATC spots the deviation right as I did, and issues instructions to Aircraft Y to proceed and enter a left downwind.Aircraft Y then turns right- and begins entering final when ATC again contacts Aircraft Y to issue corrective action.During this time I have expedited my descent by going engine idle and adopting a slightly nose down attitude. Due to low AGL, nearby towers and already having 20 degrees of flaps in, I am hesitant to enter a forward slip and descend faster (aircraft type placards state to avoid forward slips with flaps). It's possible that I'm also reaching the end of my endurance- coming back from an hour of pattern practice at ZZZ1 where conditions were gusty. My flight time at this point was around 1.6 hours, and my flights up to that point at typically max of 1.8.I have debated if I should have immediately turned right or even left. While I had the right of way (a lower craft engaged in landing), the right of way isn't going to help me if I end up in a midair. In the end I think it was correct not to turn- the pattern was extremely busy, there were higher towers to the right and planes on extended down wind to both sides. I could have caused another NMAC by turning suddenly. ATC was aware of the situation, issuing instructions to Aircraft Y and I was going to pass safely- although close- below.While I pass under (300-400 ft. estimated?) Aircraft Y either completes a right 360 or an S-turn, and ends up in an extended left downwind.Because I am below the ideal approach path to Runway XX, I put power in and arrest my descent. I actually end up too high for the runway and decide to do a go around. The go around is uneventful and I land safely. I believe Aircraft Y actually landed in between my go around and actual landing. Moderately heavy traffic relative to ZZZ, training in progress, everything under control of the Trainee until I noticed an aircraft turning base without any sequence or landing clearance yet. This aircraft was initially part of a flight of two who had just separated in the downwind, because we have to issue separate landing clearances at ZZZ, the AID (Aircraft IDentification) is Aircraft Y. Multiple inbound aircraft on either downwind and on straight in.I key up and say 'Aircraft Y and flight, both of you guys, Don't come in on base, there is traffic at the [VFR reporting point], so don't come in on base right now, you are going to follow the guy on a 3 mile final' The [VFR reporting point] is 3 mile final, Aircraft Y is starting a 1 mile right base so this is plenty of time to catch and correct this pilot. The second aircraft from the original flight of two responds traffic in sight and immediately corrects back to the downwind. I respond to 2 other calls then scan back to ensure Aircraft Y was correcting, he wasn't, I say 'Aircraft Y it looks like you are doing exactly what I said not to do, unless the radar is deceiving me here.' Pilot responds 'Aircraft Y was already on base', I respond 'OK, well I just said don't go on base, you missed that part, so let's go right turn back to the north downwind for both you and the other guy (his flight wing man, who was following instructions)' Pilot responds 'Affirm, right turn, north downwind, Aircraft Y'. I tell the original wing man to now turn base, he correctly responds, I then scan back and see Aircraft Y not following instructions, again the pilot does the opposite and starts a left turn towards final before correcting right and continuing for the north downwind. I then say 'Aircraft Y are you literally on final right now cutting someone off?' Pilot responds 'No, I'm trying to get out of here, we're turning, Aircraft Y'I advise the traffic on final 'Aircraft X, the guy in front of you is moving out of your way, Runway XX cleared to land' His response seemed to be partially blocked but I heard 'Aircraft X'.All aircraft eventually land, brasher warning was not issued. The pilot of Aircraft X called the tower a couple hours later and said he wanted to file a NMAC. He said he was aware of the situation developing and heard the controller (me) several times tell the other aircraft not to turn base and issue instructions which the pilot of Aircraft Y repeatedly disobeyed. I should have issued a traffic alert to both aircraft, but at the minimum to Aircraft X.
ASRS:1826213.s: A pilot in Aircraft X reported a near mid-air collision with Aircraft Y during a busy pattern at ZZZ, where Y repeatedly ignored ATC instructions to extend downwind and turned base instead. The controller failed to issue a traffic alert despite Y's non-compliance, forcing X to descend rapidly and execute a go-around to avoid the conflict.

ASRS:1826222.n: Departed [and] filed an IFR flight plan for 6,000 ft. Level at 3,500 ft just about the time to pick up IFR plan the aircraft's oil pressure gauge went off, alerting a loss of oil pressure. The aircraft is equipped with a Garmin G1000. 15 seconds later I turned the aircraft 180 degrees and headed back to ZZZ. Approximately 2.5 NM from ZZZ the aircraft engine seized (quit), no windmilling. Dead sticked the aircraft from an altitude of 3,500 ft. to a successful landing on Runway XX with a ground roll of 400 to 500 ft. to a full stop. All occupants safe, no injuries. Aircraft engine settings prior to low oil pressure indication was at cruise performance. I experienced no vibration, or rough engine performance prior to the engine quitting. After landing I noticed engine oil under belly, landing gear and wheel pants and large puddle of oil on the runway under the engine.[FBO Maintenance] will be dispatched to determine what failed in the engine. The aircraft is a 2009 CT206/G purchased new - approximately 460 TT on engine and airframe.I have no idea what caused the engine failure. The aircraft is very well maintained and the engine is never flown to max settings with the exception on takeoff.
ASRS:1826222.s: The pilot of a 2009 CT206/G experienced a loss of oil pressure at 3,500 ft, followed by an engine seizure and dead-stick landing on Runway XX. No injuries occurred, but the cause of the failure remains unknown pending maintenance inspection.

ASRS:1826224.n: Approx 5 to 10 miles west of ZZZ, I nearly had a mid-air with another aircraft while under ATC control. I was on an IFR flight plan but needed to return to ZZZ1 due to aircraft issue, and the controller cleared me to descend from 8000 feet to 5500 feet while asking me to turn Left, Heading 270. I continued to descend as the controller directed me next to turn Right, Heading 360. I did and was given a traffic point out to an aircraft flying slightly northwest, closing in on me. I acknowledged I saw the traffic on ADS-B. The controller asked if I could climb to 7,000 feet. After one attempt, I told him unable and watched as the other aircraft's ADS-B track closed in closely on me with the range in our altitudes decreasing. Finally when it appeared the tracks would soon be on top of each other, I turned to the right, then requested a turn to the right. The controller approved, then told the other aircraft to immediately turn left. Before pulling away, it appeared the other aircraft had 300 feet of vertical separation from me. During the position relief briefing Aircraft X reported aircraft issues and requested to return back to ZZZ. The relieved controller turned Aircraft X left heading 230 and descended them to 5,000 feet. The relieved controller finished the briefing and I took over the position. Aircraft Y was roughly 10 miles south-southwest of Aircraft X and direct ZZZ1 at 7,000 ft. I descended Aircraft Y to 5,000 feet and switched him to ZZZ. The 2 targets converged and came within less than 2 miles of each other around 7,000 ft. I missed the other controller assigning 5,000 to Aircraft Y. Maybe I should have waited to take the position until the relieved controller finished helping Aircraft X work through their aircraft equipment situation.
ASRS:1826224.s: A pilot and air traffic controller were involved in a near mid-air collision while the pilot descended from 8,000 to 5,500 feet near ZZZ1 due to an aircraft issue. The controller later admitted missing a handover detail that caused two aircraft to converge within two miles at 7,000 feet, requiring immediate corrective turns to maintain separation.

ASRS:1826245.n: Signed on with ZZZ Approach and they cleared me to descend to 8000 ft. and asked to turn to 170 heading. Shortly after I turned I realized they had vectored me right into a cell and we were simultaneously leveling at 8,000 ft. I was on the autopilot and the turbulence was severe enough that it disengaged and we caught a huge downdraft. The airplane was still trimmed nose down in a descent when the autopilot turned off. The aircraft descended several hundred feet below the assigned 8,000 ft. MSL and lost 50 kts. in airspeed in a matter of a few seconds. So as not to impose heavy load factors on the aircraft and passengers I recovered slowly and climbed back to the assigned 8,000 ft.
ASRS:1826245.s: The pilot, while descending to 8,000 ft on autopilot, was vectored by ZZZ Approach into a thunderstorm cell. Severe turbulence disengaged the autopilot, causing a downdraft that dropped the aircraft below 8,000 ft and reduced airspeed by 50 kts before a slow recovery.

ASRS:1826254.n: Near mid-air collision at the approach end ZZZ. It was almost a perfect storm that could have put us in a nearly unavoidable accident had the timing been a few seconds different. I was number one on final (RNAV Approach, VFR conditions, approximately 1/4 mile from threshold, visual landing) ahead of Aircraft Y on a survey mission landing for gas. The other aircraft was a Airtractor crop duster operating from a semi-trailer full of chemicals parked on the ramp. The pilot reported that his radio was marginal, but they had no replacement. His ground crew reported that he was using a hand-held radio. He made no calls before getting to the runway, and may not have even had the radio on until taking the runway. He certainly wasn't listening to it. He says he made a call taking the runway, but the FBO said it was more like a call after he was on the runway and rolling, and I didn't hear it or recognize it as there were also two aircraft operating same runway alignment, same frequency. I believe he took off from the midfield intersection just short of the midpoint of the 6307 ft. runway opposite direction to the one with two aircraft on final who had been making multiple position reports on CTAF. Winds were being called as calm until I was on three-mile final when they went to about 9 kts. crosswind. He obviously didn't visually clear the final approach course as he took the runway because I had all lights on (three strobes and three landing/taxi lights) and would have been quite visible had he looked.He was likely concentrating on centerline (tailwheel aircraft with a crosswind), and I was concentrating on the aim point on short final (end of the runway) so I could turn off at midfield with Aircraft Y behind me. When I was about ¼ mile on final, he came into my field of view just above the pavement less than 1000 ft. from the end of the runway. I went around and broke right, but he didn't deviate before he passed out of my view under my wing as I banked away. We passed abeam one another just south of the approach end of Runway XX. I doubt he saw me before I was wing-up passing him on his left.
ASRS:1826254.s: The pilot on final approach for a visual landing at ZZZ experienced a near mid-air collision with an Airtractor crop duster that entered the runway without proper radio communication or visual clearance. The pilot executed a go-around and turned right to avoid the tailwheel aircraft, which passed under their wing while operating in the opposite direction.

ASRS:1826255.n: Had partial power engine failure on initial climb out landed safely on runway opposite direction. Valve spring was determined to be the problem. No aircraft damage besides engine.
ASRS:1826255.s: The pilot experienced a partial engine power failure during initial climb caused by a valve spring issue. The aircraft landed safely on the opposite runway with no damage other than to the engine.

ASRS:1826318.n: Aircraft was dispatched with an improperly secured left engine thrust reverser. The thrust reverser was secured with a heavy duty zip tie by Maintenance when, to comply with the MEL, it should have been secured with a thick gauge wire. The aircraft was flown in that condition. Proper compliance with all MEL procedures by company and contract maintenance personnel. Proper review of MEL by flight crew to ensure compliance with all maintenance and operational procedures as applicable. Improved clarity in the description of maintenance and operational procedures throughout the MEL, in addition to better separation of said procedures. I was assigned to ferry this aircraft with the left thrust reverser inoperative MEL. I did not communicate at all with the mechanic that accomplished the MEL procedure. The thrust reverser lever was secured in the stowed position. I had no knowledge of the technical method that was required to be accomplished by a qualified mechanic. Today I was informed that the maintenance procedure for securing the lever was accomplished improperly. The flight was completed without incident.
ASRS:1826318.s: A ferry flight was conducted with a left thrust reverser improperly secured by maintenance using a zip tie instead of the required wire per MEL. The flight completed without incident, though the reporter noted a lack of communication with the mechanic and insufficient MEL clarity.

ASRS:1826321.n: During initial climbout from Runway XXR, the Trailing Edge (TE) flaps failed to retract from the takeoff position, flaps 1. I noticed this, as I prepared to place the Landing Gear lever to OFF and autobrakes to OFF. I directed to the FO (First Officer), who was PF (Pilot Flying), to slow to 210 KIAS while I coordinated with ATC to level off at 6,000 ft. MSL and Hold PPOS, approximately 15 miles southeast of the airport. I pulled out the QRH as we assessed our indications. The TE Flap gauge showed a slight split in the needles, with the R needle slightly retracted from flaps 1 and the L needle at flaps 1. I considered both Flap Asymmetry and Flap Disagree Checklists, and we decided the Asymmetry Checklist was more correct, despite the flap lever being UP. The PF did indicate very slight anomalous roll indications, prior to engaging the AP (Autopilot). I then informed the Passengers of our issue, briefed the FAs (Flight Attendants) that we would hold and work the problem and that we would be diverting to either ZZZ1 or ZZZ. Dispatch was very helpful in getting the Company Operations Center involved and suggesting ZZZ, editing the Release and giving us fuel and weight and balance data for worst case scenario. We began the QRH, holding at the deferred items for descent and landing. I then coordinated for the RNAV Z XXR Approach, briefed the Passengers of our decision to return to ZZZ, and briefed the FAs on the ETA and after landing plans. We briefed and commenced the approach, completed the QRH, ran brake cooling and reviewed the plan one last time. The PF flew a very nice approach at Vref 40 + 30 to a smooth flaps 1 landing with AB3 required and selected. On rollout I suggested he quickly disarm the AB and let the aircraft roll out at max reverse thrust to allow for more brake cooling. The data indicated 18 minutes of cooling at the gate so we taxied to the gate, shut the aircraft down and coordinated with Operations and [Maintenance Control]. Training and Company operational priorities had us well-prepared and allowed us to handle the issue safely and with ease.
ASRS:1826321.s: The crew experienced a Trailing Edge flap retraction failure during initial climbout, causing a slight needle split and minor roll indications. They executed the Asymmetry Checklist, diverted to ZZZ, and completed a safe flaps 1 landing with autobrakes and reverse thrust.

ASRS:1826339.n: The Captain was hand flying the aircraft on the ZZZZZ RNAV Departure off of Runway XXR from ZZZ, climbing to FL 190. ATC issued our flight an intermediate level off altitude of 10,000 ft. Approaching 10,000 ft. and about to level off, our flight received a TCAS RA to 'Maintain Vertical Speed;' due to an aircraft that appeared to be descending towards our aircraft and crossing our flight path. The Captain complied with and performed the TCAS RA maneuver. Then, the ATC Controller and what sounded like an ATC Supervisor intervening, issued instructions to the other aircraft to turn and climb immediately. At this point, our flight's TCAS RA changed from a 'Maintain Vertical Speed' to a 'Descend Now.' The Captain complied with the changing 'Descend Now' TCAS RA maneuver. Once the radio communications cleared, the First Officer was able to inform ATC of our TCAS RA. As a result of our TCAS RA maneuvering and the ATC issued turn and climb instructions to the other aircraft, the other aircraft appeared to pass our aircraft forward, above and to the right at less than 500 ft. Our flight then continued to ZZZ1 without further incidence. Departing ZZZ on the ZZZZZ ZZZZZ1 transition, we were initially cleared to FL190. Passing 8,800 ft., we were told to stop our climb at 10000 ft. The Captain was hand flying. At 9,800 ft., we received a 'maintain vertical speed' in a climb RA. ATC gave the conflicting aircraft, a light twin, an immediate climb and turn to the east. The traffic was pointed out to us and I responded, 'Roger. Aircraft X TCAS climb.' I then spotted the aircraft (conditions were VMC) but was unable to tell ATC due to radio congestion. As the conflicting aircraft began to climb away from us, we received a course reversal to 'DESCEND. DESCEND NOW' RA. The Captain followed the guidance. ATC gave us a frequency change and I read back the clearance and added 'TCAS descent' and changed frequencies. I estimate we passed within 500 ft. as the aircraft passed above us and to the right, turning away from us. The flight continued without incident to ZZZ1.
ASRS:1826339.s: The Captain hand-flew a departure from Runway XXR to FL190 when a TCAS RA occurred due to a light twin descending toward the flight path. After complying with conflicting 'Maintain Vertical Speed' and 'Descend Now' RAs while ATC vectored the other aircraft, the flights passed within 500 feet with no further incident.

ASRS:1826343.n: Shortly after setting the takeoff power with the auto throttles the airplane veered hard to the left due to the auto throttles commanding the left engine to reduce thrust to well below commanded EPR setting. Takeoff rejected at approximately 50-60 knots and all checklists and procedures accomplished per SOP. Returned to Gate in ZZZ, notified hub maintenance, Dispatch, Maintenance Control and left a voice mail with the Chief Pilot outlining the events which caused the rejected takeoff and subsequent gate return.
ASRS:1826343.s: The pilot rejected takeoff at 50–60 knots after auto throttles commanded the left engine to reduce thrust, causing a hard left veer. The aircraft returned to the gate in ZZZ, and maintenance, dispatch, and the Chief Pilot were notified.

ASRS:1826385.n: During takeoff upon rotation, LG AIR/GND FAIL" CAS message. We notified ATC and completed the applicable QRH procedure and all checklists. We also conducted an over weight landing in accordance with applicable QRH procedure. We landed at 4X;XXX lbs with 100 fpm rate of descent. After landing crash fire rescue inspected the aircraft. They found no damage. We continued to the gate and deplaned our passengers.Cause - "LG AIR/GND FAIL" CAS message and the inability to retract gear." During takeoff upon rotation, LG AIR/GND FAIL" CAS message. We notified ATC and completed the applicable QRH procedure and all checklists. We also conducted an over weight landing in accordance with applicable QRH procedure. We landed at 4X;XXX lbs with 100 FPM rate of decent. After landing crash fire rescue inspected the aircraft. They found no damage. We continued to the gate and deplaned our passengers. All in all, [everything] went well. Could improve my briefing to the flight attendant. First Officer and I worked well together. ATC support was excellent."
ASRS:1826385.s: The flight crew received a "LG AIR/GND FAIL" CAS message upon rotation, preventing gear retraction. They executed QRH procedures for an overweight landing at 4X,XXX lbs with no damage found.

ASRS:1826410.n: While I was cruising about 60 Miles off ZZZ and 120 Miles to ZZZ1, I saw the Door Warning light just came on, I knew it was from the crew hatch so I tried to re-lock it tight but the crew hatch just came off and opened but still attached with the aircraft. So, I called [Operations Control] and returned to ZZZ. I safely landed back to ZZZ on Runway XXR. Nobody got hurt or injury and everyone seem pretty good.Knowing crew hatch was not fully locked and trying to relock. While I try to tighten the Open and Lock red switch and the D ring the crew hatch was opened in Cruise. I noticed that the D ring is kind of loose and easy to unlock on Aircraft X. Better judgment and decision of fix the problem later fly the airplane as always. Knowing what it is will making you wanna fix the problem. Also having hard day of flying long flight back to back will make your decision poor and not thinking a lot.
ASRS:1826410.s: The pilot reported that while cruising, the crew hatch warning light illuminated, and attempting to re-lock the loose D-ring caused the hatch to open while remaining attached. The pilot diverted and landed safely at ZZZ with no injuries, attributing the incident to fatigue and poor judgment in trying to fix the issue mid-flight.

ASRS:1826413.n: When we arrived at the airplane the flight deck was around 34 degrees, but it soon cooled to around 28. Everything else was normal until the Captain stepped out to use the restroom. As soon as he sat down the ground crew pulled the ground power, but we had not yet switched over to the APU, so everything shut down. The Captain switched to the APU, but the right FMC did not start back up, and we got a R FMC FAIL status message. After about five minutes it did come back on without incident. We pushed back and started normally, but after about two seconds after I selected the status page on the lower EICAS we got a PACK 1 status message. The Captain reviewed the procedures, but because we had already blocked out and did not get any EICAS messages we continued. After starting up with the packs all off the flight deck warmed up quickly, but we knew as soon as we took off it should start cooling. At around 1,000 ft. the Tower gave us the Departure frequency and I checked in successfully. By the time we reached 5,000 ft. we were concerned by how little airflow there was, and the observer pilot asked for the ECS page to verify that the airplane was pressurizing. It seemed to be normal, and we monitored the air, but still figured as we climbed the flow would increase. Around FL180 Departure called us on guard and said, 'Aircraft X, if you can hear this transmission contact...' The Captain and I agreed that she hadn't called prior to that and I dialed in the frequency. I couldn't reach them, so I asked for another frequency. I didn't realize how much the heat was affecting me, but on the third frequency I asked the Captain to attempt to call. When he transmitted, I could hear that his call wasn't going out, and I finally recognized that we had lost the left comms. I didn't want to change the right radio from guard, because that seemed to be the only way they could reach us, so I used the center radio and was able to reach ZZZZ Control. Shortly after that we got an EQUIP COOLING EICAS message, and the third seat pilot began to run the checklist, and I asked for a level off altitude of FL300. ATC came back with FL290, but we were at FL288 and empty, so I said we would do our best. We ended up climbing to FL295 before we could get level, and promptly descended back to FL290. At this point we began to discuss returning when we noticed that the secondary attitude indicator was leaning to the right, but our wings were level, so we all agreed we should return. We told ATC we needed to return and explained that we were having equipment cooling issues. They assigned us the arrival and Runway XXR, but the workload was continuing to accelerate, and we were all sweating profusely, and told them we would like to get vectors to the ILS for XXR. I gave them the fuel remaining, souls on board, and tried to explain that we were safe, but needed to return soon. We completed all checklists, and uneventfully landed, taxied, and parked the airplane. I didn't realize until we were on the ground how much the heat in the flight deck was affecting me. Even with the lack of traffic in the vicinity, I am surprised how long it took me to recognize the radio failure. In the future I will be more cognizant of the heat and it's affects not only in seeming to increase workload, but also decreasing focus and clarity. I had gone to the lavatory on the ground prior to departure. Before I returned to my seat, the external power was pulled without my permission, and the power to the aircraft was interrupted, as I sat back down, I selected the APU power source and after waiting a bit, the R FMC would not come back. We called Maintenance up and the FMC returned to normal. We ensured all of the data that we had input was correct and then continued onward to push. The aircraft was extremely hot, and we know that they had just established air as we were arriving at the aircraft. The interior cabin was at 36 Celsius and we agreed that the aircraft should cool after takeoff. After starting we noticed a Pack 1 status message, but there was never an associated EICAS message. We followed our checklists and proceeded with taxi. After takeoff, the airflow never increased and the FO (First Officer) selected the EICAS page as we all were wondering if we were even pressurizing. The gaspers were blowing at about 5%, but cool air was coming out. It was still extremely hot in the aircraft, and the 3rd observer seat first officer said that he had hardly to no air coming out of his gasper. At around FL250, we began receiving radio calls on 121.5 and it was at this time with trying to transmit out, and different frequencies that we realized the radios were not working, except for the center. The Pilot Monitoring was able to get the right radio to work intermittent, and immediately we got the Equip cooling EICAS caution message. I continued to fly the aircraft while the crew ran the QRH and attempted to maintain contact with ZZZZ. At this point, we all agreed the best course of action was to return to ZZZZ. We were given a level off to FL290 after an initial climb clearance. We were given this rapidly, as were already in a climb, but I arrested the climb and descended back from FL295 to FL290. We were given vectors and further descent. At this point with descent power, there was almost no airflow. We [received priority] to get on the ground as safely and quickly as possible. My standby instruments were also showing erroneous. We landed in ZZZZ without further incident. After touchdown, the airflow suddenly increased to normal. Maintenance was briefed with the logbook, but I was not given the nature of the aircraft's issues before we headed back in to rest.
ASRS:1826413.s: The crew experienced flight deck overheating, FMC failure, and left comms loss after ground power was disconnected prematurely before APU start. They returned to ZZZZ due to equipment cooling issues and erroneous standby instruments, landing safely once airflow normalized.

ASRS:1826424.n: This was a fumes event. On takeoff, we noticed an oily odor. I thought this was something transient and continued takeoff. At about 4,000 feet the smell was not going away. I said we need to return to ZZZ. We [requested ATC priority handling for an air return] and put our O2 masks on. I called the Flight Attendants (FA's) and asked if they smelled anything. They said yes. We made an approach and overweight landing to Runway XXL. Prior to landing, I called on another radio for a gate. By this time at least one FA was on portable O2. I asked the Tower to send paramedics to Gate. I began the fumes checklist on the QRC. Once those initial actions were complete I stopped because we were getting close to a landing. Two AML entries were made. One for the fumes event and another for an overweight landing. According to the AML, the aircraft hit a bird the day before and an engine was bore scoped. When we arrived at the gate, Maintenance was powering hydraulic systems and testing reversers. When we got to the gate, I told the passengers to exit out the forward door quickly. After a couple of minutes of securing the flight deck, I opened the door and no one had gotten off. There was a fireman testing the air just inside the aircraft door. SOF Event during departure with an immediate return to the departure airport (ZZZ). First Officer (FO) was the pilot flying. Ground Ops and taxi out to runway XXL were uneventful. As soon as the engines reached FLEX power, a slight burning metal smell began. This smell, experienced from time to time when the engines run up, normally dissipates in a matter of seconds. This time it remained throughout the entire takeoff roll. All other aircraft indications were normal during rotation and clean up. The smell persisted and a dirty sock smell was now prevalent, intensifying somewhat as we made a turn to a 230 heading with a climb up to 12,000 feet. At 4,000 feet we elected to stop the climb, don oxygen masks, and [advised ATC the need of an air return]. As a side note, it was hard to hear ATC and ICS with the loud noise of breathing with the masks on. At this point I remained the Pilot Flying and the Captain informed ATC of our intention to return for an immediate landing on runway XXL. The Captain was also made aware by the #2 Flight Attendant that the #1 Flight Attendant was on oxygen and still feeling very sick. I loaded the FMS for arrival and began a descent/vectors for the ILS runway XXL approach. At this time the Captain completed the Smoke/Avionics Smoke/Fumes QRH Quick Action procedure and informed the passengers and flight attendants of our intention to land. We were over maximum landing weight by roughly 4,000 lbs., but elected to proceed with the descent checklist and land instead of working through the QRH procedure for Overweight Landing due to time. The approach, landing, and taxi in were uneventful.This aircraft, Aircraft X, had a birdstrike in the #1 Engine on the preceding flight. The maintenance actions were signed off. It is possible that the fume event could be related to this event. Fume events are a recurring issue across most fleets and airlines. I know there is a lot of attention from multiple organizations on this issue and that should certainly continue.
ASRS:1826424.s: The flight crew and cabin crew experienced a fumes event with oily and dirty sock odors during departure from ZZZ, likely linked to a previous bird strike on Engine 1. They returned for an overweight landing on Runway XXL, donned oxygen masks, and requested paramedics while the First Officer flew and the Captain managed the emergency.

ASRS:1826455.n: During the RNAV X 16L approach into RNO, we passed the KNACK approach fix at 6,900 ft., as depicted, then set 6,200 ft. for WARAX and descended. The weather was IFR and our aircraft was not equipped with vertical guidance for this approach, so we descended quickly to see if we could get below the smoke layer. Reno Tower advised us to check altitude and said that we had a Low Altitude Warning. We double checked the approach charts and our altitude settings and found no error. We continued with the approach with no further Altitude Warning and did not need to adjust our altitude. The approach terminated with a missed approach due to low visibility and a diversion. Possibly a higher descent rate than what would have been suggested by an aircraft equipped with vertical guidance.Possibly a slower rate of descent or a navigation system with vertical guidance and would be very helpful.Upon arriving at LNAV minimums on the RNAV 16L approach into Reno, we were unable to get the runway or runway environment in sight due to smoke and low visibility. We decided to go around at the missed approach point and divert to ZZZ because it did not seem that conditions would improve for a second attempt at a landing. Low visibility, inaccurate meter report.
ASRS:1826455.s: During an RNAV 16L approach into RNO in IFR conditions, the crew received a Low Altitude Warning while descending without vertical guidance. The approach was terminated with a missed approach and diversion due to low visibility and smoke obscuring the runway environment.

ASRS:1826460.n: We departed ZZZ turned northwest and was climbing out of approximately 14,000 ft. for 16,000 when we received an EICAS MESSAGE L FWD ENTRY DOOR. Also entry doors light was illuminated on the overhead panel. We seemed to be pressurizing normal but it seemed slightly louder than normal. At this time we where level at 16,000 ft. so I informed ATC that we would like to stay at 16,000 while we look at a pressurization issue. I read the QRH and it advised that if pressurizing normal that we could continue but if not we need to raise cabin altitude to 9500 ft. and land. At this point it seemed we where pressurizing but I didn't want to climb higher without being certain so I got out of my seat and went to the back of the plane to look at the door. I immediately could see the handle was about 1/4 open, lock was released, some daylight under the door and could hear whistling noise of air escaping. I returned to me seat and informed ATC that we wanted to descend to 10,000 ft. I then called and received a phone patch to flight control. I told them we have an entry door unlatched and need to land. I asked if they wanted me to return to ZZZ, ZZZ1 or ZZZ2 since they where all about the same distance. We then informed ATC that we wanted to return to ZZZ. We finished the remainder of the checklists and returned without incident.
ASRS:1826460.s: The flight crew departed ZZZ and climbed to 16,000 ft when an EICAS message and overhead light indicated a forward entry door issue. Upon discovering the door handle was unlatched with air escaping, the crew descended to 10,000 ft and returned to ZZZ without incident.

ASRS:1826531.n: On Aircraft X [a Boeing 737-900ER] I installed two serviceable Flight Control Computers (FCCs) and performed the Line Replacement Unit (LRU) replacement test in [the] Digital Flight Control System (DFCS) bite in accordance with the manual. While finding the correct software for the FCCs the mechanics ran a test on the elevator tab control. The test failed step 5 resulting in the trim tabs split when pushing the control forward or aft instead of them going the same direction like the test calls out for. All breakers were in and no flight deck effect showed. I found out that the preloaded software was 737 MAX. As soon as I installed the correct software the tabs worked correctly in accordance with the test. My concern is that if someone misses loading the software like the manual tells them to do that there might be a safety of flight issue that could result in loss of life. I know its not supposed to happen because the manual tells you to check it but in a high pressure situation or with low experience it could and I don't want to see something like that happen.
ASRS:1826531.s: A mechanic installing Flight Control Computers on a Boeing 737-900ER encountered a failed elevator tab test caused by preloaded 737 MAX software. After loading the correct software, the tabs functioned properly, though the mechanic warned that missing this step could create a safety of flight issue.

ASRS:1826542.n: While flying over ZZZ1, I became task saturated due to a malfunction with the avionics. After being called by ZZZ Center, the comms switched back to the previous control frequency as well as the PFD glitching. While I tried to sort out what happened I missed the call from ZZZ Center I veered off course and by the time I got back in radio contact with ZZZ Center, I was in the restricted airspace and had not responded to multiple attempts from ZZZ Center to contact me due to the frequencies flipping and ultimately flew into restricted airspace. After troubleshooting the comms and PFD, I was vectored out of restricted airspace and resumed en route to my destination. About 15 minutes later the PFD turned into a mix of white and pink lines before ultimately shutting off. At this time I made the decision to turn back to ZZZ where I was sure the conditions were good VFR so I could make a safe approach with the failed instrument.
ASRS:1826542.s: The pilot experienced avionics and PFD malfunctions over ZZZ1, causing task saturation, loss of radio contact, and entry into restricted airspace. After being vectored clear, the PFD failed completely, prompting a return to ZZZ for a VFR approach.

ASRS:1826549.n: The runway incursion occurred when a new CFI and myself were doing a night flight for the said CFI to become night proficient again in small GA aircraft after not flying GA in a long time. ZZZ Tower had closed 30 minutes prior and we were the only aircraft working in the pattern. I said that we should practice a power off 180 when the incursion occurred. The situation that occurred was that Airport Operations was doing sweeps of the runway and either they did not announce they were on the runway or we did not hear them due to being focused on the power off 180 maneuver. As we turn from base to final and get closer to the runway, we did not see anything on the runway that would have warranted a go-around. As we start to line the aircraft up with the runway a few hundred feet above the ground we see on the very edge of the runway two sets of stationary lights that were on the edge that we initially mistook for runway edge lights, but by the time we were about to pass, we saw it was a vehicle. Being low to the ground, still in a bank, low energy, and with nothing in front of us I determined going-around was not the optimal decision to make since the vehicle was now behind us. After seeing it was a vehicle of some sort I initially believed that the sweeper had moved off into the grass, however the driver came over after we landed and said he was still on the runway. We landed 300 ft. past the vehicle to the best of my knowledge so there was no immediate concern for a collision.I believe that the situation would not have occurred had several things happened. A breakdown of communication had occurred in the chain of events between the aircraft and the Ground Operations in terms of knowing the position of where everyone was. We made a downwind call but did not make subsequent calls due to the high workload of the power off 180 maneuver. I cannot confirm if the ground vehicle did or did not make a call, but to the best of my knowledge they did not make the call saying they were on the runway.
ASRS:1826549.s: A pilot and new CFI in a small GA aircraft experienced a runway incursion during a night power-off 180 maneuver when an unannounced Airport Operations sweeper was on the runway. The pilot attributed the event to a communication breakdown and high workload, landing safely 300 feet past the vehicle.

ASRS:1826560.n: Completed run up for departure on Runway XX at ZZZ. Normal performance during run up. Took runway. Stopped. Ran engines to 20 inches manifold. All gauges green. Released brakes. Accelerated to blue line. Rotated. Within a couple seconds and roughly 20 ft. above runway, airplane was shaking and stall warning was intermittent. Put nose down or tried. Very difficult to get nose down. Trim was set for take off and autopilot off but it felt as if that was not the case. Decided to abort take off. Put nose down and brought power back. Landed quite hard. Kept directional control and exited runway. Returned to FBO. Inspected plane. Found evidence of tail strike. Loose tail cone would interfere with elevator function. Elected to not fly the plane. Put it into FBO hangar.
ASRS:1826560.s: The pilot aborted a takeoff from Runway XX at ZZZ after the aircraft shook and gave intermittent stall warnings at 20 feet. A post-flight inspection revealed a loose tail cone interfering with elevator function, causing the pilot to ground the aircraft.

ASRS:1826565.n: Upon arrival at ZZZ, A normal landing was set up. Engine and flaps were in landing configuration. Landing gear was extended and confirmed down by green indicator light and by visual (pilot side main gear by viewing out pilot window, co-pilot side main and nose gear by wing located mirror). I landed on both main gear as normal. As the nose settled during deceleration, the nose fell to the runway. The plane slide to a stop on the center line of the runway. I turned off electronics, master switch and fuel. I exited the plane. I did not notice any fluids leaking from the engine compartment or any other location. I contacted the Manager of the airport and the Manager of the FBO. I also spoke briefly with the FAA. The FAA authorized removal of the aircraft from the runway. Upon lifting the nose of the plane by a front end loader, the nose gear limply extended. Upon kicking the nose gear a few times, the gear appeared to lock down. The plane was towed from the runway.
ASRS:1826565.s: The pilot landed a normally configured aircraft at ZZZ, but the nose gear collapsed upon touchdown, causing the nose to contact the runway. The gear later extended and locked after being manually kicked, allowing the aircraft to be towed away without reported fluid leaks.

ASRS:1826570.n: On the way back from the practice area with a student after practicing steep turns, slow flight and stalls, I called ZZZ Tower 12 miles out asking for full stop taxi back intending to do some landing practice with my student. We were advised to report our position when we are inbound over the landfill. As we are about to report the landfill inbound when my ADS-B traffic lit up and advised me of traffic same altitude opposite direct less then half a mile. Looking up I immediately saw the Piper twin on a collision course and immediately began a hard right turning decent. At the time I was aware of a TBM aircraft behind and faster then me on an GPS approach for an avionics check, as well as another aircraft 500 ft. below me passing right to left. Tower was extremely busy at the time and I was unable to report the near miss immediately due to frequency volume and traffic. Adding to the confusion there was another aircraft in the area with the abbreviated tail number being Aircraft Y, while my tail number being Aircraft X. Tower told me to turn base which did make sense to me considering I was 5 miles out. I reported to Tower that there were two [similar N-numbers] on frequencies. He then told Aircraft Y to turn base followed by an instruction to me to turn to a heading of 070. I read back 070 but confirmation bias, and still rattled by the near miss, I turned to a heading of 170 thinking that he wanted me to turn an extended base to final, essentially cutting off the faster TBM closing on me. Tower asked me to read off my current heading and I reported flying 175 only then realizing the mistake. I was advised to make a right turn to intercept the final of Runway XX and report turning through 270 degrees. Already heading south this happened in less than 30 seconds. Now inbound on final for landing I was advised to copy a phone number on the ground for a possible pilot deviation. Finally on a half mile final I asked Tower twice if I was cleared to land Runway XX, and they advised me that I was 'still cleared to land XX' when I had not previously been given a landing clearance. Once on the ground I contacted Tower via phone and we discussed the situation, agreeing that parties were at fault a that a lot of events contributed to the situation.I believe that there were 3 main human factors causes that led to this incident.First the Tower was overloaded with inbound, transit, and outbound traffic and was unable to properly give traffic advisories to inbound and departing traffic.Second that Tower instructed me turn base when an aircraft with a similar call sign was the intended recipient even though it didn't make sense to me and at the time. Lastly that because of confirmation bias I expected to receive a base to final clearance when in reality he wanted me to intercept a left downwind entry into the pattern.
ASRS:1826570.s: A flight instructor and student in a single-engine aircraft experienced a near mid-air collision with a Piper twin while inbound to ZZZ Tower, followed by a clearance misunderstanding due to similar call signs and controller overload. The pilot mistakenly turned 170 instead of 070, cutting off a TBM, but was eventually cleared to land after a post-incident discussion attributed the event to human factors and frequency congestion.

ASRS:1826581.n: Right after takeoff Runway XX at ZZZ about 1,300 feet MSL, 95 kts indicated airspeed, we had a significant thrust lost on the right engine, PFD (Primary Flight Display) indicates both right engine's ECU (Engine Control Unit) failed simultaneously and RPM drop down to about 1500 RPM, but we can tell the right engine is still producing some thrust (feels like 30-40%). We thought it might be a dual ECU failure. Copilot did the checklist on both ECU failures, didn't work, so we proceed back to ZZZ immediately, we were clear of the Runway after landing, and towed back to hangar afterward, from intersection Taxiway 1 between Taxiway 2 and Runway XX.
ASRS:1826581.s: Pilots reported a significant right engine thrust loss at 1,300 feet MSL shortly after takeoff from Runway XX at ZZZ due to simultaneous ECU failures. After unsuccessful checklist attempts, they returned to ZZZ, landed safely, and were towed to the hangar.

ASRS:1826584.n: Complete GPS Signal loss for 2 minutes without NOTAM or other notification. I have 5 devices with built-in GPS devices connected to 3 GPS antennas. Additionally, I had a portable GPS, with its own GPS antenna and power supply. All GPS devices reported a complete lost of signal. I covered about 3.5 miles while on the visual approach. Signal was restored, but the virtual glideslopes from the GPS's were not available. I reported the event to the tower. Since I was in visual condition, I was able to maintain control of the aircraft and was hand flying for the landing. Since I had been navigating with GPSS and the autopilot, this could have created a surprise in the loss of GPSS steering. Additionally, had this been in IMC, I would have lost the glideslope and needed to make changes. I do not know how the coupled autopilot would have responded. I do not know where else to report this sudden loss of GPS signal.
ASRS:1826584.s: The pilot experienced a complete GPS signal loss on five devices during a visual approach, covering 3.5 miles without prior notification. Although the pilot hand-flew the landing safely, the autopilot and virtual glideslope functions were unavailable, creating potential risks in instrument conditions.

ASRS:1826592.n: I made a residential structural sUAS using DJI GO4. Relied on DJI's GEO Fencing to alert me when I was in controlled airspace instead of checking with LAANC provider or FFA's UASFM. The mistake was caught during monthly flight review by manager.We have discussed the error in flight planning and shall verify all airspace before every flight using either FFA LAANC provider or UASFM.
ASRS:1826592.s: A pilot operating a residential sUAS with DJI GO4 relied on GEO Fencing instead of checking LAANC or UASFM for controlled airspace. The manager identified this flight planning error during a monthly review, prompting a commitment to verify airspace using official tools before every flight.

ASRS:1826598.n: Aircraft is a 2 place open cockpit Experimental tail wheel bi-plane that I had acquired a while back.Was trying to familiarize myself with aircraft by conducting 'high Speed' taxi down runway to simulate both take-off and landing.This was not the first time conducting a 'high speed' taxi, I had noticed on previous runs that the aircraft stability decreased when power was removed and while lowering the tail. Had completed one pass down runway and was in process of a 2nd pass. Had achieved sufficient speed to raise tail with elevator. Was removing power and attempting to lower tail when aircraft began weaving across runway left-right-left. Attempted to regain control and when headed towards grass on left side decided to go straight as opposed to trying to re-align down runway. Apparently struck runway light with right main gear, punctured tire, partially collapsed gear leg and ended up flipping aircraft onto upper wing. An important contributor was my inability to secure a CFI (Certified Flight Instructor) safety pilot due to recent FAA regulation interpretations regarding training in experimental aircraft.
ASRS:1826598.s: The pilot of an experimental tailwheel biplane flipped the aircraft onto its upper wing during a high-speed taxi training exercise. Loss of directional control while lowering the tail caused a runway excursion, striking a light and collapsing the gear, a situation the pilot attributed to an inability to secure a safety pilot due to FAA regulations.

ASRS:1826622.n: On base to final to Runway 10, we were turning base to final and descending to 1,500 feet to conduct a visual approach. As I looked outside to align the aircraft with Runway 10 and considering the tailwind I descended to 1,300 feet and Tower called Low Altitude Alert. I was two miles from JEANS waypoint, the final approach fix for the ILS 10. I immediately climbed and crossed JEANS at 1,500 feet. Completed the approach.
ASRS:1826622.s: The pilot descended to 1,300 feet while turning base to final for a visual approach to Runway 10 due to a tailwind. This triggered a Low Altitude Alert from Tower, prompting an immediate climb to cross the JEANS waypoint at 1,500 feet before completing the approach.

ASRS:1826634.n: After about 10 minutes at the gate, the oncoming FO (First Officer) stated the left inboard main tire fuse blew and the tire deflated. Our flight was uneventful with normal braking departing ZZZ, Auto brakes 2 used on Runway XX, smooth touchdown in the Touchdown Zone, and normal braking to exit at [taxiway] in ZZZ1. We were an average to low weight. The temperature was approximately 91 in ZZZ and 86 in ZZZ1.
ASRS:1826634.s: The First Officer reported a blown fuse and deflated left inboard main tire after 10 minutes at the gate. The flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 was uneventful with normal braking, a smooth touchdown, and an average to low aircraft weight.

ASRS:1826656.n: On a step climb around FL300, between ZZZ and ZZZZZ, we noticed a weather cell we wanted to deviate around. The Captain had already briefed the FAs (Flight Attendants) about the en route weather, that we would most likely have some bumps, that we were keeping the seat belt sign on, and to use caution. We were in full IMC and our radar return showed that a turn to the left would be best. We requested an initial left turn of 20 degrees but almost immediately we encountered heavy and extreme precipitation and ultimately had to turn 80 degrees. We were given the necessary deviations but then told to go direct ZZZZZ when able as well as climb to FL340. We also encountered moderate and possibly severe turbulence. We experienced both positive and negative G's. The speed tape never went into the red but the trend vector showed both rapid climbing and simultaneous descending trends that took up the entire top to bottom range of the speed tape. The plane was moving quite a bit as we were both in updrafts and then subsequent downdrafts getting bumped around. After about 5 minutes when we could actually get everything sorted out, we called back to check on the status of both the Flight Attendants and Passengers. FA1 answered and she proceeded to tell us there was an accident in the aisle and she would call us back. FA2 was about mid aircraft doing her beverage service when we encountered the worst of the turbulence. She thought she had hit her head and beverages had been thrown from the cart and some passengers tray tables into the ceiling. We consulted our FOM and made the decision we needed to contact Dispatch and make them aware to coordinate with [Maintenance Control]. We continued to keep checking on the FAs for the rest of the flight and as we got closer, FA1 called and said FA2 had requested In-Flight to meet us at the gate. Upon block in, [flight attendant representative] and member of [Company] met the aircraft. CA (Captain) called Dispatch/[Maintenance Control] to explain event and to assess if an aircraft inspection for severe turbulence was required. Based on our reading and interpretation of FOM on the definition of severe turbulence, we determined we encountered severe turbulence. However, [Maintenance Control] said because the autopilot did not disengage, that there was no 'momentary loss of aircraft control' and it was only moderate turbulence which does not require an aircraft inspection. The aircraft was not removed from service, boarding for the next flight started immediately, and [Company] took FA2 for a medical evaluation.Pilot interpretation of FOM differed from [Maintenance Control]. [Maintenance Control] did not accept our interpretation of severe turbulence. It kept them from having to inspect the aircraft and delaying the flight schedule. Any disconnection of autopilot is apparently the determining factor in deciding if aircraft control is lost. There needs to be a more clear definition of what severe versus moderate turbulence is and pilot experience should be held in account. Safety should always be the priority over schedule integrity. On final climb out from FL300 to FL340 between ZZZ and ZZZZZ intersection, we had to deviate for weather. Seat belt sign was on and FA (Flight Attendant) briefing and PA to passengers included weather/ thunderstorms in the area and to expect a bumpy ride on the climb out. We were in and out of IMC conditions as the weather radar depicted a buildup. We discussed a plan for deviations prior to the radio frequency change that we received at the same time. Originally asked for 20 degree left turn, ATC approved it and said no other traffic in the area do what we need to and cleared back direct ZZZZZ when able.Simultaneously, we encountered heavy to extreme precipitation which FA1 later said she could hear In the galley. FA1 started to clean up galley and observed FA2 in the middle of aircraft conducting beverage service. We continued the left turn to approximately a 270 degree heading due to the intensity of precipitation and increasing turbulence, while still trying to climb to FL340. In the turn and climb, we encountered moderate to potentially severe turbulence: VSI showed +/- 2000 fpm climb, ASI showed a white positive and negative trend vector for the entire range of speed tape, and we experienced zero G and positive G due to the turbulence.Once clear of the weather, we immediately called the FAs to get a status of the cabin. FA1 answered and she said there was an accident in the aisle. A few minutes later, she called back and reported that FA2 believes she hit her head on the ceiling and the surrounding passengers in the area agreed. Beverages had spilled on to passengers and were also dripping from the ceiling. Throughout the rest of the flight, we were in constant communication with the cabin on the status of FA2 and the passengers, as well as Dispatch/[Maintenance Control] via ACARS. FA1 requested that inflight meet us at the gate for FA2.Upon block in, a member from inflight and from [Company] met the aircraft. CA (Captain) called Dispatch/[Maintenance Control] to explain the event and to assess if an aircraft inspection for severe turbulence was required. Based on our reading and interpretation of FOM on the definition of severe turbulence, we determined we encountered severe turbulence. However, [Maintenance Control] said because the autopilot did not disengage, that there was no 'momentary loss of aircraft control' and it was only moderate turbulence which does not require an aircraft inspection. The aircraft was not removed from service, boarding for the next flight started immediately, and inflight took FA2 for a medical assessment.Pilot interpretation of company FOM definition and procedures differed from [Maintenance Control] definition and interpretation of company FOM defined severe turbulence [Maintenance Control] decided NOT to err on the side of safety and do a precautionary severe turbulence inspection of the aircraft due to their interpretation of the FOM severe turbulence definition, solely based on the fact that the autopilot did not disconnect during the event in order to save the integrity of the flight schedule. In the interest of safety, a severe turbulence inspection should have been conducted and a better definition of severe turbulence needs to be updated in company FOM defining what 'momentary loss of aircraft control' means. Safety should always be a priority over schedule integrity.
ASRS:1826656.s: During a step climb from FL300 to FL340, the crew deviated for weather and encountered severe turbulence that injured a flight attendant. Although the pilots requested an inspection based on their FOM interpretation, Maintenance Control denied it because the autopilot did not disengage, prioritizing schedule over a precautionary check.

ASRS:1826670.n: I was assigned Aircraft X ZZZ-ZZZ1 to reposition a plane that needed a mechanical issue fixed. Upon receiving the aircraft, I noticed the flight deck was unusually warm. The cockpit indication showed 32-33 degrees. The side window vents blew coolish-lukewarm air, and the gasper was blowing HOT air. The side vents air flow was weak and the gasper had strong air flow. I proceeded to write up the aircraft and have Maintenance look at it. After Maintenance did an inspection, they signed the aircraft ok for service with the cockpit indicator still reflecting 33 degrees and feeling unreasonably warm/hot. Surprised that it was signed 'OK for service;' I asked one of the technicians if he agreed with me the cockpit felt hot, he replied 'Yes, I would say it is warm.' I then asked if he agreed the gasper was blowing hot air, and although the side vents were slightly cool to lukewarm with weak airflow, it was not enough to cool the cockpit. He looked away without maintaining eye contact and replied '...well…we have to get this plane to ZZZ1. We don't have the parts here.' I then asked a second time why is the aircraft signed off as 'OK for service.' I received about the same reply. Eventually I was told 'it's your prerogative but it feels fine compared to outside. We are saying it's ok for service.' Shortly after, he left so I then called Maintenance Control and told them the temperature control knobs left in auto were not sufficient to cool the plane at any position, and that if you moved the knobs to manual, it was blowing out warm air immediately followed by hot air within 5 minutes. Maintenance Control replied that he didn't understand as the technician said it was 'OK for service, and only 25 degrees in the cockpit.' My statement to him was 'Absolutely not. It is right now indicating 32 degrees and nothing is fixed. Did you want me to send you a picture of the temperature?' I did not receive a reply as we talked about what the issue could be. I stated to Maintenance Control, 'I have seen this before multiple times and I think either a duct connection is loose, or there is a tear or leak somewhere, did you want me to send a picture of the cockpit temperature to show you what is indicating?' I still received no reply that he wanted evidence so I then asked him for the number I can send it to. When provided and after I sent a picture, he replied 'CABIN temperature looks pretty normal for a summer day' but mentioned absolutely nothing about the cockpit. He thought the plane was 'heat soaked' but I reminded him it had already been running for an hour and a half. I was then instructed and proceeded to run ground air inside the cabin and directly point it at the cockpit. It dropped 8 degrees from 33 to 25 in 20 minutes. I then had the ground air disconnected and within 20 minutes the cockpit heated back up to 31 degrees, and 5-10 minutes later it was again at 32. After writing it up a second time and being told from Maintenance Control it's still probably just 'heat soaked', the same technician from before came back and I told him what we did. He replied while mumbling something about 'maybe we got some parts lined up and we'll take a look.' The First Officer and I went back inside to cool off and let Maintenance work on it. After 5-6 hours of Maintenance continuously working on the plane, I called Maintenance Control to get an update. Apparently, the technicians did in fact discover a leak(s), and were proceeding to put a sleeve(s) on. An hour later it was still not done (about 6-7 hours of continuous work since the second write up). I then was removed from Aircraft X by scheduling.Cockpit indication and hot feeling in the cockpit.Hot airplane that would not cool down without external air and feeling pressured to take a hot airplane to ZZZ1 for service.Refused the aircraft twice.The main concern is current maintenance practice. I was able to get the technician to agree that it was warm inside the cockpit even though he signed offthe aircraft as 'OK for service' because they could not find anything wrong. I will give the benefit of the doubt that maybe the technician relayed bad information to Maintenance Control and read the temperature of the cabin instead of the cockpit, however, he still told them it felt fine when clearly the temperature control knobs were not functioning properly. There was a second technician that stated the same about it being OK for service. Since the first write up, Maintenance Control had me troubleshoot it for up to 4 hours with/without the technicians. After going through 2 large bottles of water, sweating profusely, and being asked to run the ground air into the back of the aircraft instead of the front this time as it was probably still 'just heat soaked;' I said no and needed a break. Also, I mentioned that based on experience it was probably a leak or tear. Sure enough, after having the technicians look at the aircraft a second time, this is what they found and worked on for several hours. The fact I refused the aircraft twice and they 'found an issue' the second time leads me to believe they knew all along. Especially considering the fact the technician admitted to me that the cockpit would not sufficiently cool but yet signed it off and told maintenance control it was fine. A chief pilot called me to get more information and while I did not feel pressure from him directly to take it, it was clear that the company for one reason or another needed to get this plane to ZZZ1. Again, I did not feel pressure from the chief pilot directly, but I could not help but think everyone in Maintenance knew this plane could not get stuck in ZZZ. I also believe that troubleshooting for Maintenance up to 4 hours is excessive when it was clear the aircraft was not heat soaked but instead was not self-sufficient to cool on its own. I am not a maintenance technician nor one with the most experience, however, I felt undermined from the technicians signing it off and Maintenance Control having me go through the motions of 4 hours of troubleshooting and not one person taking my advice that I had seen this exact issue multiple times. More believably I was ignored and every trick was pulled just to get the aircraft to ZZZ1, i.e., being told constantly by Maintenance Control we can get the aircraft cool enough with PC air so that we can depart but then reminding them the packs are not working properly and keep heating the plane up. Regardless, the technicians constantly tried to tie the issue to me implying that I was the problem and ultimately it was my call. If this was the case, I do not see why they would have had to work on the aircraft for several hours following my second write up.
ASRS:1826670.s: The pilot refused Aircraft X twice due to an inoperative cockpit cooling system caused by a duct leak, despite maintenance initially signing it "OK for service" to meet repositioning needs. After the pilot documented the issue and demonstrated the temperature rose without external air, maintenance eventually repaired the leak following several hours of work.

ASRS:1826694.n: The aircraft in question was operating with MEL 27-XXX open, Spoilers #2 or #4. After engine start on both legs, an ECAM message was received regarding the spoilers but this was disregarded as a result of the MEL. Upon further reflection, these messages should have triggered further investigation on my part, as the presence of such an alert was not mentioned in the MEL. However, I had noted a write-up in the MEL about spurious messages - made by a Check Airman - which was subsequently signed off by Maintenance as essentially being unimportant. The aircraft had flown 4 legs the day prior with the MEL active. Also, at the time of this incident, I had approximately 100 hours of experience in any Airbus aircraft.The first leg of the day was flown uneventfully. Immediately after takeoff on our second leg of the day with the same plane, an ECAM caution and audio alert was triggered for a F/CTL SPLR FAULT. The message subsequently cleared itself, but then a few seconds later, would trigger again. This cycle repeated itself approximately every 20-30 seconds for about 20 minutes, until the flight reached FL270, where the message stopped cycling and instead remained. Initially, after exiting the sterile period, ACARS messages were sent and a brief exchange ensued. An emergency return to ZZZ was offered as an option, but given that we were well above maximum landing weight and the ECAM did not require us to land as soon as possible, I elected to continue the climb.Upon reaching cruise altitude, I transferred the flying duties to the FO (First Officer) and verbally contacted Dispatch and eventually Maintenance Control. Maintenance had no inflight suggestions and stated that they would look at it when the plane is on the ground. At this point, the Dispatcher and I discussed our options. Since the ECAM mentioned FUEL CONSUMPTION INCREASED and FMS PRED UNRELIABLE and we still had just under 3 hours to go on a flight planned to land with just 8,000 LBS of fuel, the decision was made to divert to ZZZ1. Dispatch changed our destination and we proceeded to an uneventful landing in ZZZ1. An emergency was not declared. While on the ground in ZZZ1, one of the responding mechanics reported to me that he discovered that the MEL procedures were not properly complied with when the item was deferred and that Spoiler Pair #2 was inadvertently deactivated instead of Pair #4. Apparently, the aircraft had flown 4 legs in this condition prior to our operating it. He mentioned to me his concern that on the [day prior], a previous crew, the previously mentioned Check Airman had also apparently experienced a similar condition, wrote it in the logbook, only to have Maintenance simply clear the entry by writing 'info noted.' He expected that the aircraft would be taken out of service to fix the underlying issue. However, the decision was made to clear the write-up that I made and allow the deferral to continue. Based on the information that was relayed to me by this Mechanic, it appears that the initial error of deactivating the wrong spoiler pair was attempting to be covered up. This is very concerning.My relative inexperience with Airbus aircraft allowed me to be lulled into a false sense of security when it came to ECAM messages that appeared to relate to the MEL item. Seeing a write-up about spurious messages being handled the way it had been also led me to believe that there was nothing out of the ordinary, when realistically, there was a major error made by a certificated Mechanic. In retrospect, what was displayed on the F/CTL page should have alerted me to a problem, with both Spoiler Pairs #2 and #4, but I assumed that this was the same display that the mechanics and all of the other pilots who operated the aircraft before me also saw. The MEL does not give us specific guidance as to what should be displayed on this page with the MEL active, but I presume that the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) procedure referenced should tell the Mechanic whatshould have been displayed.More information in the MEL document detailing what exactly should be displayed on the SD (System Display) and what messages the crew should or shouldn't expect for a given MEL. Also, if there was indeed an attempt to cover up a maintenance error, I think this case should be used as an example as to how to properly correct an error. After takeoff we got an ECAM for flight spoiler fault that was reoccurring. We had this aircraft on the previous leg and got the ECAM and cleared it but this one kept returning. We still thought it was associated with the MEL on the Aircraft Spoiler Surface 4 INOP but Spoiler Surface 2 was also INOP. The Captain had reviewed the logbook before the previous flight and seen another crew had this happen and Maintenance had signed off [that] it was normal for the MEL. The Captain got in touch [with] Maintenance through Dispatch and they wanted us to divert to ZZZ1. We diverted and landed uneventfully.I think Maintenance improperly deferred the Spoiler Surface 4 and after a crew wrote it up, did not verify it was correct. The MEL should have had us view the Flight Control page instead of the HYD SD page for amber information of #4 Spoiler ONLY amber or #2 Spoiler ONLY.
ASRS:1826694.s: The Captain, operating an Airbus with an open MEL for Spoiler #4, diverted to ZZZ1 after recurring F/CTL SPLR FAULT ECAM messages. A mechanic later revealed the deferral was improper because Spoiler #2 was deactivated instead of #4, a maintenance error that was previously overlooked.

ASRS:1826848.n: Shortly after rotation, smoke entered the cockpit and cabin. The smoke smelled like something was burning and a high pitched whistling noise began. ATC was notified. ATC cleared us to land on the opposite runway. We quickly donned our oxygen masks and performed a teardrop maneuver to land on the opposing runway. As we lined up with the runway the smoke began to dissipate however our environment system was not providing cool air. A normal landing was made and vehicles inspected the exterior of the aircraft. When given all clear we taxied back to the FBO and shutdown. Maintenance was notified and the airplane was grounded until released.
ASRS:1826848.s: The flight crew experienced smoke and a whistling noise shortly after rotation, prompting an ATC-cleared teardrop maneuver to land on the opposite runway. Although smoke dissipated, the environmental system failed to provide cool air, resulting in a normal landing, exterior inspection, and subsequent aircraft grounding for maintenance.

ASRS:1826863.n: On an RNAV 34 approach into 11R, once landed on Runway 34, an aircraft landed on the opposing Runway 16. I had been switched from ZZZ Center 13 miles out and had made a 10 mile, 5 mile, 3 mile final and short final call out for [Runway] 34. No traffic was heard on the frequency until after the incursion. My aircraft could not have done a go-around as the aircraft was already on the ground and the configuration had already been changed, as well as the distance was gauged to be too close to gain the airspeed needed. I swerved to the left side of the Runway to avoid the traffic, while the other traffic swerved to the right side, relative to me. I pulled back on the yoke to provide drag to slow down, and applied the brakes heavily. We passed each other without the aircraft touching, and we were both still in motion when we passed. When my aircraft stopped I proceeded to taxi off on the next available taxiway. While doing this someone came onto the frequency asked me if I was all right and gave me their tail number. I then taxied back to the run-up area for Runway 34. Upon stopping, another aircraft came onto the frequency and gave me their information as well, the aircraft that was believed to have been the opposing traffic. With that I departed the active Runway of 34 to the north.
ASRS:1826863.s: A pilot on an RNAV 34 approach to Runway 34 encountered an opposing aircraft landing on Runway 16 after receiving no traffic advisories. The pilot avoided a collision by swerving left and braking heavily, passing the other aircraft while both were still in motion.

ASRS:1826875.n: All of a sudden, the Captain stopped mid-sentence and said, 'Look at that!' He pointed to the 1:00 right position, and we passed by a large, round, unknown object to the right at our altitude. Based on the speed of passing, it seemed to be stationary. It was large (much larger than a Mylar balloon), dark gray and silver/shiny, stripes (stripes of its form/shape) from top to bottom. It seemed to have a pinch point at the bottom. I didn't see anything attached, but the Captain said he saw a rope or something dangling behind it. Soon after our shock, ATC gave us a handoff and we reported the object. He was unaware of its presence. I reached out to the [nearby] pilots to see if anyone knew anything. One pilot responded: 'We got a message from our chief pilot this morning - balloon off SWO 100 radial 12.4nm & tethered balloon by Company.' The message the pilots in SWO received correlates with the location of our event. I've never known of a tethered balloon at 32,000 feet. Makes one wonder if this balloon got loose, especially given the rope the Captain saw. If so, shouldn't ATC have been notified? A bit more right today, and I may not have been able to write this report, along with the more than 200 people we had onboard.
ASRS:1826875.s: The crew encountered a large, stationary, tethered balloon at 32,000 feet while carrying over 200 passengers. Although ATC was unaware of the object, the reporter suspects a tethered balloon from a nearby company had become loose, posing a significant collision risk.

ASRS:1826877.n: I conducted a training flight with another experienced flight instructor for the purpose of a high performance endorsement. The flight departed from Independence State Airport (7S5) and returned two hours later. The weather was VFR with cumulous ceilings above 3,000 ft. Surface winds were northerly at 10 to 15 kts. The only flight precaution was AIRMET SIERRA for occasional mountain obscuration. We departed Runway 34 and landed on Runway 34 upon our return. The apron area for loading and unloading passengers, refueling, and parking is located east of the runway, between Taxiway A1 and A2, with taxi lanes on the north and south ends. The airport was on a north wind operation that day, so we used the taxi lane on the south end in order to make an upwind turn to access the fuel island.Five days later we start hearing from other pilots how 'pissed off' [a] hangar owner is that we used the taxi lane in front of [their] hangar adjacent to the taxi lane. Aircraft and other vehicles are often parked dangerously close to the taxi lane in front of [the] hangar, so taxiing requires great care to avoid collision. Many times the hangar occupants shut down, leave aircraft unattended, and block the taxi lane. This causes other aircraft to use the downwind taxi lanes causing unsafe operations, especially for tailwheel aircraft. Being considerate of each other is imperative to aviation safety.
ASRS:1826877.s: Two flight instructors conducted a VFR training flight at Independence State Airport (7S5), using a south taxi lane to access fuel. The reporter noted that hangar occupants frequently block this lane with parked aircraft, creating collision risks and forcing unsafe operations for other pilots.

ASRS:1826883.n: An aircraft in crosswind for Runway 29. Aircraft Z is 4 NM to the South West 1,000 feet above pattern altitude, announcing intentions to enter the downwind. My aircraft (Aircraft X) is 2 miles to the south at pattern altitude, announcing intentions to enter on the 45 for midfield downwind [Runway] 29, have the crosswind and 4 mile traffic insight. I announce to the now downwind traffic that I have them insight and will sequence behind them at the midfield downwind Runway 29. Aircraft Y departs Runway 29 and announces crosswind to perform touch and goes on Runway 29 (CFI and student). Aircraft Z announces performing a 360 for spacing. I believe that Aircraft Z was facing away from the field and did not see Aircraft Y in crosswind. I hear a radio call that Aircraft Z has cut off Aircraft Y, I look at my MFD and see the two aircraft appear very close to each other. The CFI in Aircraft Y announces that they will be performing a 360 for spacing behind the 'cutting aircraft'. I am closer than I would like to the aircraft in front of me and stay 100ft higher and slightly to the right to keep the aircraft insight. Aircraft in front announces intentions to full stop land, and I announce that I will extend downwind for spacing. Aircraft in front calls base, I continue on downwind. Aircraft in front calls final, I call and turn base. I call and turn final upon seeing the Aircraft on short final and deem spacing to be appropriate for the Aircraft to vacate the Runway. Reviewing the radio calls, my call to Final was stepped on. Aircraft Z calls base, I'm expecting him to be behind me on base. Aircraft in front calls that they are on the runway and will be vacating, I verify that spacing looks good. My passenger (2nd GA flight) calls for traffic to the left, I look and see the Aircraft Y in downwind. 5-10 seconds later the broadside of Aircraft Z passes in front of the windshield at 100ft or less, same altitude. I call 'go around sidestep left' as I can see the shadow of Aircraft Z on the right of me. I announce intentions to depart crosswind to the south. Not hearing any calls from Aircraft Z I become concerned. Using my MFD, I identify the call sign of the aircraft involved and ask if they are OK? They respond they are OK and that they are in Downwind. I believe that Aircraft Z confused my radio calls for that of the Aircraft in front of me. I believe that the near miss with Aircraft Y after his 360 for spacing caused him to lose situational awareness. I believe that my call for final being blocked did not help Aircraft Z's SA. I believe that the lack of availability of pattern work at ZZZ/ZZZ1/ZZZ2 is making non towered fields like LMO busier than they should be.
ASRS:1826883.s: The pilot of Aircraft X reported a near mid-air collision with Aircraft Z on final approach at a non-towered field, caused by Aircraft Z's loss of situational awareness after a previous conflict and blocked radio calls. Aircraft Z passed within 100 feet of Aircraft X, forcing a go-around and sidestep while Aircraft Z remained unaware of the proximity.

ASRS:1826885.n: During a normal flight lesson in the traffic pattern with my student, my student landed the plane with full brakes and the brakes locked up. The plane took a hard right toward the edge of the runway and I took the flight controls.
