With barely any directional control left I was able to keep the plane on the runway long enough to to make a taxi way. We took the taxiway at a fairly high speed and then I was able to regain directional control and bring us to a full stop. No damage was caused to the plane, runway or taxiway, or any signs or lights on the airport. Tower asked if we needed any assistance and I said negative just to taxi back to the ramp.
ASRS:1826885.s: During a flight lesson in the traffic pattern, a student pilot landed with locked brakes, causing the aircraft to veer right toward the runway edge. The instructor took control, exited onto a taxiway at high speed, and stopped the aircraft with no damage to the plane or airport infrastructure.

ASRS:1826890.n: After acceptance an IFR clearance from ZZZ to ZZZ1, myself, as PIC (Pilot in Command), and a passenger, in the co-pilot seat, departed Runway XX (ZZZ). At 1,000 feet AGL, I checked in with Departure on the climb out. All was normal until we realized the cockpit door was not fully closed and secured. The latch on the top of the door appeared to have not fully engaged. At approximately 3,200 feet MSL, the door popped open and I decided to immediately return to ZZZ. I informed Departure of my intentions to return to ZZZ. Due to wind noise in the cockpit, I could only partially hear ATC's response. I entered a right downwind for Runway XX and informed the Tower of my location and intentions. The Tower cleared me to land and I proceeded to a normal landing on Runway XX. The taxi back to the FBO was normal. Within 30 minutes we were airborne on an amended IFR flight plan, with the door properly closed and secured.
ASRS:1826890.s: The PIC and a passenger departed ZZZ in an IFR flight when the cockpit door latch failed to engage, causing the door to pop open at 3,200 feet MSL. The pilot returned to ZZZ, landed normally on Runway XX, and departed again 30 minutes later after securing the door.

ASRS:1826894.n: Recreational Drone FlyawayDeerc DE22 Drone over .55lbsBattery status: FullController charge: estimated 95% FullSet leveling, then compass. Flew to check position (5 feet straight up) noticed a slow left roll. Landed. Powered off drone and controller. Carefully checked all props. Checked arms for cracks. Reseated battery. Turned on, leveled, set compass again. Appeared to fly in place. Checked controls at 5 feet. OK to fly. Started climb. Noticed a marked right roll at 35 feet. Tried to roll to left to bring it back, no response. Increased altitude to avoid tree. Tried to turn and fly back, no response. Hit RETURN HOME. RETURN HOME button was flashing on controller (which is correct). Watched drone continue to roll to the right until out of sight. After a few minutes left controller on landing pad with RETURN TO HOME still flashing, jumped in the car to try to reacquire visual. Never saw it again.
ASRS:1826894.s: A recreational pilot operating a Deerc DE22 drone experienced an uncommanded right roll at 35 feet that became uncontrollable despite input and Return to Home activation. The drone rolled out of sight and was lost after the pilot failed to reacquire visual contact.

ASRS:1826901.n: I'm working two radar sectors combined. Total normal for the summer. Even if it wasn't normal we don't have the staffing to split it off. I'm working about X airplanes at the time. Sure, not a lot. Two airplanes are going the same direction. I separate the two airplanes via altitude separation. One's an IFR small aircraft (Aircraft Y) west bound on the airway at 10,000 feet. The other is a VFR small aircraft (Aircraft Z) west bound restricted at 9,500 feet wanting 10,500 feet. There's an air carrier jet (Aircraft A) which was a departure off of PSP heading east bound. Then there's this IFR small aircraft (Aircraft B) at 14,000 feet without a proper scratchpad flashing at me from the Center from the east. There are thunderstorms in and around the area so I suspect it's someone deviating. So I call the flight data and get a full route. Of course, thunderstorm or not, it's a bad route. I don't take radar, I have some time to deal with that issue later. Now here are the two players. The first one is what this whole story is about: Aircraft X.I release Aircraft X on the RNAV departure. I then go over and deal with the skydiver at the Banning Airport (BNG). This is a problem. It's been somewhere between 2 to 4 years since someone [opened] a skydiving joint in the middle of a pass in between two large mountains. Many reports [have been filed] about this. Now, I will give you all this much, the skydiving is finally depicted on the VFR chart.However, the folks at SCT have dropped the ball. There's no Letter of Agreement (LOA) with us and the BNG skydiving operation. We have an LOA for every other skydiving organization within SCT. There's no definitive anything on what should or shall happen with any of the procedures. We have a little piece of paper taped to the radar sector for controllers to spout off on the recorded line to invoke their Article 65 rights. Doesn't that seem like a glaring issue? Is it because no one has died yet or there haven't been enough TCAS RAs or significant event/MORs (Mandatory Operation Report) filed yet to have to worry about it? The BNG jumper calls two minutes. I give my two minute call. I call the Hemet sector and give them the notice that the jumper is two minutes out. [I have] to coordinate with a separate sector about a jump zone that is on the border of three airspaces and there's nothing written anywhere about who's responsible for what?The initial altitude for departures off of 31L is 8,000 feet. The lowest altitude you can issue off of 31L is 5,000 feet. There was about a two year period where it was 400 feet but that changed when PSP was absorbed into SCT. I'd like to mention to everyone that's ever seen the craziness of the Minimum Vectoring Altitudes (MVA) of PSP that the Cath1 departure is runway heading until about 5ish miles before it's a right turn to the east into the valley. So the Aircraft X goes up the final (if you will) to Runway 13R. The MVAs look scary but it's a pretty clear shot...albeit not for very long at all. JEXOT which is the Final Approach Fix for Runway 13R is supposed to be crossed at or above 2900 feet which is 7.5 miles north of the airport. It was also 10 miles visibility and Sky Clear that day. Upon Aircraft X's second call he checked in either at 3,000 or leveling at 3,000. Either way, it wasn't what it was supposed to be. I was literally in disbelief. I asked him again, 'Verify assigned altitude?' To see an aircraft where he was at there at 3,000 feet wasn't shocking. It gets a little warm in the summer time at PSP. Climb rates are bad. Once it was verified, it was clear there was a problem. I solved it. I issued 'Climb and maintain 8,000.' I think I said it twice just in case.[I was told] I should have issued a low altitude alert. The FAA 7110.65 says, 'low altitude alert check your altitude immediately the MVA in your area is...' The altitudes are a little hyperbolic but it's the truth. Look at the MVAs. They're insane and there are a lot of them. I didn't assign 3,000 feet. He needed to climb. I believe the .65 literally says, 'Give first priority to separating aircraft and issuing safety alerts as required in this order.' That's what I did. I separated the plane from the terrain. So Aircraft X is up to 8,000 feet. He's flying the departure. Everyone's separated. He's passing traffic so I assign a higher altitude. 'Aircraft X climb and maintain 15,000.' He reads back 16,000. I immediately catch it and fix it. He clears a higher MVA so I want to turn him on course. I tell him, 'Aircraft X turn left heading 360 when you are able proceed direct to YUCCA.' We do this 1,000 times a day. He reads back 260. I catch immediately. 'Negative, 360.' Honestly, I don't think I used his callsign. That's on me. But he reads it back. Should be fine right? I'm guessing CRM (Crew Resource Management) wasn't optimal that day. He definitely turns right, not left, to a 260 heading. I think it was at this moment that I noticed a VFR aircraft departing the BNG airport within two minutes of jumping. I say, 'Safety alert (almost ironically I know since I didn't say low altitude alert with the Aircraft X)' to the BNG jump aircraft and I inform him about the traffic.I know there are safety alerts even though the phrase safety alert isn't phraseology. It gets the message across. I hold the jumper and ask if he's talking to the departure. Unsurprisingly he's not because the departing traffic isn't on the UNICOM. That's when I notice the Aircraft X is turning right instead of left. Now he's heading for terrain and two unsuspecting small aircrafts. I deem that trying to turn back to the left would be a catastrophic decision. I felt that just continuing the right turn but stopping the climb would be the absolute safest decision. So, phraseology didn't work the first time so I go to plain language. I say something to the effect of, 'Aircraft X it looks like you turned right instead of left. That's okay, just continue your right hand turn to a heading of 030 and just stop your climb for traffic.' Not sure if it matters or not at this point but I did ask the Aircraft X, about two minutes before, when he was out of 3,000 for 8,000 that I wanted to triple check to make sure that he was assigned 3,000 by clearance delivery.So because I had said that, I was a little concerned that maybe the Aircraft X would think that he was in trouble and he might not have been as responsive as I would have liked him to be. That's why I said the whole 'that's okay' bit. I just didn't want him to go into a mountain and I didn't want him to say, 'you said right not left' all the while he's not turning. It happens way too often. So I stopped his climb. Well, I asked him to...but he didn't. He was at about 8,100 feet when I said stop your climb. He wasn't exactly climbing at 4000 feet a minute either. I could have said climb and maintain 090 but he was converging with a small aircraft that was out of 9,300 feet for 9,500 feet and another small aircraft above that guy at 10,000 feet. Sure I'd have 'separation' but I didn't want a TCAS RA. I had hoped he could level off at or around 8,500 feet or so, clear the MVA, not get a TCAS RA and be on with this show. But he kept climbing. I saw this and used a more authoritative voice and said stop your climb for traffic. I probably could have called traffic but there was a lot going on at the time. I might have called traffic but I don't think I did to the Aircraft X. Center was crying for me to take a hand off on a guy. I told them I couldn't take him. They refused to accept that an answer and kept calling. The VFR aircraft at BNG was posing a dangerous threat. The Aircraft X was turning away from a mountain. I was trying to tell the other two small aircraft about each other but I felt I kept getting blocked. Eventually, the Aircraft X stopped climbing. He said he had traffic in sight. There was no MVA violation with the high terrain. There was no TCAS RA. I got the Aircraft X back on course. I climbed him up and got him on the way. The VFR departure eventually cleared and the skydiver let out skydivers. It all worked out.The Low Altitude Alert (LA) never went off on the radar scope I was working. Hard to believe right? I thought so too. I was shocked about the LA alert going off.This is clearly a pilot deviation. It seems apparent it's a CRM issue. Please intervene and get us an LOA with the Banning jump zone and SCT.The FALCON program that SCT uses is faulted. The LA never went off on the scope. And if I missed it initially, surely it didn't go off continuously over several minutes and thousands of feet in the climb. There's a bug that needs to get addressed with that system.
ASRS:1826901.s: An air traffic controller managing a combined radar sector issued a safety alert when Aircraft X, departing PSP, deviated from a left turn instruction and climbed toward terrain and other traffic. The controller used plain language to stop the climb and redirect the aircraft, resolving the conflict without a Minimum Vectoring Altitude violation or TCAS resolution advisory.

ASRS:1826902.n: I'll start off by saying that the South Area had 6 Controllers and 1 D side trainee, but no Supervisor. The East Area had 6 Controllers and 1 Supervisor. The South Area was forced to operate while the Supervisor position was combined with the Operations Manager in Charge. While working 68, Sealord was active above my stratum for everything but W136A/B. There was a few scattered areas of precipitation around SAV, and a line west of SAV that forced the traffic between sectors 66/50 to deviate into my sector. Sector 47/48 was combined and very busy. ZDC did what ZDC does best, as they slammed the door on sector 47/48. Scrambling, the East Area begins rerouting every aircraft into ZTL. ZTL did what ZTL does best, as they then slammed the door on the East Area as well. This caused us all to put everyone into no notice holding. Like dominoes falling south, everyone stopped taking hand offs for aircraft headed towards ZDC and put everyone into holding.From here, chaos ensued. Information was limited, we had no Supervisor in the area to talk to Traffic Management Unit or the other areas to figure out what we needed to do. I basically had one hole around SAV everyone was flying through, and Sealord had the rest of my airspace. Regardless, I had to begin no notice holding. I didn't know how long this would be, so I made a plan to hold aircraft at odd altitudes in two different locations (SAV and GIPPL). My plan was to hold south at both points, so I could successfully hold a lot of aircraft if I needed to. I began by first issuing holding instructions to Aircraft X to hold south at a point just east of SAV at 33,000 feet. The next aircraft I was given was Aircraft Y at 33,000 feet. I issued holding instructions to him to hold south at the GIPPL intersection at 33,000 feet.Between every transmission of mine, I was trying to get the attention of the Supervisor in the East Area. If you listen to the tapes, you will hear me say 'say again' very often. This is because it was impossible to try and get help, while also keeping up with their check ins/requests. He was the only one around that wasn't plugged in and trying to create order from the chaos. He of course was very busy (and doing well at taking care of his own area) so it was hard to steal him away to try and figure out what was going on. At some point (I had too much going on to see the exact time) conflict alert initiated between the Aircraft X and Aircraft Y. I expected the Aircraft Y to be south of GIPPL, thus no factor for the Aircraft X when I gave the holding instructions. The Aircraft Y must have plugged in north instead of south, because he was head on with the Aircraft X. I issued traffic alerts and turns, while climbing the Aircraft X to FL340. There was a loss [of separation].I don't know at this point if I issued the holding instructions incorrectly or if I had missed a bad read back. This could have been my mistake or it could have been a pilot deviation. Either way, there was too much chaos to catch any unexpected pilot actions. ZDC giving no notice to stop all hand offs without any kind of heads up is ridiculous and dangerous. It would be a completely different story if they had put us on alert and given us routes to issue if it happens. This also would have given ZTL a heads up and then we could have all worked together on a safe and expeditious plan. There should have been a staffing trigger tonight. Any time that is brought up, everyone freaks out and refuses to ever use the word 'staffing'. This happens constantly. The South and East areas having 6 Controllers a piece is not ok. Maybe this is conversation better spent as a hotline call? What is so wrong with slowing traffic due to low staffing? It is no different than getting slower service at a restaurant because they are low on servers. It's semantics, and semantics should never interfere with safety. That is our number one job after all. Tonight was dangerous and this kind of practice needs to stop. It won't though, so I'm going to stop wasting any more time. Staffing is terrible, we constantly get stretched too thin, we don't ever really have a proactive plan, we get very little support from Command Center, and sometimes that swiss cheese thing the FAA likes to tell us about comes true and then there's a loss.
ASRS:1826902.s: An air traffic controller in the South Area reported a loss of separation between two aircraft at FL330 while managing no-notice holding due to upstream flow restrictions and understaffing. The controller attributed the incident to chaotic conditions, lack of supervisor support, and a potential pilot deviation where one aircraft entered a holding pattern in the wrong direction.

ASRS:1827007.n: At approximately XX:45 on Gate X during the arrival of Aircraft X ZZZ-ZZZ1, an aircraft maintenance truck drove through the OSZ (Operational Safety Zone) of Gate X as the aircraft was turning into the gate for arrival. The arrival ramp crew was in place to receive the aircraft, and was in fact about to begin marshaling in when the maintenance pick-up drove through the OSZ.
ASRS:1827007.s: During the arrival of Aircraft X ZZZ-ZZZ1 at Gate X, a maintenance truck drove through the Operational Safety Zone while the aircraft was turning in. The ramp crew was present and preparing to marshal when the truck entered the zone.

ASRS:1827010.n: On a flight loadout it was identified that four (4) HAZMAT quickpacks were scheduled for the same flight and pit location, B737-800. Two (2) boxes were RADIOACTIVE ll, One was (dry ice) Exempt Human Specimen 'IVF medical Biopsy', last one was (dry ice) Human Organ. Medical IVF specimens and human organs should not be shipped without proper separation distance from radioactive items. All were loaded in the same pit with about seven (7) feet distance from each other. Is there a way to ensure other employees separate such items.
ASRS:1827010.s: During B737-800 loadout, four HAZMAT quickpacks, including radioactive items and medical specimens, were loaded in the same pit with only seven feet separation. The reporter noted this violated required separation distances and questioned how to ensure proper segregation by employees.

ASRS:1827014.n: On Gate X at XA:56, Vehicle drove and stopped behind the aircraft while mid push. The vehicle was a full gate length away at the start of the push. Wing walkers were in position to stop the aircraft and were clearly visible to all traffic. No damage occurred and the push was completed after the vehicle was moved out of the gate.
ASRS:1827014.s: A vehicle stopped behind an aircraft during a mid-pushback at Gate X, despite wing walkers being in position and visible. No damage occurred, and the pushback was completed after the vehicle moved out of the gate.

ASRS:1827029.n: While reviewing the SID and release prior to departure (ABQ3 Runway 8), the First Officer and I noticed that the required climb gradient was very steep. We determined it may be difficult to meet the gradient and contacted Dispatch for guidance. I was unable to get in touch with Dispatch via phone. I then contacted a base chief pilot for guidance, who referred me to the Director of Operations. I was unable to get in contact with the Director of Operations until after departure. I then contacted another chief pilot for guidance and was referred to contact Dispatch again. I was able to talk to Dispatch and asked if we needed to run the climb analysis tool that we perform in ZZZ since this gradient was much steeper than ZZZ. Dispatch informed me that there was no need/requirement to run the analysis. I verified multiple times that this was the case, even with a steep climb gradient. Dispatch confirmed that no climb analysis was needed.I briefed the First Officer that we would need to fly a performance climb and ensure we were above 1,600 ft./min at a 200 Knot climb. After takeoff, we maintained the highest practical climb performance with E-climb, but were unable to maintain the needed vertical speed for our airspeed. We tried leaving the flaps at 9 and after that didn't work, flaps up with a climb below 200 Knots. I estimate we maxed out at 800 to 900 ft/min at 180 Knots. It was apparent that we would not be able to climb at the required rate with any configuration/speed and we made a right turn as assigned by ATC. We avoided terrain by executing the turn, but in IMC or without a quick turn crews would be in danger of CFIT. I was able to get in contact with the Director of Operations after landing to explain my concern with this departure. He pointed me to Training Bulletin XYZ, which referenced SID climb tables. This bulletin references ZZZ SIDs and it was not readily apparent (at least to me) that it would apply to other airports. After referencing the data cards, it appears that the required climb gradient of 470 Ft. per NM may not be achievable by the aircraft. While technically, there is a sentence in the training bulletin that states applicability to other airports, we have not received any training, memo, daily read, email, etc. on climb analysis at airports other than ZZZ. I was also a bit frustrated that it is recently getting harder to contact support resources by phone. I spent about 20 minutes trying to get help on a safety sensitive concern with no real available/wrong answer. While I take responsibility for this event, I followed the note on the training bulletin to contact dispatch when in doubt. I believe the company needs to issue a training, memo, etc. to make other pilots, Dispatch, and Management aware of the need for this analysis at other airports and include this on the 10-7 pages. I think this threat could result in CFIT if not corrected. While ATC would hopefully intervene, a crew could run into a situation where a GPWS (Ground Proximity Warning System) escape maneuver may not physically be able to clear the terrain without a non apparent turn in IMC. ASRS:1827029.s: The flight crew departed ABQ Runway 8 unable to meet the 470 ft/NM climb gradient after Dispatch incorrectly advised no analysis was needed. They avoided terrain by executing an ATC-assigned turn, though the crew noted the aircraft could not achieve the required rate and cited unclear training on climb analysis for non-ZZZ airports.

ASRS:1827045.n: Preflight up through takeoff on this flight was normal ops. I was sitting as the relief pilot with NAME being the PIC and flying pilot and NAME1 being the SIC and pilot monitoring. During the takeoff roll and at rotation, the flying pilot rotated normally after the 'ROTATE' call and pitched up to approximately 4 to 5 degrees and then stopped rotating any further. We were very heavy (382,094 TOW). We had a stop margin of approximately 2,000 feet and the end of the runway was rapidly approaching. After a moment or two, the flying pilot continued the rotation and we proceeded on normally. After takeoff and past sterile cockpit, the flying pilot communicated to us that the airplane just didn't seem to want to fly and he held the lower pitch attitude for a moment to allow the aircraft to accelerate a bit and avoid a potential tail strike. During cruise with my time in the seat, the flying pilot and I discussed the issue a little bit more, determined that we might be heavier than the weight and balance paperwork stated, and agreed to really check the pitch attitude on final approach at the calculated REF speed to see if that was another indication of being heavier than we thought we were. We did find that some airspeed had to be added to the calculated REF speed to maintain the normal pitch attitude during the final approach. Upon blocking in, we pulled out the landing REF speed chart in the QRH Inflight Performance section and found that with the additional airspeed we had to add to maintain the normal, fully configured, landing pitch attitude, it was conceivable that we may be UP to 20,000 pounds heavier than what was stated on the paperwork. We called the Load Master up to the flight deck and he said that flight was loaded at the point of origin in ZZZZ1, he was not involved with the loading process (or maybe more accurately, he wasn't involved in the weighing of the cargo) but was just given the numbers from those that were and that we had around 20,000 LBS of cargo in the lower cargo compartments along with all of the passenger weight. The PIC placed a writeup in the logbook to alert the outbound crew (the airplane continued on to ZZZ1 with the same Passengers and cargo) and we all agreed that we needed to make someone else aware of the issue (I elected to inform the Duty Pilot) and to ensure the outbound crew knew of the situation since we wouldn't see them ourselves. During the limo ride from ZZZ to ZZZ2, both the PIC and myself made unsuccessful attempts to reach the duty pilot through both Pilot Support and Dispatch. During the subsequent limo ride and discussing the issue further, the PIC wondered if there was a chance that the ground crew in ZZZZ1 was using KILOS as unit of measure rather than pounds (very possible given the 20,000 LBS of cargo we reportedly had vs what the potential difference in weight we noticed with the landing REF speed). The PIC was dropped off at the ZZZ2 airport for a commercial flight and the FO (First Officer) and I continued onto the layover hotel. It was agreed that the PIC would continue to communicate the issue to someone in hopes of alerting the outbound crew of the situation. I was texted later by the PIC that he did get a hold of the Fleet Captain and discuss the issue.
ASRS:1827045.s: The crew of a heavy aircraft experienced delayed rotation and required higher approach speeds, suspecting the aircraft was up to 20,000 pounds heavier than documented due to potential cargo weighing errors. The PIC logged the discrepancy and contacted the Fleet Captain to alert the outbound crew, though initial attempts to reach the Duty Pilot failed.

ASRS:1827051.n: On arrival at the departure gate, I inquired about station provision of international documents - Hawaii Reference Guide, plotting chart, and AIREP forms. Agent had no idea what I was talking about, claiming that the Hawaii flight is a domestic operation. The FOM clearly includes Hawaii operations under the flag operations description, and Hawaii is specifically addressed in the international operations sections of FOM - to include the need to use a plotting chart on random routes and the AIREP form when making non-CPDLC (Controller Pilot Datalink Communications) position reports. On this flight, the SATCOM system was placarded INOP which meant I would need to make position reports - thus, the need for an AIREP form. The Hawaii Reference Guide includes both plotting chart and AIREP forms as required paperwork to be checked prior to departure. I called Operations to ask for an AIREP form, but was told that they had no idea what I was asking for. We have been operating Hawaii and ZZZ1 flights out of ZZZ for years. If the FOM is going to require certain forms and documents, it would be very helpful to have these documents and forms available at the departure station. The same situation is now occurring in HNL as well - no international forms are being provided since they state that flights to the mainland are considered 'domestic' flying. But random routes are occasionally used and position reporting is still required. If there is no requirement for an AIREP form to be used in the CPDLC environment, the FOM and reference guides should be updated to reflect that their use is no longer required.Conflicting treatment of Hawaii operations - domestic for some purposes, international for others. Lack of clarity on what forms and documents are actually required to be used or made available for Hawaii operations. Lack of availability of international forms and documents at departure stations for international operations. If the FOM requires the use of documents and forms on international flights, it would be very helpful to have those forms actually available at the departure station. The mixed status of Hawaii operations - considered international flag operations by the FOM for some purposes but not for others - causes confusion as to which rules actually apply. This needs to be clarified.
ASRS:1827051.s: The pilot reported that ground agents and Operations failed to provide required international forms for a Hawaii flight due to conflicting domestic versus international status interpretations. This lack of availability occurred despite the FOM mandating these documents for non-CPDLC position reporting when SATCOM is inoperative.

ASRS:1827087.n: I was pilot flying, my CA (Captain) was pilot monitoring. After receiving instructions from Approach to slow down to 170 KT until a 5-mile final, we got an IDG (Integrated Drive Generator) fault message. The CA pulled out the QRH and tried to address the issue. Shortly after, we got a multitude of issues. We notified ATC and we agreed that we would be safe to land. Slat flap fail, AT/AP (Autothrottles/Autopilot) disconnect, and more. Suddenly we lost all screens and everything went black. The RAT (Ram Air Turbine) deployed and I had to continue flying using the Captains PFD (Primary Flight Display). The CA [requested priority handling] and was cleared by Approach to land and swap to Tower.CA told the FAs (Flight Attendant) we were making a precautionary landing. Tower said they had the trucks rolling and landed as best we could normally. We dropped the flaps on schedule and noticed that the Slat Flap Disagree persisted. The CA then took over the controls with ample time before the 1,000 feet call and I swapped roles to PM. We notified ATC that we could not verify [if] the gear and flaps were down. Luckily, Tower notified us that another plane verified they were down. We landed uneventfully and taxied to the gate under our own power. No passengers were hurt, only the first row or two knew something was abnormal due to the RAT vibrations, the rest of the passengers were unaware of the incident. [The cause was an] internal electrical malfunction at a time of high workload. Potentially go-around and troubleshoot If issues happen on final.
ASRS:1827087.s: During approach, the crew experienced an IDG fault followed by total electrical failure, triggering RAT deployment and loss of displays. The aircraft landed safely after an internal electrical malfunction caused multiple system failures, with no injuries reported.

ASRS:1827106.n: When trying to level off at 3,000 ft. the trim became stuck. I proceeded to pull back power and even with doing that and being in an almost standing position with all my weight down the plane was continuing to climb I tried switching it to the opposite side trim using aux trim it was still stuck. I advised ATC. At this point my arms are starting to get tired I tried flipping the trim again to reset it. I get the trim back for maybe 20 seconds but then it freezes again at this point the plane is controllable enough to maintain altitude though I'm using a lot more muscle then usual I tell Control I need to go back to ZZZZ, ZZZZ1 airport is short and has a steep descent and ZZZZ2 is too far and I'm not sure my arms would hold out that long for the longer runway and more services. I run the QRH which reading the notes I bring flaps and gear in earlier to make the plane more controllable and land.Trim motor bad.Called Dispatch, Maintenance Control. Also filled out paperwork with ZZZZ airport and called their Tower.I think memory items should include stuck trim, we have runaway but that checklist doesn't go over using flaps and gear to help you out and though once I had a second to think it made sense when you're using all your muscles to try and keep the plane from becoming uncontrollable you become very focused on just that aspect.
ASRS:1827106.s: The pilot experienced a stuck trim motor while leveling off at 3,000 ft, requiring significant physical effort to maintain altitude. After consulting the QRH and using early flap and gear extension to aid control, the pilot diverted to ZZZZ1 airport for a safe landing.

ASRS:1827107.n: We departed for an empty reposition leg from ZZZ - ZZZ1. Climbing through approximately 10,000 feet we began to experience compounding failures. First, our 60 Hz Converter failed, our left and right packs turned off, [and] our cabin pressure controller defaulted to manual control and would not reset back to auto. Our cabin began to climb excessively, cabin pressure low illuminated, cabin oxygen on - I immediately initiated a turnaround back to ZZZ and began a descent. We advised ATC and landed back at ZZZ. After several days of maintenance, it was discovered that the Mechanic assigned to fix our aircraft installed an unapproved E-INVERTER which was not listed in the IPC (Illustrated Parts Catalog) for a GIV and did not properly secure a cannon plug. These issues were later fixed by the Gulfstream FAST.From a pilot perspective this was unavoidable. The errors that occurred here are solely on the maintenance side. The IPC should have been consulted prior to ordering and installing any part on any aircraft. This did not happen.
ASRS:1827107.s: Pilots experienced multiple system failures during climb on a GIV reposition leg, forcing an immediate descent and return to ZZZ. Maintenance later revealed an unapproved E-INVERTER and an improperly secured cannon plug caused the issues.

ASRS:1827152.n: Taxiing when left brake wouldn't engage, pumped the brakes multiple times, and decided to continue in a forward direction toward grass rather than possibly tipping the plane resulting in the plane running over a light. Plane stopped. Proceeded to get back on taxiway and get back to ZZZ1 constantly engaging the brakes to make sure they were both working, which they did.
ASRS:1827152.s: During taxi, the pilot encountered a left brake failure and steered the aircraft onto grass to avoid tipping, damaging a light. The pilot returned to ZZZ1, verifying both brakes functioned correctly after repeatedly engaging them.

ASRS:1827154.n: On less than 1/2 mile final, 200ft AGL Aircraft X Destination: LAL. Local VFR Training Flight Ceiling Unlimited- Visibility 10 miles While on short 1/2 mile final, 200 FT AGL, Aircraft Y conducted a short approach descending from above and left in between us and the runway. Distance between aircraft approximately 500 feet horizontal- crossed vertically. Minimal time between sighting and evasive turn to the right at 200 FT AGL Aircraft X conducted a low level evasive turn to the right at 200 FT AGL to rejoin final for landing. No evasive action taken by other aircraft. Aircraft acknowledged our location on final and was instructed by ATC to follow traffic on final. No injuries occurred this near miss.
ASRS:1827154.s: Aircraft X, on final approach at 200 feet AGL, executed a low-level evasive turn to the right after Aircraft Y descended between them and the runway. The near miss occurred with approximately 500 feet horizontal separation, resulting in no injuries.

ASRS:1827156.n: While in cruise flight at Flight Level 380 the amber Hydraulic Overheat annunciator illuminated, the check list was performed for the corresponding annunciator which indicated no action in flight. Shortly afterward the Amber Hydraulic Low Pressure for the right engine illuminated and the Amber Hydraulic Overheat extinguished. It was also noted that the right engine vibrated briefly when the annunciator illuminated. The checklist for the Amber Right Hydraulic Low Pressure annunciator was performed which indicated no inflight action required unless hydraulics fell in which case flight would have to continue at a lower altitude (FL350 or lower) due to concerns for emergency descents. Due to the rapid occurrence of the two annunciators the decision was made to divert to ZZZ out of an abundance of caution.We landed safely without further issues and Maintenance was sought.The Right Engine Hydraulic pump had failed.
ASRS:1827156.s: During cruise at FL380, the crew experienced right engine hydraulic overheat and low pressure warnings accompanied by brief vibration. They diverted to ZZZ as a precaution, landed safely, and maintenance confirmed the right engine hydraulic pump had failed.

ASRS:1827160.n: We were cleared for takeoff on a Boeing 757-200 operating a ferry flight Part 91 from ZZZ to ZZZ1. We rejected the takeoff at high speed due to a left engine fire indication. We advised ATC immediately of the issue, cleared the runway, shut down the engine as a precaution, and taxied to a pad to allow for brake cooling. No further event took place from this rejected takeoff, it was only an indication problem.
ASRS:1827160.s: Pilots rejected a high-speed takeoff on a Boeing 757-200 ferry flight due to a left engine fire indication. They cleared the runway, shut down the engine, and taxied for brake cooling, concluding the event was solely an indication problem.

ASRS:1827163.n: I was in [an] Archer, Aircraft X, in the pattern at ZZZ with my student working on landings. After completing a touch-and-go at ZZZ we took off and began [an] out-crossing turn at 500 feet AGL. Upon reaching the crossing-to-downing turn, what looked to be some sort of Piper Cherokee cut directly ahead of us on downwind. We saw them cut us off and executed a turn to our right to avoid and then another turn once clear to follow them in the pattern. As we entered the downwind leg, I determined we were too close for a safe pattern and told the student to execute a right 360-degree turn for spacing. I announced this on CTAF and we did the turn.While this was occurring, the unknown Cherokee was proceeding down the downwind leg and failed to notice Cessna 172, Aircraft Z, on an extended downwind/base leg. Aircraft Z had announced its intentions of doing so once [it] joined its downwind leg in order to provide spacing for another aircraft already in the pattern to complete a full-stop landing. This unknown Warrior proceeded to turn a base leg too close to the runway and effectively cut off Aircraft Z on final. The unknown Cherokee then overflew final, turned its own final leg, and proceeded to fly final within 100 feet. wing tip-to-wing tip of Aircraft Z. Aircraft Z then proceeded to execute a go-around and depart the area to the south afterwards. The unknown Cherokee did not make another radio call and proceeded to go around, departing ZZZ's pattern to the north from what I could tell.After talking to the other pilot in Aircraft Z, we determined that when Aircraft Z was on its entry leg into ZZZ's pattern the unknown Cherokee was following Aircraft Z in trail very closely. To make spacing, he announced he would execute a left 360. However, in reality he turned into an opposite direction downing leg and made a 180-degree turn after to reenter downwind on the correct direction. In doing so he effectively entered right where I, in Aircraft X, was making my turn and cut us off. All of this could have been fixed by proper radio communication on the part of the unknown Cherokee. The Cherokee should have also used standard pattern procedures and not nonstandard ones. If he had completed the 360 like he said he was going to he wouldn't have cut us off and standard procedure usage wouldn't have led to Aircraft Z being cut off as well.
ASRS:1827163.s: The Archer pilot and student in Aircraft X avoided a Piper Cherokee that cut them off during an out-crossing turn at 500 feet AGL at ZZZ. The Cherokee later cut off Aircraft Z on final approach due to non-standard pattern procedures and lack of radio communication, forcing Aircraft Z to execute a go-around.

ASRS:1827181.n: At XA:34, after holding short at ZZZ Runway XX, Taxiway XX, I announced on CTAF frequency that I was departing with my Skylane C172S, Aircraft X, from Runway XX for left closed traffic. The AWOS-3 weather observation was for variable winds, 3 KT. One other airplane in the vicinity reported their position in response, stating they would fly left downwind in the pattern for Runway XX and land after my departure.When [I was] aligned with runway centerline and applying full power for takeoff, I noticed another aircraft coming in to land on the opposite runway end, ZZZ Runway XY, with no radio communication. My ForeFlight software through ADS-B input, Sentry, gives me an audible collision warning that traffic is observed 0.6 NM from me on the same altitude, heading my way 12 o'clock, a Diamond DA-40, Aircraft Y. I took immediate preventative action by pulling back power, releasing the brakes and making an emergency taxi maneuver onto Taxiway XY, west, via point XZ. The other pilot landed using full runway and passed behind me on the now vacated Runway XX, with the collision narrowly avoided.It seems the other pilot was unaware of the preferred calm-wind runway being XX at ZZZ, and made no attempt at reporting position or intentions on CTAF. I approached the pilot after he had come to a full stop on the west ramp, and he claimed he had been communicating intentions on UNICOM frequency, being unaware of the existing CTAF frequency. With the intensity in traffic on many Class D/Class E after-hours airfields, it would be better if position and intention reporting on agreed CTAF frequencies were made mandatory.
ASRS:1827181.s: The C172S pilot aborted takeoff on Runway XX at ZZZ after a DA-40 landed on the opposite end without CTAF communication, triggering an ADS-B collision warning. The near-miss occurred because the DA-40 pilot mistakenly used UNICOM instead of the required CTAF frequency.

ASRS:1827193.n: On my third touch and go of the morning taking off from [Runway] XXR at ZZZ, just after turning crosswind, there was a tremendous bang followed by vibration from the engine. I [advised ATC] and believe I requested landing on XYR. I reduced power to reduce the vibration and left the engine running at approximately 1600 RPM. The Controller wanted me to go to [Runway] XYL but I didn't think I had the power to make it so continued to XYR and completed the landing. I was able to taxi to the hangar and shut down the engine. I inspected the aircraft airframe and found nothing wrong. I removed the cowling and discovered the starter ring gear had separated from its mounting position on the alternator rotor. It was still attached by one bolt, but had destroyed some wiring and ventilation SCAT tubes.
ASRS:1827193.s: During a touch-and-go at ZZZ, the pilot experienced an engine bang and vibration after turning crosswind, likely due to a separated starter ring gear on the alternator rotor. The pilot landed on Runway XYR with reduced power, taxied to the hangar, and found the gear had destroyed wiring and SCAT tubes.

ASRS:1827200.n: Landing at ZZZ with about 40 minutes of fuel estimated upon arrival. Upon entering traffic pattern, I experienced some delays due to faster aircraft on final for [Runway] XXR. Cleared to land number two behind a military F-16 and ahead of another military jet, I believe an F15. Tried keeping my speed up, but it wasn't enough and told to go-around. Upon going around and entering the traffic pattern a second time, I was now at minimum fuel and declared minimum fuel. Tower told me they will get me down and that I'm number two behind a Company jet. Following behind the Company jet, I noticed they were taking a long time to get off the runway, so I slowed down as much as I could so I could avoid another go-around. The Company jet began to exit the runway as I was getting close to touching down and then I was told a second time to go-around. I replied 'Unable' and landed. By the time of touchdown the jet was clear of the runway completely. Tower and I both exchanged apologies as I was taxiing to the FBO and went on our way. I wanted to report this since I did land without a landing clearance, but I was uncomfortable with doing another lap in the pattern with such low amount of fuel. I felt the safety of flight would be compromised and decided to land rather than risk a worse situation.
ASRS:1827200.s: The pilot, landing at ZZZ with minimum fuel, was instructed to go around twice due to runway occupancy by military and company jets. Citing safety concerns from low fuel, the pilot refused the second go-around, landed without clearance after the preceding aircraft cleared the runway, and exchanged apologies with Tower.

ASRS:1827217.n: I was vectoring Aircraft X into ZZZ for an ILS Approach. He was vectored through final and left high for VFR traffic on the localizer. He called the field in sight over the Final Approach Fix, was cleared for a Visual and switched to ZZZ Tower. He turned towards ZZZ1. VFR aircraft above 1500 feet near the localizer are a conflict because 2400 feet is the crossing altitude for the Initial Approach Fix ZZZZZ. VFR aircraft departing ZZZ or ZZZ2 Class D southbound are in a head on conflict with any aircraft on the localizer into ZZZ. IFR aircraft often end up being too high for a localizer approach because they can't descend because of VFR traffic on the localizer and they get a Visual Approach instead. It's also not uncommon for aircraft to be vectored through the final approach course to avoid traffic or descend. Both of these courses of action can disorient pilots, but there is nowhere to break them out without creating another conflict somewhere else. A few miles east of the localizer is higher terrain. An aircraft at 3000 feet within 10 miles of the airport will not be able to climb to the Minimum Vectoring Altitude in time. If the aircraft continues on a vector north to parallel ZZZ1, they could conflict with a departure off of ZZZ1, likely a prop on a 020 heading climbing to 3000 feet. ZZZ1, ZZZ, and ZZZ2 are so close to each other that it can be confusing which airport they see when they aren't able to fly a straight path inbound because of VFR conflicts.ZZZ localizer approach course need to be controlled airspace. VFR aircraft should not be able to fly on or through the localizer without talking to ATC. It's impossible to predict the actions of a VFR aircraft not on frequency. They climb, descend and maneuver around traffic they do see, sometimes making 360's. About XA:25 PST I observed Aircraft X, who was on an ZZZ ILS Runway XXL approach, heading westbound about 2 miles east of ZZZ1. They had gone through the ZZZ final and appeared to be flying towards ZZZ1 and not ZZZ. I told the Local controller and the Cab Supervisor then called ZZZ1 Tower on the shout line advising them of the traffic and that ZZZ Tower was attempting to turn Aircraft to the north towards ZZZ. Aircraft X's data tag was then changed to Visual Approach, ZZZ VA XXL. Aircraft X landed ZZZ Runway XXL without incident.
ASRS:1827217.s: An air traffic controller vectored Aircraft X high for VFR traffic during an ILS approach to ZZZ, causing the pilot to mistakenly head toward nearby ZZZ1. The controller alerted ZZZ1 Tower, and Aircraft X subsequently completed a visual approach and landed safely at ZZZ without incident.

ASRS:1827224.n: Departing Runway XXR at ZZZ over the shoreline at approximately 1,500 feet AGL, the Pilot Flying (PF) began a required turn to the left for heading of 210. The PF immediately verbalized a flight control abnormality stating that he is feeling resistance in the control wheel and that it couldn't be turned more than about half-scale deflection to the left, as if it was hitting the designed maximum stop.We continued the climb and the PF asked the Pilot Monitoring (PM) to take controls to see if the resistance was the same on both sides. The PM took the controls and agreed that the resistance was the same on both sides. Neither the PF nor the PM tried to force the control wheel beyond the point of resistance since the plane was still controllable in the normal range of operation up to 30 degrees angle of bank.The PM pulled out the QRH section 9.8 Jammed or Restricted Flight Controls. The PF continued to fly the SID as the PM ran the QRH and discussed the situation. The first thing we noticed about the QRH was that Step 4 required the use of Maximum Force to overpower a restricted system, however, this step did not seem to apply to us because the aircraft was controllable in the normal flight regime. This step introduced some doubt and confusion with the crew.We agreed that we didn't have a jam, but the maximum control deflection was restricted. Upon reaching Step 7, we had to decide whether the controls were normal or not normal. This step also introduced some confusion because we reasoned that since we both were able to make right and left turns under normal conditions up to 30 degrees angle of bank, the controls were for all intents and purposes normal. However, we still had the restriction, which gave us concern, and that full control wheel deflection was not normal.At this point, the crew decided to contact Maintenance and Dispatch on ARINC VHF radio and use all available resources to discuss the situation. The radios were very scratchy and there was a lot of feedback when the company keyed their microphones. All parties agreed that QRH 9.8 was the appropriate checklist for the situation, but the decision to continue or divert to the nearest suitable airport was still to be determined.As a crew, we felt that we were in a gray area between normal and not-normal flight controls but relayed to Maintenance that we felt comfortable continuing on to our destination. All parties agreed. En route, we continued to discuss the situation and it occurred to us that even though we could maneuver the plane normally, it was unknown whether an upset recovery might be diminished or not in the event of an encounter with wake turbulence, jet wash, or a rudder hard-over event. Such a condition might require Step 4 of the QRH to overpower the restriction with both Pilots. As a precaution, the crew asked ATC to keep the aircraft clear of potential wake turbulence due to restricted flight controls but that we were not declaring an emergency at this time.On final approach in full configuration, the PF experienced some ground convective turbulence and verbalized that he hit the resistance once during the approach as he was trying to counter the turbulence. This was unexpected, but the crew was able to land the aircraft safely.
ASRS:1827224.s: Pilots departing Runway XXR encountered restricted left control wheel deflection at 1,500 feet AGL, limiting turns to 30 degrees bank. Despite QRH confusion and turbulence-induced resistance on approach, the crew consulted maintenance, requested wake turbulence avoidance, and landed safely.

ASRS:1827225.n: [There was a] nose gear tire issue followed by a loss of System A Hydraulics. We were flying Flight XXXX from ZZZ to ZZZ1 on (date). As we were rolling down the runway, we heard a loud bang from the nose gear area. It went away as quickly as it arrived, engine parameters were normal as well as directional control. After the takeoff, we talked about what it could have been. During the climb to our cruising altitude, we decided to call ZZZ Tower back and ask them to inspect Runway XR for any clues to what had happened during our takeoff roll. It took a while before we got an update from ZZZ Tower. They had found a two feet by two piece of rubber. We immediately contacted Dispatch and Maintenance, and we discussed various options. We were now in cruise and still bound for ZZZ1, when all of sudden the Number 1 Eng Hyd A LOW PRESSURE light started to come on and off a few times. We got the QRH Checklist and ran the HYDRAULIC PUMP LOW PRESSURE.I looked down on the instrument panel and noticed the System A Hydraulics quantity was down in the low 20's percent. We could watch that number was dropping fast. We now went quickly over to another chapter in the QRH, to LOSS OF SYSTEM A. We also [requested priority landing] with Center, and they immediately gave us direct to ZZZ1 airport. We determined that it was likely that a possibly piece of rubber had hit some of the Hydraulic lines. We quickly updated Dispatch about our loss of Hydraulic A quantity, and that we had [requested priority landing]. Dispatch gave us the Landing Distance information data, and we compared it to our own. We were all in agreement to continue and land in ZZZ1. We informed our Flight Attendants about our situation and what they could expect from our landing. We flew overhead ZZZ1 airport, and manually extended our landing gear per QRH. After completing all the steps in the QRH, we lined up with Runway XXL and landed. I immediately noticed the tiller was «locked» and unusable upon landing, and had to use rudder and differential braking to get back on center line. Both NORM and ALT nose wheel steering where both unavailable. We elected to stop the aircraft on the runway, and asked the Fire Trucks to visually inspect the aircraft from the outside. After getting the OK from them, we had Company Maintenance meet us on the runway with a tug, and to tow us clear of the runway. We had just cleared [Runway] XXL when the tow bar snapped, and they had to get another one. Once we got the second one, we were towed over to Gate X where our passengers were able to deplane. Departed ZZZ Runway XR. On takeoff roll, prior to rotation, a noise was heard similar to a hand slap on the front of the aircraft. Takeoff was continued with no adverse indications. As we continued to climb, the Captain and I assessed the probable cause of the noise. ZZZ Tower was advised of possible FOD on the runway. Before we were out of range of ZZZ Tower, we inquired for any findings of the FOD. Tower advised a piece of tire rubber was found on the runway. Still unsure whether the rubber was from our aircraft or a piece we hit on takeoff roll, we continued the assessment. Dispatch was brought into the loop and we all agreed to continue. As we continued to discuss the current situation, the #1 HYD LOW PRESSURE light illuminated and we ran the HYDRAULIC PUMP LOW PRESSURE QRH Checklist. SYSTEM A HYDRAULIC quantity was noted to be around 20 percent. SYSTEM A HYDRAULIC quantity continued to drop. LOSS OF SYSTEM A QRH Checklist was started. [After] reassessment of the loss of HYDRAULIC SYSTEM A and the noise heard at takeoff, [they] led us to believe that we had blown a tire which had damaged the hydraulics. A [priority landing was requested] with Center and direct ZZZ1 was issued. We continued discussions with Dispatch, as well as informed the Flight Attendants of our current conditions, plans and what to expect on arrival in ZZZ1. All went as planned with the completion of the LOSS OF SYSTEM A Checklist and landing on Runway XXL in ZZZ1. The only unexpected item on landing was no nose wheel steering on landing. Both NORM and ALT nose wheel steering was inoperative upon landing so we were unable to exit runway. CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) met the aircraft on the runway to assist. Aircraft was towed to the gate from the runway.
ASRS:1827225.s: The flight crew experienced a nose gear tire failure during takeoff roll, likely causing debris to damage System A hydraulics and resulting in a rapid fluid loss. They executed the Loss of System A checklist, landed at ZZZ1 with inoperative nose wheel steering, and were towed to the gate after a tow bar snapped.

ASRS:1827261.n: Prior to pushback we receive a planned Dangerous Goods printout but not a final dangerous goods summary. The Captain spoke with the ramp Lead, Operations, Dispatch, the Chief Pilot, and Load Planning. We could not get a definitive answer or paperwork to confirm if the Dangerous Goods had been loaded or not. We did find out that the planned Dangerous Goods had not been loaded but 391 pounds of lithium ion batteries had been loaded. Lithium Ion batteries are listed in the manual as exempt from pilot notification but also they have certain prohibitions depending on packing and voltage. We had no way of knowing without paperwork. I expressed my concern about safety and legality to the Captain since I have read about numerous incidents with consumer product lithium batteries on aircraft as well as the NTSB's final report on the 787's that lists oversight on battery safety by Boeing and the FAA. Since we were on a duty time extension, the batteries were removed and we departed. Before push back we received a planned DG [Dangerous Goods] message that was not followed by a final DG message. We asked load planning and operations what we had onboard but no one could give us a straight answer. So we contacted dispatch to gain clarification. Still no answer. The lead in ZZZ sent a picture of what he showed on the final DG but we never received a copy. We were then notified that the planned DG had not been loaded but that we had 391# of lithium batteries. We were uncomfortable with that so called the Chief Pilot, who pointed out the page reference regarding pilot notification and lithium batteries. We elected to pull the pallet in question so we could depart with all crew members comfortable regarding the safety of the items being transported.
ASRS:1827261.s: The flight crew discovered 391 pounds of lithium-ion batteries were loaded without a final Dangerous Goods summary or clear confirmation from operations. To resolve safety concerns regarding the lack of documentation, the crew removed the batteries before departing on a duty time extension.

ASRS:1827283.n: Aircraft X joined taxi line for runway 4L. During the 45 minute taxi the flight was operating on upper antenna and all radio communications broadcast and received were normal. Flight was cleared to line up and wait 4L, comms normal. While in position a garbled, indistinct transmission was heard. Flight was expecting a takeoff clearance and called tower to verify they were broadcasting to us. No reply. Tower then came on and cleared flight to vacate runway, comm was loud and clear. Tower received our reply as well. Tower was then heard giving directions to a go around aircraft. The initial go around call to that flight was not heard by either pilot of our flight. Flight taxied back to departure end. Flight was cleared to line up and wait again, comms normal. Takeoff clearance was received and acknowledged. During initial takeoff roll tower came on frequency asking us if we were taking off. We replied we were and had acknowledged our takeoff clearance. Airborne tower wanted us to have our radio checked. Subsequent radio checks and communications with ATC were loud and clear for remainder of flight. I believe the transmissions during first takeoff clearance were blocked by a radio shadow. While in position for takeoff on 4L at EWR both the Captain and I did not here the takeoff clearance given by tower which resulted in a go-around for another aircraft on final. We did hear a garbled 'takeoff;' but that was it. We both questioned it and when the Captain tried to clarify with tower were told to hold position and then received clearance to taxi off the runway, via BB and P. Neither the Captain or I heard the takeoff clearance or the tower directed go around of the landing aircraft, but obviously the other aircraft did. We than taxied back into position and it took the tower at least two tries to get us the takeoff clearance. We only heard it once. Upon departure we verified the VHF one was working correctly with multiple ATC agencies. Sterile cockpit procedures were followed and there were no conversations while in position on the runway. Neither the Captain or I heard the original T/O clearance or the wave off call to the landing aircraft. The 10-7B pages for EWR state, 'Radio shadows exist in the vicinity of the first 1800 feet of the runways.' This is true and is an obviously known issue. Not sure what causes this, whether it is certain airplanes or position of other planes on the taxiways. At the time of the incident there was a line of 20+ airplanes on taxiway B. This condition is unsafe and needs to be corrected.
ASRS:1827283.s: Pilots of Aircraft X at EWR missed takeoff clearance and a go-around call due to radio shadowing while holding on Runway 4L. The crew vacated the runway, returned for a second attempt, and successfully departed after verifying VHF functionality.

ASRS:1827331.n: Just prior to push out of ZZZ we received and Air Bleed Message. Maintenance interrogated the system and MEL'd the message iaw MEL XX-XX. Enroute the Purser called and stated 'we have an issue, in reviewing our manual we have a Class A fume event in the forward galley. It smells like dirty gym socks.' I've had fume events in the past and I know the ramifications to the safety of the crew and passengers. We also have received good training during [Flight Attendant Training]. In the cockpit we didn't smell anything. All three flight attendants confirmed the same smell. With a Jump seat rider in the cockpit, I made the decision to take a quick bathroom break. Upon reaching the front right galley is was prevalent, mild and persistent. Upon returning to the cockpit I had the purser remain in the cockpit. I used air cell to call Dispatch and maintenance. With pilots, purser, dispatch and maintenance all on the phone call we jointly made the decision it's best to divert to a suitable airport. Over the vicinity of ZZZ2 and ZZZ3 we evaluated diversions to outstations, continue to ZZZ4 or ZZZ5. We were 570 miles from ZZZ4 and 240 from ZZZ5. Knowing ZZZ5 was just as close as spiraling down from FL380 and the aircraft would be grounded, we took into consideration passengers re-accomodation, medical response, inflight support and aircraft replacement. ZZZ5 was the best option and the joint decision was made to proceed to ZZZ5. I asked the First Officer (F/O) to [request priority] from ATC and we proceeded direct to a fix on ILS [Runway] XXR and landed and taxied to the Gate. With the jump seater being pregnant and the review of other events where fumes become hard to smell after long exposure, I requested everyone in cockpit to wear oxygen. I ran through QRC and [other procedures] multiple times to make sure we didn't miss any steps. Managing and reassessing the issue I think we did a pretty thorough job. I even turned on APU and ran bleeds to trouble shoot and nothing was working. The smell persisted in a mild to moderate amount especially in descent according to Flight Attendants (F/As). The purser had F/As rotate to mitigate one persons exposure. With a full aircraft we couldn't move anyone. Upon landing and shutting down we de-masked and opened up flight door. The first officer immediately noticed the smell and we left shortly after securing the aircraft. I was not aware that the F/As had on the previous leg noticed any smell. They all reported after the event that the dirty socks smell was present on the previous flight. When I took over the aircraft I was again blind sided by this. The F/A in aft galley even said she replaced her socks thinking it was her feet. So my suggestion is to continue to encourage communications from the cabin and have these experiences validated and documented even if there is the slightest question to certain smells. I don't know if the Air Bleed message would have an impact on this event but if so maybe adding instructions to confirm with crew no odors prior to MEL. Having these Name (Purser) able to locate his references on his tablet was huge in assisting me with my QRH. In cruise Flight Attendant (FA) reported odor in galley. Ran QRH odor in cabin, Captain (CA) Flight Attendant (FA), Dispatch, Maintenance Control agreed best course of action divert to ZZZ5 as best suitable airport for landing. Received priority diverted direct ZZZ5, landed without incident.
ASRS:1827331.s: During cruise, flight attendants reported a Class A fume event with a "dirty gym socks" odor in the forward galley, while the cockpit remained unaffected. The crew, dispatch, and maintenance jointly decided to divert to ZZZ5, where the aircraft landed safely after the odor persisted despite troubleshooting attempts.

ASRS:1827345.n: On final approach to SEA 34R, Tower gave us a 'Low Altitude Alert' Call. Indications within the cockpit showed we were on glide slope. I informed the Tower. Approach continued to uneventful landing. I suspect the 2 aircraft that departed as we were on short final causing glide slope fluctuation, coupled with the 2.75 glide slope for Runway 34R ILS caused us to momentarily go below the threshold. Multiple departures on short final coupled with a 2.75 glide slope.
ASRS:1827345.s: The flight crew received a Low Altitude Alert on final approach to SEA 34R despite being on glide slope. The pilot attributed the alert to glide slope fluctuations caused by two departing aircraft and the runway's 2.75-degree glide slope, resulting in an uneventful landing.

ASRS:1827379.n: Contract Autel EVO II being used to inspect Antenna Structure Registration infrastructure and briefly contacted the Antenna Structure Registration lightening rod. Operation was being conducted by contractor with vendor oversight. Pilot immediately backed away from structure with no loss of vehicle control and landed for inspection. Extremely minor prop damage was observed, new props attached, field debrief accomplished, and operation continued. UAS flight plan was changed by request of vendor to closer inspection pictures of the top radar antenna. The lightening rod on each corner extend above the top altitude of the radar antenna. The Remote Pilot in Command was relying on the UAS rear collision avoidance, which did not detect the narrow lightening rod. Due to geometry and distance of the structure made depth perception for Visual Observer not possible. 1)Vendor should include policy to land and brief if flight plan is changed 2)Vendor should include expected crew action in the event situational awareness with structure is lost or obstacle clearance is uncertain 3) In inspections of complex structures, crew may need to do walk around and locate best places for Visual Observer and potentially have more than 1 Visual Observer present.
ASRS:1827379.s: A contractor operating an Autel EVO II UAS briefly contacted a lightning rod while inspecting an antenna structure due to collision avoidance failure and poor depth perception. The pilot landed for minor prop repairs, and the operation resumed after a field debrief.

ASRS:1827391.n: Fumes were initially observed by the #4 flight attendant while standing with myself in the forward galley. Once I observed the odor, I went to the Captain and told him about the smell. He proceeded to turn off the APU, and the smell of the odor dissipated. He restarted the APU, and the odor returned. He decided to try it once again by shutting it down and after a few minutes restarting it, and the odor was gone and again returned upon restarting. The Captain called Maintenance and it was later decided that we would have to remove passengers and crew from the plane and take that particular aircraft out of service and get another plane for the flight.
ASRS:1827391.s: Flight attendants and the Captain detected fumes in the forward galley while the APU was running. The odor returned each time the APU was restarted, leading to the decision to evacuate passengers and crew and take the aircraft out of service.

ASRS:1827427.n: Instructing student on dual flight from ZZZ. Pre-flighted aircraft and fueled up and sump check good. Taxied to [Runway] XX. Run up checks were all within tolerance. Took off [Runway] XX and had normal performance for the weight and heat of the day. Getting around 300-400 FPM climb after crossing through 50 feet above the runway. Did our check of engine gauges, all green. Contacted Approach around 800 feet MSL and were told on course heading, started turn to NW and experienced partial power loss from 2,250 to 1,800 RPM. Instructor said 'what was that?' I took controls from my Student and remained Pilot Flying till we landed. Checked mixture full rich, throttle full, fuel pump on, and switched fuel tanks. Made a call to Approach and turned back to the airport. Was switched over to Tower and requested priority as we could not maintain altitude and safe airspeed. Did not lose total engine power until after we landed. Made sure Student was OK and calm. Picked a field and put in one notch of flaps, then full flaps once the field was made. Turned 180 degrees at 30 degree bank and aimed for first 3rd of runway. Touched down as smoothly as possible and used parking brake to come to a stop. Engine died as we rolled to a stop. Called emergency personnel, no injuries or visible damage to the plane, surprisingly. Plane overhead spotted us. We did the run up and pre-takeoff checklist and everything was checked out. We made a call to Tower and were cleared for takeoff on Runway XX. We took off with 10 degrees of flaps and full power and started climbing, and engine was sluggish due to high heat index, but within normal operating range. We did our initial climb check with engine gauges and Departure was contacted. Altitude was reported as 800 feet MSL and climbing, we took out the flaps, and turned toward our heading. At 1,000 MSL we had a partial power loss before we reached our heading. I noticed the partial power loss right away and exclaimed, 'What was that?' to my Instructor and instructor took controls. We switched the fuel pump on and then verified mixture and throttle were full and then switched fuel tanks. Nothing changed. We established proper pitch for best glide. My Instructor made a call to Departure, but then was switched to Tower and made a call. We were cleared to land Runway XY, but aborted landing because we were too far from the runway. Instructor put in 10 degrees of flaps and found a field. Instructor put in full flaps and did 30 degrees of bank to align with the field while descending rapidly. At 100 feet AGL, instructor pulled power to idle. Instructor then flared to land and we touched down. We immediately pulled the parking brake as the engine had total power loss and the propeller stood still. We stopped before the trees and switched off fuel pump, master, and turned off magnetos. We got out and started contacting the appropriate people. We opened the engine compartment to check things out and made sure the propeller was OK. An airplane found us and began circling and emergency personnel arrived. We left the airplane in the field and walked to meet with the personnel and they took it from there.
ASRS:1827427.s: A student pilot and instructor experienced partial then total engine power loss during a dual training flight shortly after takeoff, likely due to fuel system issues. They executed an emergency landing in a field with no injuries or visible damage to the aircraft.

ASRS:1827436.n: I was taking a Student out to do basic maneuvers and slow flight. On the way out to the practice area at 2,500 feet already making practice area traffic calls. I was going to do a clearing turns until on my left side I saw something move so I looked up to my left and saw a light blue colored twin-engine already making a hard right turn to avoid me. With me seeing this I made the quick decision as well to reduce the engine to idle, and bank right and descend as well to avoid the traffic. The aircraft was close enough to see a tail number on the plane, but because the twin was a low wing and was turning I was not able to see the tail number.
ASRS:1827436.s: A flight instructor and student in a single-engine aircraft at 2,500 feet encountered a light blue twin-engine aircraft during a clearing turn. Both pilots executed immediate avoidance maneuvers, with the instructor reducing power and banking right to prevent a collision.

ASRS:1827448.n: Was instructing in owner's aircraft. He wanted to practice takeoff and landings in the pattern at ZZZ. We did three three pointers. They were acceptable. Not greasers but nothing fundamentally wrong. We then did two wheel landings. Again, acceptable but not greasers but no warning flags. It was getting hot and thermal activity was affecting the landings so we decided to do one more and then call it quits. He did an acceptable wheel landing and at first everything was OK. Straight on the runway and wheels down. He then put the tail down - prematurely in my judgement as we still had a lot of speed (not excessive). The plane immediately yawed to the right. I intervened and applied full opposite rudder (I think he did as well) but it did not stop the yaw. This aircraft has no brakes on the instructor side so unable to apply brakes. The pilot did not use brakes to control the yaw. We ended up in the grass next to the runway. The pilot was pretty shaken up so I taxied back onto the runway and to the tie down. We determined there was no damage to the aircraft. I recommended to the pilot to have the tail wheel inspected in case there was some issue with it.I was surprised that we had the yaw to the right after what appeared to be an acceptable wheel landing. There were no wind gusts or other factors that I was aware of. It was either a result of lowering the tail too quickly (gyroscopic precession) or there is an issue with the tail wheel mechanism.
ASRS:1827448.s: An instructor and student practicing wheel landings in a tailwheel aircraft at ZZZ experienced an uncommanded right yaw after the student lowered the tail prematurely. The aircraft veered into the grass without damage, likely caused by rapid tail lowering or a tail wheel mechanism issue.

ASRS:1827463.n: While taxing, a situation arose where the aircraft I was operating, Aircraft X, and a separate C172 training aircraft were instructed to taxi in opposing directions on Taxiway XX at ZZZ Airport. I was instructed 'to taxi via XX and XY to [Runway] XZL and maintain right of XX for opposite traffic' after leaving FBO.Abiding by this instruction, I maintained right of the taxiway and an opposite Grumman aircraft passed our left side of the taxiway, with us on the right. Having believed the opposing traffic no longer a factor, I returned to normal taxi while still maintaining right of taxiway, however, with less vigilance, believing traffic no longer a factor. My instructed taxi procedure at the Skydiving Facility is to taxi nose high to alleviate nose wheel pressure thus putting less wear and tear on the nose wheel Oleo Strut. This can make distant traffic difficult to see. We are also urged to taxi rather quickly to save time by skydiving management to save time. As I approached a 45 degree bend in Taxiway XX, eastbound on the Taxiway, my aircraft briefly went over to the left side of the Taxiway. I was unaware that there was another opposite bound Aircraft, having thought only the Grumman was the traffic I should have been looking out for. Our quick taxi, and brief cross to the left, startled the opposing C172 traffic--who was instructed to taxi right side of XX, from XA, to FBO. This prompted them to alert Ground Control that we were too close and a possible collision existed. I applied brakes and moved further to the right of the Taxiway to make room for the opposing traffic and passed with normal intended separation.To avoid a recurrence of a similar situation, I believe it would be helpful to alert pilots of specific traffic when special bidirectional operations are in use on Taxiways. This will aid in helping pilots to stay more alert of specific traffic to be aware of. Also, skydiving operators should be advised to use caution when bidirectional taxiway operations are in effect. Ground Control holding conflicting traffic could also improve safety, by holding traffic at originating positions to allow for non-opposite direction use of the Taxiway with only one permitted on the Taxiway at a time.
ASRS:1827463.s: The pilot of Aircraft X and a C172 nearly collided while taxiing in opposing directions on Taxiway XX at ZZZ Airport. The incident occurred because the pilot crossed to the left side of the taxiway while taxiing nose-high and quickly, failing to see the opposing C172 until it was too close.

ASRS:1827469.n: I was working two sectors combined during a west flow. We were ILS XXR and visuals to Runway XY. I was trying to lay off of Runway XY because I just didn't have time to vector and hit the ghosts. I am already busy vectoring for space to [Runway] XXR and I had a couple that I was taking to Runway XY. Aircraft X popped up from ZZZ and I just didn't have a good way to take them to Runway XXR. I decided to assign them Runway XY. All my arrivals to XXR are already descended to 6,000 feet. Aircraft X came to me at 6,000 feet and I needed to get them under my ZZZ1 arrivals. I then descended Aircraft X to 5,000 feet and didn't see the traffic in front of them who ZZZ1 was working. By the the time I noticed it Aircraft X was already responding to an RA. After coming off of a COVID-19 reduced staffing schedule a lot of A siders are a little rusty in the radar room. I think that sectors should have been split.
ASRS:1827469.s: An air traffic controller managing combined sectors during a west flow descended Aircraft X to 5,000 feet without seeing preceding traffic, resulting in a resolution advisory. The controller attributed the incident to reduced staffing and rusty skills, suggesting sectors should have been split.

ASRS:1827473.n: Aircraft X was assigned the unadvertised XYL for arrival (advertised as a departure only runway) to accommodate for the required runway inspection by airport ops after this type of aircraft arrives or departs. It's easier to stop traffic and inspect the departure runway. Aircraft Y checked on 10 to 15 miles out and I cleared them to land and advised that traffic would Line Up and Wait/depart prior to their arrival. I was very focused on my sequence because we were in weather reroute program and there were numerous in-trail restrictions over most (all?) departure fixes. I got too focused on the departures and did not appropriately scan for the arrivals progress. When I instructed Aircraft Y to Line Up and Wait, Aircraft X advised that they were going around. I responded with a subsequent go around and maintain 3000 feet shortly after followed by a 300 heading after coordinating with Local Control. Aircraft Y crossed the Hold Short Lines but not the edge line. I will add a memory aid to my personal technique to prevent this from occurring again. I plan to use an empty strip holder to conservatively predict where the arrival will fit in with my departures. For example, if the arrival is 10 miles away I would put the blank strip 2 departures back and not depart beyond the blank strip without reassessing the situation. This will force me to periodically check on the progress of the arrival to my departure runway.
ASRS:1827473.s: An air traffic controller cleared Aircraft Y to land while managing departures of Aircraft X on an unadvertised arrival runway during weather reroutes. The controller failed to monitor the arrival's progress, causing Aircraft X to go around after Aircraft Y crossed the hold short lines.

ASRS:1827500.n: Aircraft X checked on approximately 30 [miles] north [of] CUL airport requesting to descend. Marginal VFR to IFR conditions in airspace. Attempted to request type approach and verification from pilot. Pilot advised they could not hear me and switched radios. The pilot switched but was broken and unreadable and when the pilot called back, I attempted to switch to standby transmitter but the pilot could only get me '2x5'. I told the aircraft to proceed direct the IAF for the RNAV 18 approach at CUL. The pilot responded 'proceeding direct HGOOD, cleared RNAV 18 approach.'
