I chose not to respond to the pilot as the pilot seemed to be having difficulty possibly with radios or navigation with the weather, so I chose not to reiterate 'cleared RNAV 18 approach'. Moments later I observed the aircraft at 2,000 feet level direct to the IAF (not on a published portion of the approach). The MVA in the area is 2,500. I then pulled the approach plate to verify the crossing altitude at the IAF (2,100 feet) and pulled up the VFR chart located above the position to verify obstructions in the area. There were no obstructions on the route of flight above 800 feet which the aircraft was more than 1,000 feet above. I chose not to climb the aircraft and accepted the altitude as variance of what I thought was an appropriate altitude considering the following: 7110.65 4-8-5 Specifying Altitude:'Specify in the approach clearance the altitude shown in the approach procedures when adherence to that altitude is required for separation. When vertical separation will be provided from other aircraft by pilot adherence to the prescribed maximum, minimum, or mandatory altitudes, the controller may omit specifying the altitude in the approach clearance.' Additionally, I was thinking of the example given in 4-8-1 for RNAV approaches of the 7110.65:'Aircraft 1 can be cleared direct to CENTR. The intercept angle at that IAF is 90 degrees or less. The minimum altitude for IFR operations (14 CFR, section 91.177) along the flight path to the IAF is 3,000 feet.'After the event a controller who had seen the altitude asked what was going on with the Aircraft X from earlier at 2000. I told him the situation and what I thought was an appropriate response. He told me that he does not believe that applied to this circumstance. I followed up with two additional more senior radar controllers who agreed that an altitude should be given but didn't know what 4-8-5 was in reference to. The next morning I asked a supervisor about the scenario and asked what 4-8-5 refers to, he showed me an approach plate for ORD with multiple crossing altitudes on the approach. I asked him how he knew that this is what that paragraph referred to and he just noted experience.I would recommend clarification of 4-8-5 in the 7110.65 to be more easily understood to which scenario this applies. Additionally, in the example given in 4-8-1 for RNAV application, the use of minimum IFR altitude is confusing as this altitude could be lower than an MVA for the area. I would change this to MVA, or DVA if applicable, to ensure better understanding that a lower MIA than MVA is not acceptable on an unpublished route.
ASRS:1827500.s: An air traffic controller cleared Aircraft X for an RNAV 18 approach at CUL despite poor radio contact, allowing the aircraft to level at 2,000 feet below the 2,500-foot MVA. The controller later questioned their decision not to specify a crossing altitude, citing confusion over 7110.65 regulations regarding minimum altitudes on unpublished routes.

ASRS:1827504.n: Aircraft X was given a descent to the Minimum Vectoring Altitude of 9,000 feet which he read back correctly. I observed him starting the descent and responded to another aircraft checking onto the frequency. The other aircraft failed check on properly so I had to query the check on information, issue a heading and an altitude to descend to. The other aircraft did not read back altitude or give a complete read back so I was in the process of getting him squared away. I then noticed Aircraft X was exiting the edge of the 9,000 foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude and descending through 8-something. He had obviously descended through the assigned altitude. He was already in the 7,000 foot (next) Minimum Vectoring Altitude so I issued a new altitude to maintain of 7,000 feet which he read back and complied with. [I recommend] proper staffing levels, [and a] standalone Supervisor in the TRACON. Had there been another set of eyes scanning as well this may have been avoided.
ASRS:1827504.s: An air traffic controller issued Aircraft X a descent to 9,000 feet but lost track of its progress while managing another aircraft's incomplete readback. The controller noticed Aircraft X had descended below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude and assigned a new altitude of 7,000 feet, attributing the incident to understaffing.

ASRS:1827510.n: We were working the Radar Assist position with training in progress. Runway 02 in use at GPI, skydiving was occurring at 58S. Aircraft Y departing on the SID climbing and making a left hand turn over 58S. Traffic advisories had been given most of the afternoon between Aircraft X and departures, also GPI Tower had been advised of skydiving operations. Aircraft X started descending down into GPI and presumably switched to advisories while Aircraft Y was climbing out of GPI. Traffic was called to Aircraft Y and then Aircraft Y responded to an RA. We recommend that jump operations be moved away from the arrival and departures procedures used at GPI. Until this is done we expect further incidences between jump aircraft and GPI departures and arrivals.
ASRS:1827510.s: Air traffic controllers managing Radar Assist at GPI reported a conflict between a departing aircraft climbing over skydiving operations and an arriving aircraft descending. The departing aircraft responded to a Resolution Advisory, prompting a recommendation to relocate jump operations away from arrival and departure procedures to prevent future incidents.

ASRS:1827517.n: We operated the ZZZ to ZZZ1 flight. The landing numbers were run for Runway XXL with the ATIS showing south winds at about 7 kts. and temperature about 90 degrees. Normal flaps 30 approach was flown and I used thrust reverser to about 100 kts. before getting on the brakes. Normal brake pressure was used and we took the high speed taxiway. Taxi time to the gate was about four minutes, and I released the parking brake once we were in the chocks.The Operations Agent came in and asked if we 'got on the brakes'. I said no and he said that our Company has blown about six plugs in the last couple weeks. I received a call from the Operations and was told what happened. I also called Maintenance and answered some questions regarding the flight. Everything on this flight was normal and I believe we did not brake the aircraft down more than a normal landing. We actually mentioned there was no reason to brake hard due to the three minute limitation on the MAX.Might consider leaving the gear down on such a short flight. Using the carbon brakes, it would be nice to have a temperature gauge for the brakes. Our first indication that there were any concerns was as the Operations Agent met us upon arrival in ZZZ. He asked if we had used heavy braking on landing because recently he had seen 6 events where the wheel fuse plugs had deflated the tires on this particular flight. The Captain immediately ensured that the parking brake had been released to allow for improved cooling. The oncoming FO (First Officer) met us after he completed his walk-around. He noted that the brakes seemed pretty warm. However, at this point the fuse plugs had not melted yet. We turned the aircraft over to the new crew and headed to the hotel. The Chief Pilot called the Captain at the hotel to inform him that the fuse plugs had melted and deflated the tires after we left. I do not believe the landing data indicated that brake cooling was required. Once at the hotel I tried to re-run the landing data to confirm that there wasn't a brake cooling message. There was not, as far as I could tell, but I could not recall the actual landing weights. I also tried to run the brake cooling module but couldn't get it to run because the release data had expired. This led me to go dig in the books for the brake cooling charts. I believe the brakes on speed was approximately 100 kts., because I remember seeing the runway exit coming and checking the speed as I felt the increased deceleration from the Captain applying the brakes. Using this and estimated landing conditions I used the Landing Data Charts in the MAX performance manual. This indicated that no special brake cooling procedures were required. However, I noted some interesting facts in this section of the airway manual: If we had used Autobrakes 3 and VRef 145, it puts a lot of additional energy in the brakes, requiring at least 40 minutes of cooling time, and possibly into the 'Caution' for hot brakes, depending on the landing data used. The cooling time chart seems to suggest that 7.3 minutes of cooling Inflight Gear Down is equivalent to 50 minutes of cooling on the ground. The text in that section states, 'Total energy is the sum of residual energy plus energy added.' This is important to note since the previous flights of this particular aircraft had landings at high elevations on high temperature days.
ASRS:1827517.s: The crew operated a MAX flight to ZZZ1, performing a normal landing with manual braking at 100 kts. Despite the pilot's belief that no special cooling was needed, the aircraft's wheel fuse plugs melted and deflated the tires after departure, likely due to residual heat from previous high-energy landings.

ASRS:1827555.n: While coming off A PREVIOUS flight I had flight ABC with 68 mins to load after I printed out the card. While working ABC the crew had 3 leads total. While loading the front another lead said I'm going to take care of the manual pit 51. I responded OK he continued to load the back. After completion of loading the cans, I tried closing the flight it wouldn't close so I went to the loading program. While at loading program, I still can't close the flight. I call load planner and we determine there isn't enough weight in pit 51 as I'm on the phone I noticed the plane went by and I called zone to let them know I need them to return to gate to add more weight. Apparently, they were calling me for weights on zone 1 but I was on channel X till the flight is closed out. I never authorized the plane to leave the gate. Also, when verifying the Hazmat, the scanner never showed pit 51 it showed the Hazmat in the forward cargo holds.
ASRS:1827555.s: A load planner reported that a flight departed the gate without authorization because the crew misinterpreted a Hazmat scanner error and failed to add required weight to pit 51. The departure occurred while the planner was on a different radio channel, preventing them from stopping the aircraft.

ASRS:1827568.n: Maintenance Control wanted this flight to completed. Name in Maintenance Control at Company told me that he can defer the engine inspection up to 25 flight hours after FOD is ingested. This might be true, but the bird that was sucked in was very large according to the crew that hit it. Airport Operations also told me they had been chasing a large bird before the bird strike. I feel that Maintenance Control would have sent this plane flying with passengers had the contract maintenance not have stood their ground. Name in Maintenance Control told me he has flown planes with bullet holes in the engines, and that he has handled FOD and bird strikes hundreds of thousands of times. I do not think that Maintenance Control erring on the side of caution, I believe that they would have sent this plane flying with passengers had the contract maintenance not stood their ground. The airplane is still out of service in ZZZ1 as of Date at XA:27, the event happened on Date1 at about XA:30.Bird strike during landing at ZZZ with reverse thrustMaintenance Control needs to consider the safety of the passengers, when FOD and bird strike are ingested into the engine. When Maintenance tells me that they can defer the inspection for 25 flight hours after a large bird has been ingested it concerns me. I fly these planes multiple times per week moving hundreds of passengers all over the country and it concerns me that they would delay the inspection and fly passengers on the airplane. I suggest that the Company start putting people first, this includes passengers and crew members.
ASRS:1827568.s: A pilot reported a large bird strike during landing at ZZZ1 with reverse thrust. Maintenance Control proposed deferring the engine inspection for 25 flight hours, but contract maintenance grounded the aircraft, which remains out of service.

ASRS:1827576.n: This report concerns the unscheduled separation of the #4 - outboard right main wheel - from the aircraft on takeoff from Runway XX in ZZZ. We began the trip receiving the aircraft from the previous crew at the gate in ZZZ1 one leg prior. There were no abnormalities on the pre-flight, no abnormalities that had not been cleared, and no major abnormalities of any kind recorded in the logbook or in the previous logbook that was in the can for the aircraft. The previous crew verbally told us that it was performing well when we received it from them. The first leg, ZZZ1 to ZZZ, operated smoothly with nothing out of the ordinary occurring. The post flight after that leg revealed no discrepancies of any kind. We pushed back from ZZZ, and our taxi route towards Runway XX included left- and right-hand turns as well as brake applications, and the aircraft continued to operate normally with no signs of any abnormality on the wheels.When we performed the takeoff, shortly after we selected the landing gear up, Tower called us and told us it looked like we lost a tire on the runway. The takeoff was so smooth that we weren't sure if we had in fact lost a tire as we had no indication in the cockpit of any system abnormalities, and the aircraft felt like it was operating normally. We knew there was construction around the runway in about the position we would have lifted off the ground at, so I thought that perhaps it was misidentified construction debris - although we hadn't seen any debris on the runway prior to takeoff. We asked them to perform a runway inspection to determine if it was our tire while we contacted Dispatch to obtain some identifying information about it, as well as to make a plan of action in case it was our tire. We contacted ZZZ Operations after some attempts, and asked them to remain at the airport to assist in identifying the tire and in case we needed to return to ZZZ.We decided not to relay to Dispatch through Operations because we initially had trouble reaching them and we believed that their Operations radio was a handheld and would not have good signal at altitude and location we would need to hold at. We decided to continue climb so that we could contact Dispatch through AIRINC. We discussed the possibility of flying by ZZZ Tower to have them identify if we were missing the tire and which one it was, but at that time we were still not sure that it was our tire and we were unsure if we would have enough fuel to do that and still proceed to ZZZ1 if that was what Dispatch wanted us to do. We made the judgement call that Dispatch would most likely have us continue to ZZZ1 due to the long runways, good emergency services, and having the finest Operations and Maintenance staff there to assist. We continued to climb along our filed route while ATC attempted to identify the tire. Shortly after that, we advised the Flight Attendant (FA) of the potential situation and that we were most likely continuing to ZZZ1, and we would wait to advise the passengers until we were sure and close to ZZZ1 to avoid panic. She said that she would take the time to review some information in her manuals. We chose to continue at a speed of long-range cruise or slower - 180 IAS being the safe speed used when structural damage is suspected - because we were unsure if there was debris on the wheel assembly that could become dislodged and damage something else, or if losing the tire had already damaged something.It took about 30 minutes to 45 minutes for us to make contact with Dispatch after that. We attempted AIRINC, Station Operations on 4 or 5 different local frequencies, relaying through company aircraft, or through another frequency. We attempted using different transmitters in case there was debris from the tire that had damaged an antenna. We were unsuccessful, so ATC attempted to call Dispatch. This took time because ATC was attempting to call using an old company number with an old area code. It was further delayed because we werebeing handed off to new controllers periodically and we had to apprise them each of the situation and have them attempt to make contact. ATC did make contact and Dispatch instructed us to continue towards ZZZ1. After that, we were advised that it was in fact our tire. We requested priority handling and continued to ZZZ1. After this determination, it took roughly 15 - 30 minutes longer for us to contact Dispatch on AIRINC.We had time with a low workload in cruise because we couldn't contact Dispatch through AIRINC yet, so we used the time to review our manuals and the QRH for the related procedures. In the QRH we decided that the Landing with Abnormal Landing Gear Procedure was the most applicable. We began to brief and discuss this procedure while trying to make contact with Dispatch through AIRINC. When we did make contact with Dispatch, [they] advised us that they thought it was the #1 wheel - the left main outboard. We told him that the procedure called to induce a fuel imbalance and to burn off as much fuel as possible before landing. We asked his opinion of going into holding on the way in to ZZZ1 to do so, and he agreed.After this determination was made, we said we would call back again and terminated the call because our radio transmitters made it very difficult to talk to ATC and Dispatch at the same time - there appeared to be interference or override between VHF 1 and 2. We began cross-feeding fuel to make the left side as light as possible and briefed the FA assuming that the #1 wheel was the one we had lost. We told the FA that there was a good chance that it would be a normal precautionary landing and that we would most likely come to a stop on the runway, or exit the runway if able, but most likely would not taxi to the gate. We decided to request for fire trucks, busses, a tug, and a GPU to be standing by. After we were done briefing the FA, we continued to discuss the procedure for approach and landing. The first step of the checklist was to notify the passengers, so we used some time to create an agreed-upon script to brief the passengers without inducing panic - which I would later administer when we were holding near ZZZ1. We noticed that this procedure appeared to be designed to cover both structural landing gear issues as well as tire and wheel problems. We were not sure if we had structural problems or not resulting from the loss of the wheel, so we briefed the procedure including several decision times - such as what we would do if the gear extended normally vs. if the gear did not extend normally vs. if we lost the hydraulic system when the gear was extended, etc. The result which did occur which we briefed was that the gear extended normally and the remaining tire, brakes, and steering operated normally for the landing.The decisions which we briefed involved in this were as follows. We left the GPWS switch in the on position because that switch's function is to silence alerts when the gear is not sensed down and locked. No fuel imbalance was established, and with our and Dispatch's agreement due to the relatively light weight of the aircraft, small practical difference the imbalance would make, and for ease of procedure application in the interest of safety. We did not pull the emergency gear extension lever due to the gear extending normally and indicating locked down by both indicating systems. Our understanding is that the emergency gear extension handle simply opens the uplock boxes, which had already been opened successfully, and that pulling the emergency gear extension handle could potentially impede us during egress if an evacuation was needed. We discussed at what time the bleeds should be selected off for approach. I had never selected the bleeds off in this aircraft in flight before, so the Captain and I had different opinions about when it should be done. We ended up selecting them off at 500 ft., which I now agree with in hindsight. The remaining items of the checklist would be completed after we were already on the ground. We briefed that we would complete these steps if there was some kind of fire, severe damage, or loss of control evident at touchdown, but we would otherwise move slowly and discuss these steps due to the potential hazards of aircraft control involved with performing them.While we were discussing this, Dispatch called on AIRINC again and corrected that we had actually lost the #4 - outboard right main wheel - rather than the #1 as said earlier. I asked him if he was sure and made sure that Maintenance had checked the serial numbers on the wheel to be positive. After Dispatch told us this we re-briefed the Flight Attendant for the #4 wheel.After we were all thoroughly briefed, we began our delay vectors around ZZZ1 to burn down to roughly 2000 lb. as instructed by Dispatch, I gave the PA to the passengers. When we had burned enough fuel, we began the ILS to Runway XYR - the longest and most familiar runway for us in ZZZ1. The gear extended normally and we saw no abnormal flight characteristics or any system abnormalities. On touchdown, as briefed, I began using the tiller to steer the aircraft early, and we felt it pulling slightly toward the right. However, not nearly enough to warrant the emergency engine shutdown. We were able to control the aircraft throughout the rollout to maintain centerline. We chose not to try to turn off the runway as it would be a left turn-off, which would put the most weight on the right side, and we were unsure of the quality of braking that we had. We used reverse only until we were at a slow walking speed and only then used brake application to bring the aircraft to a stop on the runway centerline abeam the XX taxiway exit where the firetrucks and Operations were waiting.Tower gave us the discrete frequency to use. The firetrucks came onto the runway and asked us to shut down the #2 engine so they could inspect. We complied and they said the remaining tire seemed to be in good condition and asked us if we wanted to exit. We said no, we would like to deplane the passengers and then be tugged. While Operations was setting up to deplane the passengers, we briefed how we would manage shutting down the #1 engine in order to deplane, and requested the GPU to be connected so we could deplane with lights on without killing the batteries. When the GPU was ready, we connected, Operations pinned all 3 gears, we shut down #1, checked the after-landing and -parking checklists, called the Flight Attendant, and then began deplaning to the busses. While the passengers were deplaning, Operations connected the tug. When the passengers were clear we prepared to sit in the cockpit while Operations tugged us to Gate XX. We monitored the tug process, arrived at the gate, and began conducting the postflight inspection and filling out the logbook. I completed the logbook while the Captain called the Chief Pilot to begin debriefing.I suggest that Station Operations be provided with better radio systems, or that the ACARS system be utilized in our aircraft. It was difficult for us to establish a reliable communication with Dispatch due to a combination of poor-quality radios and not many base stations being occupied due to the time of day. A communication with Dispatch was very necessary in order for Maintenance to verify which tire was missing so that we could adjust our procedures.
ASRS:1827576.s: The flight crew experienced an unscheduled separation of the #4 outboard right main wheel during takeoff from Runway XX in ZZZ, initially misidentified by Dispatch as the #1 wheel. The crew followed abnormal landing gear procedures, managed fuel and systems, and landed safely at ZZZ1 with normal gear extension and control.

ASRS:1827584.n: We were holding short of [Taxiway] 1 on Taxiway 2 at ZZZ. ATC cleared Aircraft Y into position and hold Runway XXL. In the meantime Aircraft Z was on short final to the same runway at approximately 1,500 ft. AGL (just a wag). Aircraft Y turned left on Taxiway 1 and crossed the hold lines for [Runway] XXL and continued till he came to a screeching stop as I assume he then saw the Aircraft Z coming down the ILS. Aircraft Y was well across the hold lines but had not crossed onto displaced threshold portion of the runway. ATC nor anybody else said anything. There was this weird silence, and without hearing anyone else saying anything I keyed the microphone and said 'Hey Aircraft Z go around;' and Aircraft Z immediately started a Go Around. Then finally ATC came on the radio and gave Aircraft Z, go around instructions, and told Aircraft Y that it'll be a few minutes for take off due to wake turbulence. Eventually Aircraft Y was cleared for take off and then we were cleared onto the runway. As we crossed the [Runway] XXL hold lines we saw fresh tire skid marks, approximately 20 ft. in length from Aircraft Y. Interesting thing is Aircraft Y never queried ATC during this event. We happened to have a jump seater commuting home and he provided me some data from the website Flight Aware. Flight Aware shows Aircraft Z at 475 ft. when they started to climb/Go Around, and ATC had previously cleared Aircraft Y to depart. On departure ATC said 'Sorry to Aircraft Z' and Aircraft Y acknowledged with 'Yeah we were confused.' I told/instructed Aircraft Z to 'go around;' after nobody else would say anything and the fact the two planes were on what appeared to be a collision course. It seemed as though ATC was unaware they had two planes going to the same runway.
ASRS:1827584.s: A pilot on Taxiway 2 at ZZZ observed Aircraft Y cross Runway XXL hold lines while Aircraft Z was on short final at approximately 1,500 ft AGL. The pilot instructed Aircraft Z to go around after ATC failed to intervene, revealing ATC was unaware both aircraft were cleared for the same runway.

ASRS:1827593.n: On the final phase of the Visual Approach, backed up by the ILS Runway XY to ZZZ, with the intention to capture the glide path from above, the Auto Pilot (AP) and Auto Throttles were disengaged. Prevailing conditions were Good Visibility and varying Tail Winds of up to nine (9) Knots. During the final portion of the descent to touchdown, with a visual transition to the PAPI reference already established (PAPI were showing 3 RED-1 WHITE), the Aircraft descended below the referenced visual glide path, with the tendency to fly over the Runway XY overrun area at an altitude (AGL) of less than 50 ft. The moment the Captain, having the Pilot Monitoring (PM) duties, mentioned his estimation for being low on the glide path, the aircraft was overflying a point short of the RWY by about 500 feet. He consecutively called for a Go Around, which was immediately executed by the PF (Pilot Flying). The Flight landed after a RADAR pattern on the same runway uneventfully.[The cause was] Human Factors / Pilot Flying error on visually estimating the projected Glide Slope to Runway XY, with the current Tail Wind conditions. Root cause is the initially higher angle of descent / rate of descent to capture the glide slope from above, that ended up to an over correction - reverse situation of flying finally lower than the projected/correct slope. [I suggest] earlier Aircraft configuration for the Final Approach Phase and timely request from the ATC for lower altitudes / earlier descent to the recommended altitudes that lead to a better projected sequence of flying tasks. FO was flying pilot. Performed visual approach and FO had a hard time trying to catch the glide slope from above because he was trying to slow down and put flaps down while on OPEN DESC. FO called for 'the bird', which caught me off guard because it is the first time anyone has asked for the flight path vector while trying to intercept the ILS and while disconnecting the AP. He not only disconnected AP but also eventually the auto thrust without previously briefing it. I told him to never disconnect the auto thrust again while trying to save a visual approach. Finally he was established on the ILS. Below 500 feet he said he was going to follow the PAPI. I glanced down at the VSI to make sure we were stable and when I looked backed up we had 4 red on the PAPIs and at the same time we received a GS GPWS warning. Became unstable. I loudly and sternly called 'unstable, go-around.' Performed go-around as RA called 50 feet. FO performed a soft go-around. I overrode his decision after he brought back TL (Thrust Lever) to CLB and I pushed TL to TOGA since we were in ZZZ (high airport elevation) with high OAT. I honestly could not tell you the altitude when the FO brought back the TL to CLB. I wanted to make sure we were safe since the go-around was performed at 50 feet from an unsafe position. At 50 feet RA, aircraft was not anywhere near the approach end of the runway. Came back for an uneventful landing.FO descended below glide slope and PAPI showed 4 red.Soft Go-around procedure should be changed or at least highlight the need to take into account airport elevation and OAT when deciding to make a soft go-around from a low altitude with an obvious performance deterioration.Soft Go-around procedure should be changed or at least highlight the need to take into account airport elevation and OAT when deciding to make a soft go-around from a low altitude with an obvious performance deterioration.
ASRS:1827593.s: During a visual approach with tailwinds, the First Officer descended below the glide path and PAPI reference, triggering a GPWS warning and an unstable call at 50 feet. The Captain executed a go-around due to the First Officer's visual estimation error and improper auto-throttle disconnection, followed by an uneventful landing.

ASRS:1827596.n: After takeoff at approximately 500 ft. AGL, we received an EGT (Exhaust Gas Temperature) Overtemp ECAM. We continued to thrust reduction altitude, requested priority handling, and followed the ECAM protocol which resulted in shutting down Engine #2. We completed all necessary tasks associated with an event of this nature and returned for an uneventful overweight landing at ZZZ.Contributing factors were a slight tailwind (new T/O data was obtained), heavy weight due to fuel tankering resulting in an APU bleeds on takeoff.Difficult to say, OAT was not excessive but perhaps there was an issue of some kind with the engine resulting in it exceeding EGT limits. Before departure at the gate, my Captain and I discussed possible threats prior to briefing. While the weather was nice, the two that came to mind were that while the ATIS reported wind as calm, it is not unusual to have a takeoff clearance with a tailwind, and secondly that if we had to return to field, we would be overweight for landing. As a matter of technique, I always load a return ILS into the longest runway at the departure airport in the secondary flight plan in case of a return to field, we discussed this and agreed it was a good idea.After discussing these threats, we noted that our Performance Data showed a TOGA takeoff, APU off. We requested a Performance Data with 5 kt. tailwind applied, which showed a TOGA takeoff, APU on. We entered the data for normal takeoff, but kept the we new Performance Data if needed.Upon switching to Tower upon approaching Runway XXC, we noted that the previous takeoff clearance included a tailwind. We entered the new data, ensured that flaps and APU were set appropriately, and verified that all were correct. Shortly after, we were given clearance to takeoff.The takeoff roll, takeoff, and initial climb were all normal. Somewhere around 500-800 ft., we heard the 'ding' from the ECAM. The Captain stated 'my aircraft', and after noting that it was not an quick action or ECAM exception, I noted it was simply an advisory ECAM with no actions, 'ENG 2 EGT High Temp'. I noted a temperature as high as 971. After thrust reduction, the ECAM then displayed the actions 'Thrust lever 2 ... idle, ENG Master 2 ... off'. We were now aware that we would be shutting down the number 2 engine. We requested priority handling and leveled at 4,000 ft. With the autopilot on, we changed controls so that I was the Pilot Flying, my Captain running the checklists, and we shut down the engine.With a maximum landing weight of 171,519 lbs., and we were over 188,000 lbs., we elected to slow the aircraft and deploy flaps in order to increase our fuel burn and get as light as we could before landing. My Captain completed all appropriate checklists while I coordinated with ATC. Reprogramming the MCDU for our return to field was now as simple as hitting Secondary Flight Plan and Activate Secondary. After all QRH checklists were complete and everyone was notified, my Captain asked me 'is there anything you can think of that we have missed?', which I answered, 'No, I cannot.' We concluded with our approach briefing, with emphases on single engine and overweight procedures, completed the descent checklist, and got vectors to final. The Captain resumed control of the aircraft for approach and landing.Approach and landing were uneventful, landing at a weight of 184,400 lbs., approximately 157 kts., and 100 FPM descent rate or less. We came to a stop on the runway for inspection from ARFF (Airport Rescue Fire Fighting), and we immediately turned on the brake fans and monitored brake temperatures. ARFF did not note any high temperatures or leaks. We then taxied to Gate XX with ARFF following us.The takeoff clearance with a tailwind made us change from TOGA, APU off, to TOGA, APU on takeoff. This change in takeoff thrust may have been enough for the engine to overtemp shortly after takeoff. A takeoff clearance with a headwind would have been a lower thrust takeoff. In our case, the Performance Data even indicated that [Runway] XXC would have been a reduced thrust takeoff.ZZZ airport needs to be better about airport operation being in line with wind direction in order to minimize the frequency of tailwind takeoff and landing clearances.
ASRS:1827596.s: The flight crew experienced an Engine 2 EGT overtemp shortly after takeoff, likely caused by a tailwind requiring APU bleed use and higher thrust. They shut down the engine, burned fuel to reduce weight, and completed an uneventful overweight landing at ZZZ.

ASRS:1827609.n: GPS jamming over Russia beginning at waypoint LOGMU, FL 340 w/associated alternating ADS-B, l and R alerts. Jamming continued to waypoint NIBIM when unable RNP alert received. Jamming continued to waypoint UBONA, FL 340, when alerts cleared and GPS reception returned to normal operation. Max ANP indication 5.0. Additional alerts received were runway sys, GPS, terr pos, and ADS-B out R. All QRH checklists were accomplished for each alert with no resolution. Aircraft remained in VHF radio contact with Moscow control during entire event. Aircraft position verified on-course with Moscow at each waypoint on flight plan until jamming ceased and GPS updating returned to normal.
ASRS:1827609.s: The flight crew experienced GPS jamming and multiple alerts between waypoints LOGMU and UBONA at FL 340 over Russia, causing an RNP alert. Despite completing QRH checklists, the issue resolved only when GPS reception returned to normal while maintaining VHF contact with Moscow control.

ASRS:1827613.n: We received GPS jamming at FL370 around LAKTO.
ASRS:1827613.s: The crew experienced GPS jamming at FL370 near LAKTO. The report does not specify the aircraft type, phase of flight, or the cause and outcome of the interference.

ASRS:1827640.n: Arriving SEA, ATC cleared us to follow aircraft ahead to visual approach 34L. We were given 170kts to final fix due to ATC spacing us just over 3 miles behind a B737. I was Pilot Monitoring, the First Officer the Pilot Flying had our plane on autopilot using heading select and vertical speed to navigate onto the localizer and glideslope.Just as the plane was joining the localizer, a mild buffeting was felt followed by a rapid roll in direction of the turn. Aural warning 'Bank Angle' annunciated. The First Officer immediately disconnected the autopilot and reduced the bank angle to normal parameters. The rest of the approach was uneventful.On visual approaches, especially with close spacing, fly above the path of the preceding aircraft. While on dogleg to final for RWY 34L, descending to 2,400 feet MSL following preceding B737 by 3.5 NM encountered wake turbulence while on autopilot. As autopilot initiated turn to join the localizer the aircraft encountered the wake turbulence causing a rapid roll to the right (in the direction of the turn). The aircraft rolled past 30 degrees of bank and an aural warning 'bank angle' sounded. The Pilot Flying recognized the excursion and disengaged the autopilot and reduced the bank angle to normal range. Pilot Flying continued the approach and landed uneventfully.Consider staying above preceding aircraft's altitude/flight path to avoid wake turbulence or increase range between aircraft.
ASRS:1827640.s: During a visual approach to SEA RWY 34L, the crew encountered wake turbulence from a preceding B737 while on autopilot at 2,400 feet MSL. The resulting rapid roll triggered a bank angle warning, but the Pilot Flying disengaged the autopilot, corrected the attitude, and landed uneventfully.

ASRS:1827641.n: On Runway XX approach into ZZZ, I attempted to lower the gear by placing the landing gear handle down to extend the gear. During the extension process, both main gear green lights came on but neither the red or green light came on for the nose gear. I told ZZZ Tower that I needed to go around due to a system malfunction. After completing the go around, I followed the QRH procedures. The QRH procedures did not correct the unsafe nose gear condition. I then asked for priority handling and I contacted Tower for permission for a low pass to have them see if they could confirm the status of the nose gear. They said it appeared like all my gear was down, but they were not certain as it was night and it was difficult for them to have good visibility of the nose gear. After the low pass, I went back through the QRH checklists again to try to correct the condition. Once it was determined the nose gear would remain in an unsafe condition, I prepared for a potential nose gear up landing. At that time, I took the time to brief the Jump Seater and we reviewed the egress checklist. Since the Jump Seater was an experienced pilot, I handed the egress checklist to the Jump Seater and had him read through it. We discussed egress options in the event I became incapacitated. We briefed the scenario several times to ensure we had a clear understanding of what to expect and what actions we may need to take. After all appropriate checklists were ran and briefed and the approach reviewed and briefed, I elected at that point to land. I flew the ILS for Runway XX. I followed QRH guidance to land on the mains and hold the nose off the runway while gently lowering it as appropriate. In accordance with the procedures, I pulled the stop and feather pressed the stop button and turned the fuel and hydraulics off. After safely coming to a stop on the runway center line, I asked the Jump Seater if he was ok or if he was injured he said he was not injured and was safe. I assessed myself and reported to ATC that we were both safe. I completed the remaining items of the egress checklist and we exited the aircraft.Nose wheel door failure.Run the checklists, keep the Jump Seater informed and remain calm.Metro nose gear door inspections more often.
ASRS:1827641.s: The pilot experienced a nose gear door failure during approach to Runway XX, resulting in an unsafe gear indication and a go-around. After unsuccessful QRH attempts and a low pass, the crew executed a safe nose-up landing and egressed without injury.

ASRS:1827657.n: Thunderstorms were quickly approaching XXL final approach course upon our arrival at ZZZ. ATC provided significant vectoring and cleared us for visual XXL during base leg of approach. Base leg was squared off toward final approach fix due to approaching weather. During turn to final approach course, pilot flying went below GS (Glide Slope). Tower issued low altitude warning. Pilot initiated corrective action. Aircraft Landed uneventfully.
ASRS:1827657.s: The pilot flying descended below the glide slope while turning to the final approach course at ZZZ due to thunderstorm vectoring. Tower issued a low altitude warning, the pilot corrected, and the aircraft landed uneventfully.

ASRS:1827661.n: We flew four legs in the B737 MAX over a two day period. We found the runway proximity alert system (whatever it is called) [Runway Awareness and Advisory System, RAAS] to be an amusing distraction at times, but a safety hazard at other times. At the same time that crews are likely to receive takeoff clearance with altitudes, headings, and frequencies there is a loud runway alert system talking over ATC and cockpit communications. It is a real problem that needs to be looked at.
ASRS:1827661.s: B737 MAX crews reported that the Runway Awareness and Advisory System (RAAS) created a safety hazard by loudly interrupting ATC communications during takeoff clearance. The alert system distracted crews by talking over critical altitude, heading, and frequency instructions.

ASRS:1827696.n: TOGA APU bleed on config 2. Cleared for takeoff, at about power stable and 1.5 EPR Engine 2 FAIL message (no fire indication) and single chime. Notified ATC of reject and needed to clear runway. Started ECAM procedures, at the same time another airline notified us over air that we had a fire on our number 2 engine. We then proceeded to extinguish fire with push button and squib. After finishing up procedure and coordination with CFR to make sure no fire was present we set up to be towed back to gate with no further incident.Apparently, Airbus is having issues with this config for takeoff. TOGA APU bleed on.Coordination with Airbus on reliable and safe max effort takeoff configurations. Day 3 of a 3-day, early departure, last leg home. Gate XXX, short taxi to runway XXR. Allowed the engines to warm up for three minutes while on the ramp to get the five minutes required before takeoff. Winds were reported 280 degrees to approx 300 degrees. From previous experiences from flying the Airbus in and out of ZZZ, the winds can switch to a tailwind component very quickly when they use runway XXL/R for departure, so I expected a potential tailwind.We were cleared to line up and wait on runway XXR. The aircraft was lined up with the center line and the parking break was set. Control was then given to the FO as we awaited takeoff clearance. Once it was received and we read it back, we immediately experienced a single chime, which normally would indicate that perhaps the airplane was not configured for takeoff. Upon looking at the ECAM, we had an ENG 2 FAIL ECAM alert. Normally when we encounter ENG FAILs in the simulator, we are presented with a master warning and three chimes. This was a singular chime. I immediately told the FO we needed to clear the runway as there was a 90 degree taxiway (1) on the right side of the runway just 50 yards or so from us. FO advised tower we needed to clear for a warning.At this point I initially thought this might be a false warning. There was definitely a surprise factor to all of this. As we were clearing the runway (right turn) at taxiway 1, I glanced at the EGT and it was red. At the same time, another airplane that was getting ready to take the active runway said he saw fire coming out of out right engine. I stopped the aircraft on taxiway 1. I had the FO call for the CFR vehicles. The FO wanted to run the ECAM procedure, but I had him check the Quick Reference Card first as I remembered there was either a quick action or ECAM exception procedure that needed to be run prior to executing the ECAM procedure. The FO started to look that up... I called back to the cabin and asked the flight attendants to check to see if there was any smoke in the cabin or any sign of fire coming from the engine. The answer was that there was no evidence of fire or smoke, from the #3 or #4 FA. When I returned to the FO, he said the QRC procedure he found was for an ENG FIRE on the ground. After considering a possible evacuation, my focus shifted to getting the engine shut down. Since we had no indication of a fire from the cockpit (other than high EGT) nor any evidence from the cabin, we ran the ECAM ENG FAIL procedure and elected to discharge a fire bottle into the #2 engine. I made a PA to the passengers telling them we exited the runway due to an alert we received in the cockpit and to expect some emergency vehicles come around the aircraft. The fire trucks were not present at this point, so we asked the other airplane if they could see any evidence of fire. They couldn't see from their vantage point, so I taxied the aircraft South on taxiway 2 to taxiway 3 (50 yards?) to see if they could see any evidence of continued fire. They still could not see, so I stopped the aircraft at taxiway 3 and waited for CFR to show up. No fire indications in the cockpit, such as aural fire warning or ENG FIRE ECAM, other than the excessive EGT with the ENG FAIL ECAM.Once CFR arrived, communications were hampered as they were not on a dedicated frequency yet. I queried the tower and they gave us the right frequency to be on, when they arrived. CFR scanned the aircraft and did not find any hot spots. At this point, we had finished the ECAM procedure and were looking for any follow-up procedures (which is the next step in Airbus, non-normal methodology). The FO couldn't find them. They used to be in the QRH and were on [specific] paper... easy to find. Since a previous, major QRH revision, they are no longer on [specific] pages but are found within the QRH itself. I told the FO not to worry about finding them... that much of the material was not going to be applicable. I redirected our focus back to the STATUS page so we could discuss the current situation of the airplane. The big thing was that we had no nose wheel steering, so we summoned ops to get us a tug and advised CFR to follow us under tow. It took an inordinate amount of time to get a tug out to us (maybe 30 minutes or more), but seemed like hours. Made several PA's explaining that we were still waiting on our tug.Eventually towed back to the gate. Maintenance met the aircraft and asked about EGTs, duration, and the fire bottle status. I told them I remembered seeing an EGT of 669 at some point... maybe for 30 to 60 seconds. AML entry was made indicating all of this.When all of this was occurring during a short amount of time, I originally thought that maybe this was a false alert (only a single chime). After exiting the runway and realizing the extent of the emergency, I thought that perhaps we had the presence of flames due to a compressor stall, exacerbated by a wind that may have shifted to a tailwind.After returning to the gate, I was in contact with the Fleet Captain... who asked if the APU was ON for takeoff. I replied that it was. In Airbus world, you can do a Max power takeoff and run the packs from the APU, freeing-up the engines, giving you a little more power for takeoff. That was the case this morning. The Fleet Captain indicated that the ENG FAIL ECAM was caused by having the APU bleed ON. Apparently, this causes back pressure on the engine bleed and is a known issue. Tech Ops is increasing ground idle to prevent thisAfter speaking to the Fleet Captain, he mentioned that the QRC procedure (requiring completion before doing the ECAM alert) entitled ENG FIRE on GROUND is a procedure used when there is no electrical power to the aircraft. It is a procedure that is to be used in that situation. Perhaps I misunderstood him as our conversation occurred after the adrenaline started settling down a bit, but maybe it needs to be explained to the flight crews (the correct use of that particular QRC procedure).Also, the FO had difficulty in finding the ECAM follow-up procedures, to the point where I said we need to move to the final step of assessing the STATUS (page) of the airplane.Finally, communication from the tower on how to communicate with CFR/ARFF when they arrived could, be improved upon. In retrospect though, we never said the word 'emergency' to them. My instructions to the FO were to get the trucks rolling now... not very clear perhaps and maybe was a factor in the initial comm problems with CFR.Advised the Duty Chief that we were done flying for the day. The adrenal rush was subsiding and he was very helpful in accomplishing that for us.
ASRS:1827696.s: The flight crew rejected takeoff on an Airbus due to an Engine 2 FAIL alert caused by APU bleed configuration, which created back pressure. After another aircraft reported fire, the crew discharged a fire bottle, confirmed no fire with CFR, and was towed back to the gate.

ASRS:1827710.n: HP bleed valve would not open after start, refused aircraft after MEL'd and known and forecast icing conditions.
ASRS:1827710.s: The pilot refused the aircraft after the HP bleed valve failed to open following engine start. This decision was made due to known and forecast icing conditions, which rendered the aircraft unairworthy under the Minimum Equipment List.

ASRS:1827759.n: Upon configuring flaps from 25 to 30, Trailing Edge Flaps indicated a split and stopped tracking at 27 degrees. LE FLAPS TRANSIT light was also illuminated (amber light). A go-around was accomplished to enable time for non normal checklists to be run. LEADING EDGE FLAPS TRANSIT checklist was run which led us into TRAILING EDGE FLAPS DISAGREE checklist. Flaps were left at 27 degrees with flap handle at 25 setting. Vref15 +5 was the approach speed selected and an uneventful landing and taxi to the gate was accomplished. On Final Approach to XXL in ZZZ and configuring from flaps 25 to flaps 30 at about 1,500 feet the trailing edge flap needle indicators displayed a split and the flaps stopped at approximately 27 degrees. The LE FLAP TRANSIT light was also illuminated. After taking a few seconds to realize what was happening and coming through approximately 1,000 ft the Captain called for a go around. I executed the go around, however upon attempting to retract the flaps we realized they were stuck at 27 degrees and would not retract at all. I continued to fly the plane and the Captain advised ATC and then ran the non-normal LEADING EDGE FLAP TRANSIT QRH followed by the TRAILING EDGE FLAP DISAGREE QRH. We received vectors from ATC and took our time setting up for a flaps 27 landing using the VREF15+5 knot wind additive. While being vectored back to the final approach course the Captain TEST and the FA's and made an announcement to the PAX. We landed and taxied to the gate uneventfully.
ASRS:1827759.s: During final approach to XXL at 1,500 feet, the crew executed a go-around after trailing edge flaps split and stopped at 27 degrees with an illuminated LE FLAP TRANSIT light. Following QRH checklists, the aircraft landed uneventfully with flaps fixed at 27 degrees using Vref15+5.

ASRS:1827797.n: Flight planning, preflight, ground operations, and takeoff were accomplished per SOP and were uneventful. Captain was pilot flying. Passing 18000 STD, altimeter was selected and AP 1 was selected. At XA:17, we got a master caution light, with HYD G RSVR LO LVL, HYD G ENG 1 PUMP LO PR, and HYD G SYS LO PR displayed on the upper ECAM. After confirming no Green Hydraulic QTY, I asked the FO (First Officer) to request to stop climb and return to field. Captain continued to fly and handle radios. FO accomplished the ECAM procedures, turning off the PTU and Green Eng 1 Pump. QRH was referenced after ECAMs completed, screens normal.We requested priority handling with ATC. Advised Dispatch through ACARS that we had lost all Green Hydraulic QTY, were returning to ZZZ, and would require a tow off runway due to loss of nosewheel steering. Purser was advised of the malfunction, that we were returning to field in 20 minutes, and a cabin prep was not required. A visual approach to XXL was briefed after runway assignment and the descent checklist was accomplished. Aircraft was configured early due to slow flaps/slats and alternate gravity gear extension. Approach and landing were accomplished per SOP and were uneventful. Aircraft was stopped straight ahead on centerline. Engines shut down with timing after starting APU. Aircraft was inspected by Fire Response Team, confirming gear doors down and fluid [was] leaking from under plane behind gear. Super tug arrived and towed us clear of runway to Gate XXX. On climbout passing approximately 21,000 feet, we got an ECAM indicating loss of the green system, LO G Press, and another green system ECAM but I cannot recall it now. We ran the ECAM action items which had us turn off the PTU and Eng 1 G pump. As soon as the ECAM action items were complete, we communicated with ATC, advising them we needed to stop our climb, and requested priority handling and requested a return to ZZZ. The CA (Captain) and I split up the flying and comm duties, he advised the FA's (Flight Attendant) of our situation, and sent a message to Dispatch. I talked to ATC and flew the aircraft for a brief time while he handled the message to Dispatch.We got the expanded checklist and discussed the effects of [a] loss of the green system in terms of manual cranking of the gear and needing to stop on the runway due to loss of steering, which the CA sent an ACARs to the station to start working on a tow for us to minimize us sitting on the runway. I also advised ATC to let ZZZ know we would be a full-stop on the runway and would need to be towed. We were given priority handling back to ZZZ and we briefed the approach and threats of a go-around since the gear could not be retracted once it was hand-cranked down. The CA flew the approach XXL and the landing and stopping at the end of the runway was uneventful. We dropped the landing gear pins to the tug team and got towed back to the gate. We debriefed once we were off the aircraft and the passengers disembarked. The CA was cool, calm, and collected and flew a textbook approach. We worked well together as a team, I can't think of much that we could have done to improve on how the situation was handled.
ASRS:1827797.s: The crew experienced a total loss of Green Hydraulic quantity at 21,000 feet, causing slow flap/slat operation and loss of nosewheel steering. They returned to ZZZ for an uneventful landing with alternate gravity gear extension and were subsequently towed off the runway.

ASRS:1827811.n: We were flying from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I was sitting in the right seat doing LCP (Line Check Pilot) training. Mr. A was in the left seat doing CP (Check Pilot) training. The captains side airspeed and altitude became unreliable. We transferred controls to the first officers side. Mr. A ran the QRH. The captains airspeed read 123 knots and we went down 500 feet. There was a 500 ft difference between the captains and FO's [First Officer] altitude. SPS (Shaker and Pusher System) Advance was displayed on the EICAS. The FO's airspeed was at 270. We descended immediately to FL240. While in the descent we were given an altitude to descend to of FL220. We continued to ZZZ1 without incident. We elected to continue to ZZZ1 due to all the weather in the area. Around FL220 the captains airspeed seemed to return to match the FO's side. I still continued to fly and still proceeded as if the airspeed was unreliable. We landed with out incident .
ASRS:1827811.s: During LCP training on a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1, the captain's airspeed and altitude became unreliable, triggering an SPS Advance warning and a 500-foot altitude discrepancy. The crew transferred controls to the first officer, descended to FL220, and landed safely after the captain's instruments appeared to normalize.

ASRS:1827813.n: At FL329, Captain's airspeed indicator dropped from approximately 280kts to 115kts and altimeter stopped indicating. Controls transferred to FO (First Officer) side, QRH was completed and performance tables referenced. Momentary altitude deviation. ATC alerted. Landed normally and contacted Dispatch and Maintenance. Cruising at FL 320 PF (Pilot Flying) (Captain in training) noticed airspeed slowly bleeding off then rapidly bled off. Upon getting IAS comparator flags PF called for PM (Pilot Monitoring) to get out unreliable airspeed QRH. Airplane started pitching up and looking down noticed ALT comparator flag as well on PF side. Transferred controls of the plane to PM noticing his side appeared to be working fine. Notified ATC of unreliable airspeed and altitude deviation. Requested descent to get out of clouds. ATC told us to descend FL 220. Jumpseat pilot had unreliable QRH pulled up on tablet and handed it to upgrade training CA (now PM) to run checklist. Descended down to FL 220 and just before reaching altitude airspeed and altitude came back on CA side. LCP (Line Check Pilot) in FO seat continued to fly and landed without incident.
ASRS:1827813.s: A Captain in training and Line Check Pilot experienced unreliable airspeed and altitude indications at FL320, causing a momentary deviation. After transferring controls and descending to FL220 per ATC clearance, instruments recovered, and the aircraft landed normally.

ASRS:1827823.n: After takeoff, passing approximately 2,000 feet MSL, the First Observer noticed a status message and a momentary Bleed 2 EICAS message. Upon review of the bleed control panel, he noted #1, #2, and #4 bleed off lights were illuminated with the bleed switches selected open. He quickly looked at the synoptic page and verified #1, #2, and #4 bleed valves were closed. I directed a climb to 10,000 feet to get above most VFR GA aircraft, and we leveled at 10,000 feet to begin assessing the situation. Radios were transferred to the Pilot Flying from the right seat and the First Observer, Second Observer, and I began to assess the situation.We observed the following Status MessagesENG 3 FIRE LP BBLEED OVPRESS 2BLEED PRV ENG 3There were no EICAS messages present.ECS (Environmental Control System) Synoptic was reviewed and we confirmed that only the #3 Bleed Valve was open.To assist ATC, we climbed to FL180 and leveled off, continuing to assess and evaluate the situation. We elected to cycle each malfunctioning bleed valve independently, but the #1, #2 and #4 valves remained closed. We did not cycle the #3 valve as it was the only source of air available to the aircraft.I initiated a conference call with Dispatch and Maintenance Control. The decision was made to return to ZZZ. Since we would be overweight I asked Dispatch if they wanted us to dump fuel, or burn it off. I was given approval for either choice.The crew agreed the best course of action was to return to ZZZ and burn down to the maximum normal landing weight by creating excessive drag. We held at low altitude for approximately 15 minutes to burn down to normal landing weight, uneventfully landing on XXC with flaps 30 and Autobrakes 3.It should be noted that during the descent, and any time engine thrust was reduced, the #1, #2, and #4 Bleed Valves opened and operated normally. The malfunction re-manifested itself anytime thrust levers were advanced.Our collective assessment was the #3 PRV had failed creating a manifold over pressure situation. However, we did not conduct any inflight trouble shooting of the #3 Bleed Valve to preclude compounding the loss of three bleed systems and the potential to lose all bleed air on the aircraft.ATC Controllers provided excellent assistance throughout the malfunction.
ASRS:1827823.s: The crew experienced a bleed system malfunction shortly after takeoff, causing valves 1, 2, and 4 to close due to suspected #3 PRV failure. They returned to ZZZ, burned fuel to reduce weight, and landed uneventfully after ATC assistance.

ASRS:1827829.n: Overloaded TakeoffPush back, engine start, fuel indications all normal. Initial taxi took additional power to move aircraft, which is unusual in a B777-200 at typical [long distance] weights. On takeoff roll, initial acceleration was sluggish even though we were TO2 max, the takeoff roll seemed longer than normal and climbout was less than usual. We were filed for initial cruise FL350, but given option of FL370 as FL350 taken, so we climbed FL370 (FMC said Max FL391). Upon level off at FL370, aircraft struggled to maintain normal cruise Mach speed .83, and I noticed amber hook was seemingly higher than normal (about 245 kts).Shortly after level off, EICAS caution 'FUEL DISAGREE'. Followed Emergency Check List and Progress Page 2 indicated totalizer about 10,000 lbs. higher than calculated. Determined no fuel leak, and followed up with QRH review of ETOPS failures, selected fuel probes synoptic display from maintenance section in FMC, and noticed many center tank fuel probes inoperative. We called Dispatch/Maintenance conference call on satcom and sent fuel maintenance display to them, all three parties agreed no fuel leak, use calculated fuel, determined it was appropriate to continue flight.We started to burn substantially above plan, and we started to suspect we were heavier than closeout. We referred to performance manual cruise pages, 1.3g maneuver data, and .84 cruise data, and our suspicions were confirmed: amber hook was indicating maneuvering speeds for approximately 50,000 lbs. heavier aircraft, also fuel flow predictions the same.We called Dispatch and Duty Pilot, asked them to contact ZZZ Station Personnel to obtain FUEL UPLIFT in gallons from fuel company. Prior procedures required us to check this information from the fuel slip. It would have caught this serious error. Initially fuel company kept sending info strictly off our aircraft gauges, but we explained to Dispatch this was not correct, due to inoperative center fuel probes, and we strongly suspected fueler had overfilled the amount required for the flight to ZZZ1.After an hour or so, Dispatch confirmed that we were approximately 50,000 lbs. (7500 gallons) heavier than planned.Our performance data/climb, cruise, descent, and landing data were invalid. The flight crew, not knowing this situation at the time of departure, could have encountered serious consequences, if an emergency such as engine failure occurred the crew may not have acted appropriately because of the unknown situation. implications for engine failure at V1 on takeoff, implications for stopping on wet runway from V1, implications for enroute engine out performance and drift down, implications for correct Vref in ZZZ1.This is an extremely serious incident in my opinion, possibly could have been caught with a simple fuel slip check.Inexperienced fuelers, lack of back up checks by the pilots, cross checking required fuel vs actual loaded fuel, possible fuel sensor failuresRecommend having someone in the crew cross check the fuel slip provided by the fueler against the master flight plan. We used to check this information from the fuel slip, it would have caught this serious error. Initially fuel company kept sending info strictly off our aircraft gauges, but I explained to Dispatch that was no good due to inoperative center probes, and I strongly suspected fueler had overshot the mark substantially and not checked uplift gallons from bowser.After an hour or so, Dispatch confirmation came through: 50,000 lbs. (7500 gallons) extra fuel had been loaded by accident.Our performance data was invalid, we were going to be just barely under max landing weight in ZZZ1, implications for engine failure at V1 on takeoff, implications for stopping on wet runway from V1, implications for enroute engine out performance and drift down, implications for correct Vref in ZZZ1.We prepared for the landing in ZZZ1 using max landing weight assumption for Vref and distance calculation. The difference in Vref for FMC calc weight and max wt was nearly 10 kts., and at the higher speed green AOA band was correct. Landed normally.This is an extremely serious incident in my opinion, possibly could have been caught with a simple fuel slip check.Lack of due care by fueler combined with fuel probe failure. Lack of fuel slip check in procedures.Recommend a fuel slip check prior to departure by crew.
ASRS:1827829.s: The flight crew of a Boeing 777-200 discovered an accidental 50,000 lb fuel overload caused by a fueler error and inoperative center tank probes. This invalid performance data resulted in sluggish acceleration and climb, though the crew adjusted speeds and landed safely after confirming the excess fuel.

ASRS:1827915.n: Getting a lot more non-compliance of mask wearing. I am sure it is due to CDC uncertainty and vaccinations. We (the flight crews) need clear procedures on how to move forward with the new Delta Variant, vaccines, and the federal mask mandate. Every flight is a struggle.
ASRS:1827915.s: Flight crews reported increasing passenger non-compliance with mask mandates, attributing it to CDC uncertainty and vaccination status. They requested clear procedures regarding the Delta variant and federal mandates, describing every flight as a struggle.

ASRS:1827947.n: Flight Attendant 4 boarded and almost immediately smelled a burning electrical smell, when Flight Attendants 1;2;3 came aboard they confirmed smell and we notified First Officer who confirmed he smelled it too and went down to tarmac to check unit. Captain also smelled and called Maintenance. We were advised to leave aircraft and wait on jet bridge. Name came and confirmed she smelled it too, she contacted Operations and they advised us to go to [the] clinic, after we asked several times, if they would be able to do the necessary tests for fume events, they reassured us it was the right place to go. we were unsuccessful in reaching [the] SAFETY line till after we had been at clinic for more than an hour already. SAFETY advised us we needed to go to ER not clinic. We then took a ride to ER. The First Officer was professional and helpful, the Captain unprofessionally dismissed us. Fume events need to be taken seriously and all stations and bases should have strict protocols on hand to deal with them. They need to be aware of where to send crews for correct testing as it is time sensitive.
ASRS:1827947.s: Flight attendants, the First Officer, and Captain detected a burning electrical smell upon boarding, prompting a maintenance check and crew evacuation. Operations initially directed the crew to a clinic, but Safety later advised an ER visit after a delay, while the Captain was criticized for dismissing the fume event.

ASRS:1827953.n: We are currently assigned to the tire shop in ZZZ by bid. We were instructed by previous tire shop techs of the current procedures and practices. We questioned a few of the issues of different part numbers and CMM (Component Maintenance Manual). We were told to follow the work card and that they have already addressed the procedures with engineering and all was okay. We then, to this day, were building both wheel assemblies as status quo. We continued down that path calling other company for build numbers, built and shipped wheels according to their directions. We received wheels on DATE. After reviewing accompanying paper work noticed the amount of work that was performed on one of the wheel assemblies and the references. [It was] noticed the CMM reference on paperwork was different to the reference on the work card that we follow. Work card only calls out for CMM XX-XX-XX. We tried looking up the references for XX-XX-XY in the CMM. Unable to find reference we reached out to engineering for assistance. Proceeded to ask if we could get an ECRA (Engineering Change Request Authorization) or if work card could be modified to reflect both CMM references. We were advised by engineering to send wheels with certain part number X back to the vendor for service. As soon as we received engineering response we immediately went to the aircraft assigned to ZZZ and physically checked for wheels that were built by X tire shop with specific MFR part number and had them replaced. All wheels have been removed from our ZZZ fleet and serviceable ready line and will be sent back to vendor for overhaul. We are currently assigned to the tire shop in ZZZ by bid. ASRS:1827953.s: Tire shop mechanics in ZZZ discovered a discrepancy between work card and CMM references for wheel assemblies built by vendor X. Engineering advised returning the wheels, prompting the crew to immediately remove and replace all affected wheels from the ZZZ fleet and serviceable line.

ASRS:1827954.n: I completed my service check with all tires at normal press. at around XA00. Sometime around XA42 when the aircraft was released, The Pilot thought the #1 MLG tire press. looked low. upon checking the tire press. It was found to be 8 PSI below normal at 217 PSI. The corrective measure is to re-inflate and check in 24 hours. The aircraft departed late because of this incident. This seems to be a common occurrence with the 737 MAX aircraft, on regular basis often requiring replacement of the tire and sometimes the opposite tire.
ASRS:1827954.s: A mechanic reported that after release, the pilot found the #1 main landing gear tire on a 737 MAX at 217 PSI, 8 PSI below normal. The aircraft departed late after re-inflation, with the reporter noting this is a common occurrence often requiring tire replacement.

ASRS:1827956.n: During the track and balance of A/C S/N XXXX, there were issues getting the blades to fly together, blade swapping took place as well as blade replacements. I was doing the paperwork portion and trusted that the information given to me was correct. When I was told which S/N's were swapped and which were replaced. Logbook entries were made and signed off reflecting those actions. Fast forward a few weeks I was sent an RO (Repair Order) to get unserviceable blades sent out for repair. I printed out the RO's placed them in the blade boxes and got the blades sent out. Nowhere in this process did I physically check the S/N's of the blades. I trusted the mechanics to give me the correct information which was a huge mistake and I should have physically verified the P/N's and S/N's as outlined in our procedures. This is the end of my statement.Do not rely on others to verify P/N's S/N's. Physically Verify P/N's and S/N's. Double-check other mechanic work to ensure completeness and that what was said was done was actually done. Follow published guidance, policies, and procedures.
ASRS:1827956.s: A mechanic performing track and balance on aircraft S/N XXXX failed to physically verify blade part and serial numbers during swapping and replacement. Relying on incorrect information from other mechanics led to unserviceable blades being sent for repair, highlighting the need to follow procedures for physical verification.

ASRS:1827967.n: On DATE, Time, the Internal Baggage Door was placed on MEL by a different Controller. In the morning of DATE1 I unassigned this MEL, techs could not complete this MEL and Ops needed aircraft for a flight the next day. I didn't review the MEL 52-11 and assumed it was a good MEL and removed it from the work order to be troubleshot at a later date. The aircraft flew during the day of DATE 1 and landed in ZZZ to be worked for maintenance. Tonight, on DATE 1 this MEL was back in a work order to be worked again, I was researching parts and reviewing the MEL when I noticed that 52-11 excludes the internal baggage door and that there is no relief. I immediately notified the Duty Manager NAME and grounded the aircraft. MEL 52-11 Internal baggage door does not close properly. It slides open occasionally.Review MEL's in Work Orders before unassigned them.
ASRS:1827967.s: A maintenance controller unassigned an MEL for a faulty internal baggage door without verifying the specific exclusion in MEL 52-11, allowing the aircraft to fly. The controller later discovered the error, notified the Duty Manager, and grounded the aircraft to prevent further operation with the inoperative door.

ASRS:1827974.n: On a VFR flight from HTL to 48D in day VMC with unrestricted visibility and high ceilings, with a right seat Private Pilot passenger. Briefed that Runway 09/27 at 48D was NOTAMed closed, and elected to land Runway 22 given westerly winds and NOTAM. I made multiple callouts on CTAF including base and final. During rollout, the pilot passenger noticed and informed me of a remote-controlled RC aircraft ahead, apparently above Runway 09/27 but overflying the extended centerline of Runway 22, about 600ft from the end of Runway 22. I did not myself see the RC aircraft. Upon safe landing and shut-down we became aware that there was an RC aircraft group operating at a series of RVs south of Runway 09/27 and that this was the reason for the NOTAM. While it is completely acceptable to have RC aircraft operations in an airport environment given NOTAMs, RC operators should be briefed to avoid overflight of an extended centerline for an active runway. Alternatively, if RC operations require the overflight of an extended centerline of another runway, that runway (or the airport) should be NOTAMed closed as well.If we were either performing a touch-and-go, or had to perform a go-around, the RC aircraft would have been directly in our path and would have posed a collision risk.
ASRS:1827974.s: A pilot and passenger landed a VFR flight on Runway 22 at 48D after Runway 09/27 was NOTAMed closed for RC aircraft operations. The passenger spotted an RC aircraft overflying the extended centerline of Runway 22, creating a potential collision risk had a go-around been required.

ASRS:1827998.n: I took off from ZZZ in my 2008 CAW SportCruiser, an aircraft that I had recently purchased. This was my first flight from ZZZ where I had based the aircraft. I flew around the local area to familiarize myself with landmarks in a 15 NM area near ZZZ. When I returned to land, an aircraft that was returning to the airport announced their intention to land on runway XX. I set up to enter the pattern for that runway about 5 NM away and went over the approach in my mind. Then, when I was about 3 NM away, I heard a pilot announce he was entering a left downwind for runway XY. I was surprised and concerned and made changes to my power setting and flaps setting from downwind settings. I changed my approach to enter a crosswind for runway XY. I was still a little shaken by the sudden change in approach for landing. The downwind and base legs were uneventful. The final approach started well, but as I neared the runway threshold, the PAPI system indicated that I was below the glide slope. I added a little power to get back on the glide slope, but I was too far into the landing. The aircraft hit hard and then the nose gear collapsed. The aircraft slid about 250 feet on top of the nose gear fairing and cowling. The prop struck the asphalt and one blade snapped off. Fortunately, I was thoroughly strapped into the four-point restraint harness and was uninjured.In retrospect, I should have abandoned the approach when it became unstable, and initiated a go-around. This will be a very expensive lesson. I am grateful that I emerged from the experience physically unscathed.
ASRS:1827998.s: The pilot of a 2008 CAW SportCruiser landed hard at ZZZ after an unstable approach caused by a sudden runway change and PAPI indications of being below glide slope. The nose gear collapsed, the propeller struck the runway, and one blade snapped off, though the pilot remained uninjured due to a four-point restraint harness.

ASRS:1828001.n: While performing a night flight operation as the sole occupant and PIC, I was en route to the New York Skyline Route via Direct the Verrazano Bridge. I was receiving flight following at the time from New York Approach. I was cruising at 2,000 feet VFR. At XA:44 EDT I spotted a White Drone that came into alignment and coverage with my left-wing landing light about 20-30 feet away. The drone had 4 props. My spotting and reaction time was within 2 seconds and I performed an evasion maneuver with a quick bank to the right and turned about 10 degrees with a bank angle of about 20-30 degrees. The drone barely missed my left-wing. I immediately then radioed New York Approach and reported the near-miss of the drone. The controller asked for a description, altitude, and if I had to perform an evasive maneuver.There was nothing I would have done differently in this case, however, it does once again bring around the constant issue of drones in the NAS. I believe that drones need to be programmed to not be able to exceed a specific altitude at any time without an FAA waiver. I know some manufacturers already have these restrictions in place but there is no valid reason a drone should be at 2,000 feet AGL along the New Jersey Shoreline area during the night (or day).
ASRS:1828001.s: The sole pilot flying a night VFR flight at 2,000 feet encountered a white quadcopter drone 20–30 feet from the left wing. The pilot executed a right bank evasion maneuver to avoid a collision and reported the near-miss to New York Approach.

ASRS:1828018.n: Cruising 9,500 ft. MSL indicated from ZZZ direct ZZZ1 in Grumman Traveler AA5. Sudden loss of engine rpm followed by severe vibration. Emergency procedures followed and [requested priority] with ATC. Received heading from center to HSI 20 miles north north west. Could not maintain altitude but had enough partial engine power to reach HSI and circle to descend and land. Determined intake valve broke on cylinder #3 and caused power loss.
ASRS:1828018.s: A pilot flying a Grumman Traveler AA5 at 9,500 ft MSL experienced sudden engine RPM loss and severe vibration due to a broken intake valve on cylinder #3. The pilot followed emergency procedures, received a heading from ATC, and landed at HSI using partial engine power.

ASRS:1828065.n: Close call event on short final to Runway 13 and unstable approach at ZZZ after finishing a long cross-country home from ZZZ1. Event occurred after being cleared for the visual approach to Runway 13 from Approach and switching to the local advisory frequency. I made a call on the advisory frequency on a 5 mile initial to the left downwind for Runway 31, intending to enter the traffic pattern. The aircraft was descending and I was very fast, 130 KIAS, with the intent to slow the aircraft in the pattern. Switching back to Approach frequency to cancel the IFR flight plan I decided on a straight in approach to Runway 13 to save time, while on Approach I missed the local traffic call of an aircraft taking Runway 31 to depart. After switching back to the local advisory frequency I made an advisory call for a 3 mile final to Runway 13 and I was switching the landing runway. The ADS-B data link immediately showed a traffic target directly ahead and climbing from Runway 31, passengers in my airplane spotted the traffic, and the other aircraft and I communicated to ensure we would avoid each other. Being distracted by the traffic close call, handling the radio swaps, and changing our approach I did not slow the aircraft down or add full flaps. Attempted to land with two notches of flaps and very fast, floated the aircraft most of the runway with braking in the final 1000 ft. Factors and Chain of Events:1. Long day of flying, and being tired from week at ZZZ1 contributed to wanting to be home. Additional time pressure of needing to pick up the family dog from the boarder affected decision making on speeds to fly and ultimately the runway selection.2.
