Concerns about forgetting to close the IFR flight plan, especially when tired, under time pressures, and distractions of passengers (kids), etc, contributed to cancelling in the air very close to the local airport operations. I should have stayed on the advisory frequency whenever within 5 miles of the airport that is known to be busy. Without ADS-B I would not have known about the departing traffic.3. Long two weeks of very good, challenging, and very safe flying supported an overconfidence in flying the airplane outside of SOPs, which contributed to flying way too fast on short final and almost floating the entire runway. Established patterns, speeds, altitudes, and power settings are practiced and used for good reason...to take variability out of flying and allow for handling of non-routine issues. Flying outside of SOP adds variability and multiplies risks that could overwhelm the pilot.4. Inaction of sticking with the originally stated plan to enter the downwind for Runway 31, the radio call is not just an advisory of what I am doing, but provides information to other operators on how the airport is flowing. Changing the plan adds risk to all of the other operators.
ASRS:1828065.s: A fatigued pilot flying a long cross-country to ZZZ deviated from SOPs by switching runways and cancelling IFR early, causing a close call with departing traffic and an unstable, high-speed landing on Runway 13. The event resulted in a long float and late braking due to distraction, time pressure, and overconfidence.

ASRS:1828075.n: While practicing short field landings, I came in on final at 70 kts. for Runway XX at ZZZ. I touched down on the runway with a slight right crosswind as I had done on the landing 5 or so minutes before, where I felt the same thing had happened, being only two of the three wheels initially touched. On the first landing this was not a problem and we took off again without issue, but during this approach I attempted to fix the problem by putting in right rudder as my Instructor told me to, which would have been fine if I had not also hit the right brake as well, causing the Aircraft to turn sharp to the right and drift sideways into the ditch between the runway and the taxiway. Both me and my Instructor were ok, and the plane seemed intact. My Instructor took the controls swiftly after we veered off course and maneuvered the plane gently into the ditch. After this we turned the engine off. I am a Flight Instructor and was practicing landings with my student. We were practicing short field landings and were inbound for the second landing at the airport. On final the student had made the remark we were coming in slightly fast and began correcting for the correct airspeeds. The approach to landing itself was not abnormal. It was on centerline and at a proper glidepath, just slightly fast. Due to the fact that we had been practicing short field landings, the student was aiming to flare at a point that likely should have been extended. As we flared, a little bit of crosswind caused there to be a slight sideload on the left wheel and at the time it was the only wheel touching the ground. As the Instructor, I had mentioned right rudder to get us realigned with centerline and reduce the sideloading. The student used right rudder but accidentally had his foot on the brake as well as the rudder. This caused the plane to brake solely on the right side and begin skidding down the runway. Out of fear, I believe the brake was pushed slightly more as opposed to less. At this time I started calling that I had the flight controls and the student took his hands off of the controls. At this point, the aircraft was perpendicular to the runway. Momentum had the plane still rolling slowly. I was not sure at the time if there was any damage to the tires due to side load or skidding and did not want to apply brakes in an effort to reduce damage. At this point I treated the plane as if it was a soft field landing, I used minimal braking and let the plane come to a stop in the grass directly next to the runway. I have a very small feet and know for myself that if my heels are on the ground I am on the rudder. In order to touch the brake, my leg needs to be lifted. This is not the case for most other people. In the future, I have now learned that to reduce the chances of this happening again, I will verify on short final that the students have their feet only on the rudder and not touching the brakes. Instead of teaching 'heels on the ground' I will now specify that 'balls of feet should be on the rudders'
ASRS:1828075.s: A flight instructor and student practicing short field landings veered off the runway into a ditch when the student accidentally applied the right brake while using right rudder to correct a crosswind. The instructor took control to stop the aircraft safely in the grass with no injuries or reported damage.

ASRS:1828079.n: [We were] operating in a military restricted area where range rules [were] to remain in VMC. Due to increasing cloud coverage, we had to knock off our planned flight early and began preparing for return to base (ZZZ). The PIC was managing the descent while I managed the checklists. We leveled at 10,000 ft. MSL to stay below cloud deck. We were flying southbound with mountainous terrain to the west. Cloud coverage was along the entire route ahead of us, and a hot restricted area was to the east (with cloud coverage). As a crew, we discussed the forward visibility which we estimated to be about 30 NM from our present location. It looked like some rain showers ahead down the valley, and cloudy conditions over the mountains (with maybe a little better clearance in the immediate direction). On board, radar was not indicating anything appreciable returns, and weather showed just a few pixels of green.As we approached the weather, the PIC said we should turn right as he thought the weather looked better towards the mountains. I stated that the weather ahead looked better in my opinion, as it looked like we would go under some of the rain showers in the valley. PIC said he thought it was IMC ahead, and started turning right towards the mountains. I reiterated that going down the valley was our best option, especially due to the mountainous terrain to our right. He mentioned he has flown in this area hundreds of times and he knew this would be better. I again reiterated that not only were we turning towards mountains, but there was a National Park over there which required us to stay 3,000 ft. above the terrain, and would limit how low we could go to avoid weather. I estimated that going down the valley could have got us as low as 5,000 ft. MSL safely (about 2,500 ft. AGL). PIC stated that going down the valley would be impossible for us to stay VMC and maintained the heading towards the mountains. I told him that I did not see what he was seeing, and he stated it would work fine.As we approached the first ridge the PIC climbed to 11,000 ft. MSL to stay safely above the terrain (although I estimate we needed to be about 13,000 ft. MSL to avoid National Park overflight). As we continued south, we could see that it was closing in and that the bases were getting lower, so the PIC started stepping down in altitude to approximately 8,500 ft.' MSL. At one point, the PIC was getting nervous, and asked me if we should turn around. As I was super focused on trying to stay ahead of the PIC, I told him whatever you do, do not turn right, as the Terrain display was showing a 10,200 ft. peak while we were descending through about9,500 ft. MSL. The visibility was becoming much reduced and we entered some light rain showers. As we were navigating mountainous terrain in visibility that were maybe 1 NM at times, the GPWS alerted us to 'TERRAIN, TERRAIN' followed immediately by 'PULL UP, PULL UP, PULL UP.' I immediately called climb-climb-climb. The PIC's only response was to pull back on the yoke (as opposed to our training which calls for disconnect AP (Auto Pilot)/AT (Auto Throttles), pitch to PLI (Pitch Limit Indicator) and max power). I put my hand on the throttles and started to push up about the same time the AT's responded to increasing power. As the climb commenced the Terrain Warning silenced, however we did encounter solid IMC. Shortly after we broke through the line of showers, [we] proceeded back to the airfield [in] VFRThere were multiple opportunities to prevent this from happening. The first and foremost that comes to mind is that as soon as we disagreed on the course of action, we should have entered a hold to discuss it. This would have given us time to regroup and may have resulted in a better decision. Additionally (in hindsight), we could have requested an IFR flight plan back to the landing airfield per the range rules. However, we were so focused on remaining VMC that we overlooked that option, probably due to task saturation. Personalities and organizational culture are also paramount to conducting safe flight operations, and these subjects will be presented to leadership as a result of this incident.
ASRS:1828079.s: A two-pilot crew flying VFR in mountainous terrain entered IMC after the PIC ignored the co-pilot's advice to avoid a restricted area and turned toward mountains. The aircraft triggered a GPWS "PULL UP" warning at 9,500 ft MSL, forcing an emergency climb into solid IMC before returning to base.

ASRS:1828100.n: On very short final for a landing on runway XX with a landing clearance, we were ordered to go around by ZZZ Tower. My humble estimate was that we were at about 50 feet altitude. Aircraft Y crossed runway XX at taxiway 1 heading east bound and was directly in front of us on the runway. A go around was executed and we were cleared to 4,000 feet and took radar vectors for a landing on runway XY. The rest of the flight and landing was uneventful. First Officer was the pilot flying and did an excellent job. I highly commend the tower controller for their quick actions and decision making in making the immediate call for us to execute a go around. Had the timing been just seconds later, this incident could have had a very different outcome as we would have touched down.
ASRS:1828100.s: The pilot flying executed a go-around at 50 feet on final for runway XX after ZZZ Tower ordered it due to Aircraft Y crossing the runway. The crew was cleared to 4,000 feet and vectored for a safe landing on runway XY, avoiding a potential collision.

ASRS:1828101.n: About 45 minutes into my flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 at 7,500 MSL, my aircraft engine experienced a sudden and what appeared to be total power loss leaving the prop wind milling. The engine did not cough or sputter. The fuel gauges indicated approximately 1/4 tank in both left and right tanks. Attempts to restart the engine were made but were unsuccessful. I trimmed for best glide speed and turned toward nearest airport on my VFR chart. Upon arrival I found the airport to be unsuitable for landing due to a large barn constructed at approach end of runway and multiple vehicles parked on pavement of the former runway. Houses and trees were also obstructing the runway sides. Subsequently, I made a forced landing in a clearing adjacent to former runway. The aircraft occupants egressed safely and noticed that fuel was leaking from the airplane's right-wing root and left wing fuel cap.Remove 0OR9 (Hanel Field) airstrip a defunct and non-operational airport from the FAA sectional charts and the airport facility directory. There is no possibility to safely land on the runways there. This should also apply to any other non operational airports which have runway obstructions.
ASRS:1828101.s: A pilot flying a single-engine aircraft at 7,500 feet experienced a total engine power loss with fuel gauges showing one-quarter tank. After finding the nearest charted airport obstructed by a barn and vehicles, the pilot made a safe forced landing in a clearing, discovering fuel leaks from the right wing root and left fuel cap.

ASRS:1828115.n: I was given a low altitude alert after being cleared to land. I think that I was given the alert due to having a close in base turn due to rain off the south end of the airport.
ASRS:1828115.s: The pilot received a low altitude alert while cleared to land. The reporter attributes the alert to a close-in base turn necessitated by rain at the south end of the airport.

ASRS:1828128.n: Check flight for camera filters over unoccupied playing field. While maneuvering UAS approximately 200 feet horizontally from pilot, and rotating UAS for different orientations to sun, message 'Center board failure' appeared on controller. UAS continued its forward path until distance to controller showed 1,250 feet, then 'Disconnect' warning followed by total lack of control. Return to Home feature did not function.Attempted to locate UAS by searching as close as possible to last recorded position. UAS not found.
ASRS:1828128.s: During a check flight over an unoccupied field, the pilot maneuvered a UAS 200 feet away when a "Center board failure" appeared, followed by a "Disconnect" warning and total loss of control at 1,250 feet. The Return to Home feature failed, and the UAS was not found after a search near its last recorded position.

ASRS:1828250.n: [Company] Leadership for years under hydration program created several locations housing ice makers, ice merchandisers, filtered water dispensers and water cooler sanitizing station.Yesterday [the gate] crew was seriously upset as aircraft maintenance team was working on [an aircraft] to clear clogged sewer line in aft, once maintenance team was done they walked to the sanitizing station at [an adjacent gate] meant for washing only drinking water coolers to wash their used tools. Even before [the] team could actually approach and prevent the act the maintenance team had already started the unbelievable act.Maintenance washed their dirty sewer tools and left. The act was reported to Supervisor on duty who reported to [operations] and Manager on duty about the act, who suggested to create a work order and have [facility maintenance] clean the sink which is not an acceptable solution to restore employee confidence and support [the company safety campaign.] OSHA has set firm rules for these kind of bio hazard cleaning / removal / similar process and this act committed by maintenance team is clear violation and disregard to fellow employees well being. [At the gate] water cooler sanitization station. Aircraft Maintenance group worked on [an aircraft] and according to the gate crew worked on sewer lines of lavatory on [the aircraft]. After completing their work they walked to the water station and washed the tools on drinking water cooler sanitization station. The incident was reported immediately to the Supervisor. It is very gross bio-hazard and unacceptable by any hygiene standard.
ASRS:1828250.s: Aircraft maintenance personnel working on an aircraft lavatory sewer line washed their contaminated tools at a drinking water cooler sanitization station. The gate crew reported this biohazard violation to supervisors, noting the act disregarded hygiene standards and employee well-being.

ASRS:1828260.n: I attempted multiple conversations with local zone/gate leadership and I was advised that we WOULD use an aircraft that just had returned to the gate due to excessive heat in the cabin. The aircraft gate returned as Aircraft X which was ZZZ to ZZZ1 and was planning to go out immediately as Aircraft Y ZZZ to ZZZ2. It appears that flight Aircraft X was swapped with flight Aircraft Y. I was not able to locate any repairs on Aircraft Z after its return to block. I spoke with [the Captain] who was taking the ZZZ2 trip and after making some calls, he refused the equipment.The ZZZ1 passengers came off the plane yelling, to almost screaming, and were visibly wet and beyond agitated. The ZZZ emergency line had to be called for backup at the gate return to protect our team.I overheard a conversation between the ZZZ1 FAs and the flight deck that they could hear the screaming over the intercom from the passengers.This is not humane treatment for our coworkers nor should our passengers have to deal with extreme heat.
ASRS:1828260.s: Gate leadership assigned a heat-damaged aircraft to a departing flight, causing passenger distress and requiring emergency backup. The Captain refused the equipment after discovering no repairs were made, preventing the flight from operating with the compromised aircraft.

ASRS:1828309.n: During takeoff roll no 2 ENG EGT was just below limitation. At rotation EGT exceeded limitation. EGT temperature was 975 Celsius. Requested priority handling. Continued departure and cleanup. Performed ECAM actions and follow ups. Returned to ZZZ runway XYC. Overweight landing at 193.4 lbs. Landed and stopped on the runway. Taxied to [the gate].The engine was written up with the same problem and priority 2 days earlier. Maintenance performed a engine run up and bore check but did not have the airplane flown. Flying the airplane would had been a more prudent and accurate test that would had most likely given the same result as we experienced. The change in the AOA during rotation is when the engine exceeded EGT temperature limitation.Put the aircraft in a more realistic and accurate situation that would produce actual information for maintenance to make a greater determination of airworthiness.
ASRS:1828309.s: The pilot reported that during takeoff, engine 2 EGT exceeded limits at rotation due to angle of attack changes, prompting a priority return and overweight landing. The reporter noted maintenance had previously performed a ground run-up instead of a flight test, which would have likely identified the issue.

ASRS:1828389.n: The event occurred because Greenville-Spartanburg (GSP) is working a busy airport with one controller utilizing all three frequencies. This is a major safety of flight issue as multiple links in the safety chain were broken that day. If the sharpness of the crews from Air Carrier X and Air Carrier Y had not utilized full four ear policy and patience it could have been an issue. The actions taken by the ATC operation in GSP are uncalled for and unsafe. If this is overlooked there could be fatal consequences in the future. There are a few local airports in the area of Greenville-Spartanburg that are non-towered. If the Tower Controller delayed any further for us to be handed over to Departure, we could have had a collision or RA with an unknown aircraft all due to the unsafe actions of one controller handling a workload bound for a minimum of two personal.I was in command of Aircraft X. The Greenville Tower had one controller working all three frequencies: clearance, ground, and tower. This was a busy morning with Air Carrier Z, Air Carrier X, Air Carrier A, and us to ZZZ all departing at roughly the same time. When we called for our clearance on the delivery frequency, we noticed there was some bleed over as the controller was issuing take-off clearances. We had to repeat our request for a clearance but were given it with no issues. I released the brakes and we called for push shortly after. Air Carrier X also called for push after us. In the middle of our push back the controller called on the ground frequency to inform Air Carrier Z of a delay for them. The two began to have a conversation on ground of a game plan to be made. As their conversation occurred our ramp crew disconnected the tow bar and gave the wave off for an all clear to a taxi. I noticed Air Carrier X had pushed off gate and we were pushed off with our nose in the direction of travel to only exit with a head on collision. We finished our 'After Start Checklist' and cleared the area to begin our taxi. I switched on our taxi and nose lights and noticed Air Carrier X did the same. With the controller and Air Carrier Z conversation occurring to what was now a clearance being given with a read back to follow there was no way for me or Air Carrier X to have confirmation one was waiting for the other. There was dense fog and low visibility on the ramp that morning. Tower does not control the ramp and a courtesy call is requested. The weather was so bad we had a take-off alternate of ZZZ1 that morning. It was a frustrating situation as Air Carrier X and I could barely make out the 2nd half of each other's aircraft, so it was a game of chicken. I tried to call over the radio and speak over the clearance being given but it did not work. Ultimately, I turned off my lights to give Air Carrier X the right of way. As we began our taxi to Runway 4 Air Carrier A called clearance to get their clearance to Houston (IAH) and that now was being broadcast over the ground frequency adding to the safety issue that no one moving on the aircraft surface could talk to each other. The Tower issued Air Carrier X their take-off clearance and told us we were next. After we got our take off clearance, we began the take-off roll with no issues. As we continued our take-off climb Carrier called the controller over the ground frequency. All we heard was the controller responding over the tower frequency meaning he was working all three frequencies still. This delayed our hand off to Departure and made us uneasy as the tower radar could not see our path beyond a certain mileage. As we checked in with GSP Departure we were given an instruction to contact Center as our time had been too long and radar services with GSP could not be utilized further.This told me the GSP airport controller took too long to hand us off and impeded the Departure Controller from doing their job properly. We did not have sufficient air traffic control separation all due to the unsafe practices of the GSP airport and Air Traffic Control operation at the airport of GSP. GSP needs to hire another controller! There must be at least one person working Ground and Delivery while another separate controller works Tower. The operation in GSP has been compromised and it is scary to think that the unsafe actions are acceptable to those working in the ATC system. If this issue were to happen again, I'm worried it could turn out like the Tenerife airport disaster with KLM and Pan Am but scraping metal on the ramp or taxing into each other.
ASRS:1828389.s: The pilot of Aircraft X reported a near-collision with Air Carrier X on the ramp at Greenville-Spartanburg (GSP) due to dense fog and a single controller managing all three frequencies. This overload prevented effective communication and coordination, forcing the pilot to yield right of way and delaying the handoff to Departure.

ASRS:1828418.n: ATC direct failure to advise hold short of Runway 9C in the initial clearance. After the switch from Ground to another Tower frequency no instruction was given to hold short 9C. We were given clearance to taxi M1, M, right onto Runway 22R hold short of E. Aircraft Y was ahead of us given the same clearance hold short E monitor Tower 132.70. The Aircraft Y encroached Runway 9C as Aircraft Z was on its takeoff roll on 9C. ATC Controller yelled Aircraft Y stop! Immediately after Aircraft Z cancel takeoff clearance STOP! The Aircraft Z appeared from behind the hangars with the nose wheel off the ground in a slight right bank as the Controller said 'Do you see that plane'? Aircraft Y was given a number to contact the Tower. There are no 'wig wags' installed at any intersections along this runway. There are no stop bars installed. There are multiple obstructions to visibility. Taxiing into the sun is a factor. Runway markings and signage is unacceptable for the size and scope of the runway, and it's intended use. New construction all around the airport with pilots returning to work from furlough, and layoffs or leave of absence. Trust bias that ATC is correct in the instructions given. Attempting to move aircraft with expedience rather than a structured taxi route. No designation of any 'hot spots ' on aeronautical charts. Cease and desist using Runway 22R as a taxiway! The use of this Runway as a taxiway is the inevitable set up for a mass casualty accident!
ASRS:1828418.s: Pilots reported a runway incursion where Aircraft Y crossed Runway 9C while Aircraft Z was on takeoff roll due to ATC failing to issue hold-short instructions. The reporter attributed the event to using Runway 22R as a taxiway, poor visibility, inadequate signage, and a lack of stop bars or hot spot designations.

ASRS:1828441.n: Never called [in] fatigue in my over 20 years with the company until now, but schedulers are pushing (we) reserve flight attendants to the limit since we are short staffed. It is unsafe for us to have 14 hour days or even more, with 4, 5, 6 legs a day during many consecutive days. We are not able to have a good rest, since all hotels are crowded and loud, in most places we stay at. On my 5th consecutive day flying, I experienced exhaustion due to the heavy schedules, heat, and lack of rest. I requested the schedulers a different flight, if possible, since they wanted me to fly for another 14 hour day period. They denied my request, saying that all schedules were over the same 14 hour on duty time or even more due to delays because of the short staffing. I told them it was unsafe for me to fly with the symptoms I was experiencing and asked to be removed. It took me literally more than 24 hours to get some recovery after what I experienced.Overworked flight attendants make our job unsafe. Just because [it] is legal in paper does not make right to be flying and perform our duties SAFELY or in an accurate manner.
ASRS:1828441.s: A reserve flight attendant reported exhaustion on their fifth consecutive day due to heavy schedules, heat, and poor hotel rest. The crew member requested removal from a 14-hour duty day citing safety concerns, but schedulers denied the request due to short staffing, forcing the flight to proceed.

ASRS:1828483.n: Aircraft was on final approach segment of GPS36 at M41. Conditions were hazy with scattered clouds at 3000 ft MSL (2500 ft AGL). Subject aircraft was VMC prior to FAF and had cancelled IFR and switched to CTAF. At two miles from touchdown end of Runway 36, with aircraft at approx 1000 ft AGL, pilot not flying (PNF) called traffic off right wing. PF noted rapidly approaching target and banked left. Both PF and PNF noted a large UAV (drone) pass within 1/4 mile of right wing. PF switched to Memphis approach frequency and reported near miss. A missed approach was not required and PF was able to recover to stabilized approach and land without further incident. Subject aircraft had ADS-B in/out capability (L-3 Lynx NGT-9000 transponder). The UAV did not show on display (Traffic Information Services).Operating a drone on final approach course to airport, in MVFR conditions is extremely careless and reckless. Due to haze conditions, the unlighted drone was difficult to spot and subject aircraft was fortunate to have rated pilot in right seat watching for traffic. Due to conditions, PF was focused on maintaining stabilized approach in marginal VFR conditions.
ASRS:1828483.s: The pilot flying and pilot not flying on a GPS36 final approach at M41 avoided a large unlighted UAV that passed within 1/4 mile of the right wing. The drone was not displayed on the ADS-B Traffic Information Services, but the crew recovered and landed safely without a missed approach.

ASRS:1828505.n: Cleared by ground to taxi to runway XY via taxiway 1 and taxiway 2, Hold short of taxiway 2. Approaching 2, cleared to cross [runway XY]. I read back clearance. Captain acknowledged and said 'cleared to taxi.' ATC was busy with additional traffic and an approaching thunderstorm. While referencing aerodrome chart I looked up from my airport chart to reference the runway designated sign to see that we were crossing runway XY with an aircraft conducting its takeoff roll, I called 'Go go go aircraft left' Departing aircraft was rotating and passed behind and 300+ feet above.We should have held until we both confirmed the appropriate taxi route, and verified correct route.Contributing factors: Captain unfamiliar [with] aerodrome. ATC workload, multiple commuter flights and firefighting aircraft. Approaching thunderstorm.Corrective actions: Improve CRM and aerodrome familiarity with expected taxi route verses cleared taxi route. Aircraft should not move until taxi route has been confirmed. Taxi instructions were from [our present location] to RWY XY via left on taxiway 1, 3 to hold short of 2. Instructions were read back by the CP (Check Pilot) and verified by CA (Captain). Upon reaching taxiway 2, ground control amended clearance to RWY XY via 2 and by clearing us to cross RWY XX. The CP read back the taxi instructions and the CA acknowledged. The CP pointed out another aircraft on 2 that was holding for us and the CA acknowledged. The CP proceeded to verify the amended taxi route on an EFB. The CA proceeded to cross 2 and RWY XX at 3. The CP went heads up to notice departing traffic on RWY XX and stated 'Go Go Go'. Once clear of RWY XX the crew was notified by ground of a possible pilot deviation. Weather was CAVOK at the airport.Contributing factors were a takeoff brief being conducted at critical points on the taxi route and a large amount of traffic on the ground control frequency due to adverse weather in the area. Preventive measures in the future are to minimize briefings while the aircraft is in motion, for the pilot taxiing the aircraft to ensure proper taxi clearance is understood by stating their intentions at trigger points along the taxi route and for the pilot not taxiing the aircraft to ensure the correct taxi route is being followed while query the pilot taxiing the aircraft if any deviations start to develop.
ASRS:1828505.s: The flight crew crossed an active runway while a departing aircraft was taking off due to the Captain's unfamiliarity with the aerodrome and high ATC workload during thunderstorms. The incident resulted in a near-miss with the departing aircraft passing 300 feet above, prompting recommendations to improve crew resource management and taxi route verification.

ASRS:1828534.n: Prior to taxiing onto Runway XX/XY at ZZZ I observed the pattern and both approach ends for landing or departing aircraft. None in sight, I radioed back taxiing Runway XY for departure. Approximately 500 ft from the threshold of Runway XY, I noticed Aircraft Y banking hard onto the final of Runway XY about 45 degrees to the left of my nose. The pilot appeared to have entered on a right base in what is otherwise a left traffic pattern. I called again stating back taxiing XY, assuming they would hear and also see me during their base turn. No response and they were lined up for XY head-on with me at this point so I applied 70% power to accelerate to a turn out at the threshold area. Aircraft Y proceeded to land shortly after I had pulled out of the way. A private jet [Aircraft Z] was holding short of Runway XY at the ramp at this point and also likely observed the situation. Given the size of the jet (wouldn't have fit in the small turn out at the end of Runway XY) and how the pilot never attempted a go-around, this could have been a real incident if it were the jet on the runway instead of me which is what concerns me. I received communications from the jet (jet that is based at ZZZ) that was holding short as well.After later talking with the operator, they did state the aircraft has no radios but insisted they were in the right.While landing aircraft have the right away, this aircraft was not yet in the pattern when I had began to back taxi. I believe they entered the pattern directly on a right base, making a right turn to final which was unexpected given this is a left traffic pattern. Furthermore, I was in a position where I could not easily turn my aircraft around and exit the runway which should've been clear from their view point, making a go-around the best option for the landing aircraft. Instead they proceeded to land, needlessly making a dangerous situation for the both of us.Ultimately nobody was injured but this entire scenario could have been mitigated by Aircraft Y following the established landing pattern, making himself more visible and giving any aircraft on the ground or the landing aircraft to take the appropriate evasive action.
ASRS:1828534.s: The pilot back-taxied Runway XY at ZZZ while Aircraft Y entered a right base in a left traffic pattern, creating a head-on conflict. The pilot accelerated to avoid the runway as Aircraft Y landed without a go-around, causing a dangerous situation due to the unexpected pattern entry.

ASRS:1828535.n: We were on final for Runway XX, in Aircraft X, and my student accidentally put in flaps 40 on about a mile final (this is pretty easy to do as the flaps are really touchy and the indicator is above the students eye level). This caused him to get low and slow. I asked if he wanted to go around and he decided to continue. His focus was mainly on that and he failed to notice he was coming in crabbed to the right. I told him to use left rudder to straighten, which he did about 10 ft above the ground but at that point we were extremely left of center line and he panicked banked to the right, very hard, I told him to go around but he did not respond and we touched down completely side loaded and fairly hard. I took the controls and went around, but with all the flaps in it took a bit to get off the ground and the tail dragged on the runway. Once we got off the ground, I told the tower we were going around and that we were making this a full stop because we had a hard landing. [They] responded by telling us to set up for a left downwind for Runway XX1, and that we were cleared to land. In the meantime I did hear the tower send maintenance to inspect the runway, and they found no damage. This landing was fine and we taxied back and had maintenance (Name) inspect the tail. He said there was nothing but cosmetic damage to the left elevator and tie down. The plane was flown again.
ASRS:1828535.s: A student pilot in Aircraft X selected flaps 40 on final, causing a low, crabbed approach that resulted in a hard, side-loaded touchdown and tail drag. The instructor executed a go-around, and subsequent inspections revealed only cosmetic damage to the left elevator and tie-down.

ASRS:1828544.n: On Date at approximately XA:00 Hrs, I was in Olympia, WA for an unrelated event and decided to see if I could fly my drone on the Capitol complex to take videos or photos of the legislative building for recreational purposes. I checked the airspace using the ALOFT B4UFLY app, and could see that the airspace near the Capitol was Class G, but very close to Class E airspace for OLM to the south. I saw no signs or warnings of NO DRONE flying Zones. The areas for which I would take off and land were either flat, mowed grass, or empty concrete sidewalks. The temperature was in the high XA's, low XB's, and the skies were clear with a light breeze out of the south. There were very few vehicles or people in the area because the State Legislature is not in session currently. I parked on N Diagonal road and took off from the sidewalk area there. I completed 4 flights. I maintained VLOS for all my flights. The first I took off from the sidewalk near where I parked, and I elevated to 200 feet AGL, and then flew a path to the Winged Victory Monument and circled it before I returned to the area I took off from. I also walked down to the area in between the Legislative Building and the Temple of Justice and took off from the flag pole area directly in between. I elevated to approximately 330 feet AGL and completed about a 100 degree panning video to the north side around the dome of the Legislative building and then centered the drone and landed in the same spot I took off from. I did this twice for video purposes. Again, I landed safely back where I started. I then took off from mostly the same spot in between the buildings facing towards the Temple of Justice. My focus was on taking a video of the Temple of Justice from the south side of the building while I placed the drone at the same height as the tallest flag pole on the building, then scanning down the front. My last flight I walked back to where I originally parked my vehicle on N Diagonal, then I took off again from the sidewalk area and flew around the Tivoli fountain over the grassy areas, never going higher than approximately 150 feet AGL. I had no problems or concerns at the time during these flights. Now, 5 days later, I am speaking to a friend who is also a drone operator, but also a commercial pilot about my recent drone flights. After discussing these flights, he stated that it was not authorized to fly a drone on the Capitol complex. I said I checked the B4UFLY app, and did not see any signs or postings while on the grounds of the campus. Following our conversation, I then went and did more research now looking at non-aviation sites, as well as searching Sectional Aeronautical Charts on a commercial website and found that it is indeed not authorized to fly on the Capitol grounds and apparently numerous areas around there. I also then went an checked an aeronautical section chart (learning to read them) and do now see that there is airspace restrictions over the Capitol complex. My friend advised me I should report this incident to help ensure others like me potentially won't make this same mistake. As a recreational pilot, who is working on getting my Part 107 certification, I have been attending training using the FAASafetey.gov site, and am operating under the understanding that any airspace restrictions, would be listed on the B4UFLY app. This is obviously NOT accurate. Following my friends notification that I may have violated airspace, I checked again on the B4UFLY app and again found no Special Use Restrictions, no TFR's, or any indication of not being able to fly on the Capitol grounds in the areas I flew. It was an open area and clear weather. The Class E restrictions appear to start to the south of the building. I would have never even considered flying if the Legislature was in session due to the amount of people on the ground and in the area. I will continue learning where to best get information about the areas for which I am permitted to fly and abide by the restrictions I am aware of, or should be aware of. I think this can be avoided for others in the future if the training for recreational or Part 107 pilots via the FAA, included ALL the locations to gather flight data prior to flight. Additionally training on the clear expectation that flying a drone requires you to know, use and understand Sectional Aeronautical Charts, as well as placing that information in the most accessible place to Recreational pilots. I have downloaded and used all the apps for flying a drone that have been pushed to use by the FAA on their websites. In my course of attempting to earn my Part 107 certification, I have taken the classes through the FAA websites to prepare me, and I feel very unprepared given this mistake I apparently made. I of course want to do the right thing, fly safely, and abide by the rules. I will continue to make efforts to learn and improve.
ASRS:1828544.s: A recreational drone operator conducted four flights over the Olympia Capitol complex, reaching up to 330 feet AGL, believing the airspace was open based on the B4UFLY app. The operator later learned from a commercial pilot that the flights were unauthorized due to unlisted airspace restrictions, highlighting a gap between app data and actual regulatory requirements.

ASRS:1828551.n: I was working the R-side [Radar Controller] position on Shelbyville Low Sector 60. I was working Aircraft X who was headed to BNA. The aircraft came to me descending to 12,000 from ZTL. Per the LOA with Nashville I descended the aircraft to 8,000 [feet] and initiated the handoff to Nashville Approach. I switched the aircraft to the correct frequency. When Aircraft X was about 5 miles outside my airspace, the controller at Nashville called me to say that no practice approaches were allowed at BNA and that Aircraft X was being put on a heading of 180 and coming back to me to return to his airport. I asked the Controller what was his airport? I had no flight plan information on this aircraft, just that he was going to BNA. The Controller said he would call back. When he called back a couple of minutes later, he said there was a flight plan for a BNA departure to ZZZ. The Controller told me they put him on his new squawk code and was coming to me on that 180 heading. Nashville never entered a departure message on the new flight plan. I had to remove the flight plan on the Nashville arrival and then enter the departure message for the new flight plan. I was able to tag up the aircraft and then I had to re-clear the aircraft back to ZZZ.My main issue with this event, is that this is a very unsafe situation to just turn an aircraft and reverse his course without approval from the new sector. I had other BNA arrivals descending and I had to keep Aircraft X on the 180 heading for about 5 more minutes before I was able to put the aircraft on course. Another issue I have is the Controller at Nashville refusing to help an IFR aircraft. I get it if you are busy and cannot approve practice approaches at your airport. Nashville has 6 more airports in their airspace, maybe send someone there. Just to reverse this aircraft's course is pretty bad. How are aircraft supposed to know that no practice approaches are allowed at BNA? I have been working traffic for XX years and this had only come up in the past two weeks of me being at ZME. The area across from me, Area 6, had a similar situation a few weeks ago with an aircraft being refused to be worked by the Nashville Approach Controller and had to spin for about 20 minutes until they knew exactly what was happening.One of my fellow controllers overheard what was going on and he stated that Nashville did the same thing to him about two weeks ago as well. This time it was a general aviation aircraft that Nashville refused to have the aircraft enter their airspace, and the controller had to spin the aircraft at the last minute and he returned just back to somewhere in Alabama. In Aircraft X's case he flew from Georgia all the way towards Nashville, gets 35 miles out and is turned right back around back to Georgia. I felt bad for the aircraft that we were not able to provide a service to the aircraft. There are no NOTAMs for BNA saying anything about practice approaches. There were no comments in Aircraft X's flight plan saying he wanted a practice approach at BNA. How are these aircraft supposed to know this procedure? I am not real sure the process to help alleviate this issue. Again, how is any aircraft supposed to know about this? And how am I supposed to know this exists as I am working traffic to Nashville? There needs to be more clarification on this procedure.
ASRS:1828551.s: A Radar Controller in Shelbyville Low Sector 60 reported that Nashville Approach turned Aircraft X back to its departure airport without prior coordination after denying a practice approach at BNA. The controller cited the unapproved course reversal and lack of flight plan updates as unsafe, forcing a delay while managing other arrivals.

ASRS:1828584.n: We taxied into Gate XX after a rain shower passed over the field shortly before arrival. Both the First Officer and I were unable to see the lead-in line or J-line with all the exterior lighting illuminated. Those lines are either non existent, obliterated or no longer have reflective capabilities. Either way we were only able to get some semblance of alignment with aid of clear and directive marshalling. I was very uncomfortable taxing into the gate under these circumstances and believe it is a significant safety issue. The lead-in line along with the J-line associated with Gate XX needs to be repainted with paint containing some reflective properties. In addition more ramp lighting would certainly help the situation.
ASRS:1828584.s: The Captain and First Officer could not see the lead-in or J-lines at Gate XX due to rain and poor reflectivity, requiring marshalling for alignment. The pilot reported this as a safety issue and recommended repainting the lines with reflective material and adding ramp lighting.

ASRS:1828595.n: I departed ZZZ without the final dangerous goods manifest. To my knowledge, we did not receive one. I did a communications uplink review and could not find the manifest. I do not know if Load Planning failed to send the manifest. We had a communications disruption from a maintenance issue that may have cleared the communications cache before we received it. We recognized the error in flight and had Load Planning send a copy. Regardless, the responsibility is mine to depart with a final Dangerous goods (DG) manifest. I received the planned DG manifest and placed it in my usual place as a reminder to get the final version before departure. My reminder failed. This is in no way an excuse for my error. For the record, the contributing factors follow.Threats.- Distractions. A maintenance issue to resolve an Autopilot Backdrive Wheel EICAS caution and status messages, plus accompanying Bank Angle Protection inop issue had three mechanics in my flight deck for 30 minutes, including a total power down of the aircraft. The resulting flow disruption had me out of my seat and out of pre-flight flows. The mechanics stated they needed boarding stopped and passengers seated for the power down. I was preoccupied coordinating with Customer Service and Flight Attendants on passenger enplanement to assist with the maintenance issue. As part of the power down of the aircraft, the interior would go (relatively) dark. When power was restored, it took several more minutes for the lighting configuration to reset before we could continue with boarding. I was also coordinating with dispatch as the maintenance action would produce MEL items.- Perceived time compression to get the flight out as close to on time as possible. We finally departed XA41 for a scheduled XA00 out time. When the mechanics completed maintenance, we had to redo the FMC initializations and accompanying preflight items. At this point, everything else was ready and departure depended on the flight deck to finish pre-flight procedures.- Fatigue. It was close to midnight, body time. Even though I rested before the flight and managed a brief nap in the early evening, I was tired. That may have contributed towards me missing the final DG manifest.Errors.- Failure to follow standard operating procedures. I did not get the final DG manifest before pushback as required by company procedures.- Failure to execute Crew Resource Management/Threat Error Management. I did not perform effective leadership and communications during the disruption to mitigate the potential for missing the DG manifest.- Poor task management. I tried to do everything to manage pre-departure issues. This trait was identified during LOE. Management.- Delegate. I need to better involve my other crew members. In retrospect, I should have asked one of my co-pilots to manage the cabin boarding/seating issues with the Flight Attendants and Customer Service.- Communicate. Ask other crew members to help remember the final DG manifest. I only mentioned the planned DG to the 'flying' PM. The relief PM was doing the walk-around. I did not ask them to help remember.- Change habit patterns. My preflight cues to remember the final DG manifest did not work. I need to come up with a new method.- Modify leadership methods. I need to revisit the LOE observation that I take too much on to myself and develop techniques to mitigate that leadership shortcoming.
ASRS:1828595.s: The pilot departed without the final dangerous goods manifest due to distractions from a maintenance-induced power down, time pressure, and fatigue. The pilot accepted responsibility for failing to follow procedures and manage crew resources during the pre-flight disruption.

ASRS:1828650.n: This report is submitted due to concerns regarding return-to-service preparation of our long-term stored aircraft. This aircraft had a number of issues which precluded an on-time departure and caused us to question the true airworthiness of the aircraft. Specifically, the aircraft had massively incorrect fuel loading, such that it required ~4+ hours to move fuel to the appropriate, legal-for-flight, locations. Second, upon the first engine start, we were surprised to see to ECAM Caution messages for 'ENG 1 (and ENG 2) REV INHIBITED.' Thrust reverser operation was, indeed, inhibited, so we encountered another half hour+ delay while computer settings were changed to allow thrust reverser operation. (Maintenance Control advised that these messages were likely the result of a release-from-storage checklist item being left undone/missed.) Our total delay ended up being five hours as our Dispatcher and us concurred that additional fuel was required for our flight to ZZZ due to incoming weather, which added another 20 or 30 minutes to the delays. Our concern is that the number of time consuming and potentially unsafe items we encountered in successfully launching our aircraft suggest that either the team at ZZZ1 was rushed to accomplish these tasks, and/or given insufficient time or staff to complete them. Another possibility is that the appropriate training and task cards were not been provided? Regardless of the causes, with so many aircraft coming back into service, it behooves us to look into the events of this return-to-service flight so as to preclude them from occurring again, thus enhancing flight safety. Simply suggesting an investigation or evaluation of what transpired in this return-to-service flight so as prevent compromised flight operations going forward.
ASRS:1828650.s: Pilots reported a five-hour departure delay on a long-term stored aircraft due to incorrect fuel loading and inhibited thrust reversers caused by missed release-from-storage checklist items. The crew attributed these safety concerns to potential rushing, insufficient staffing, or lack of training during the return-to-service preparation.

ASRS:1828651.n: During landing roll between 80 and 60 kts tower rattled off taxi instructions ([Taxiways] XX-XY-XZ hold short [Runway] XXC) and I read them back. During the taxi in, while doing my after landing flow, we turned from [Taxiway] XY to [Taxiway] XA, this being the standard taxi route in ZZZ off of [Runway] XXL I didn't think twice until ATC came on and advised us we turned onto [Taxiway] XA and the instructions were [Taxiways] XY-XZ. Tower then gave new instruction [Taxiways] XA-XB-XZ short [Runway] XXC. We complied with the new instructions and continued to the gate without further incident. Receiving a taxi clearance during the landing rollout is never ideal. I was able to read back the instructions, but didn't register they were different expecting the standard taxi in in ZZZ. Tower waiting till we exit the runway to give taxi clearances, instead of between 100-60 kts.
ASRS:1828651.s: The pilot received taxi instructions during the landing roll between 80 and 60 kts but mistakenly turned onto the standard taxiway instead of the cleared route. The error occurred because the pilot expected the standard procedure and did not register the specific clearance, though ATC corrected the route without further incident.

ASRS:1828652.n: Immediately after takeoff from ZZZ all communication was disrupted by extreme static which inhibited the ability to transmit or receive any communication by either VHF 1 or VHF 2 radio through headsets, hand mics, or speakers. The static continued throughout the entire flight with brief periods of communication possible for 1-5 minutes. Crew elected to continue normal departure and climb and adhere to our filed route clearance while squawking 7600. Dispatch was notified via ACARS and was requested to coordinate down link ATC communications. During brief periods of open communication we informed ATC of our intentions to fly our filed route, arrival STAR and land on runway XXC at destination ZZZ1. Captain and FO discussed and agreed that the safest course of action was to fly our filed and comply with lost communication procedures and not complicate the current flight plan by returning to departure field or an unplanned alternate. FO flew the aircraft from takeoff to landing and captain handled the communication and ATC coordination issues. Arrival landing, taxi and parking at ZZZ1 were uneventful and flight was completed safely.
ASRS:1828652.s: The flight crew experienced total VHF radio failure due to extreme static immediately after takeoff from ZZZ. They squawked 7600, followed lost communication procedures, and completed a safe landing at ZZZ1 after coordinating via ACARS.

ASRS:1828655.n: Aircraft X was scheduled for a XZ41 departure ZZZ-ZZZ1. We were delayed due to being short one flight attendant. During the preflight and logbook review, the Captain (CA) brought to my attention a previous write up from Date that the number 2 engine was shut down in flight due to an EGT over temp and that a subsequent overweight landing was made. Both discrepancies were signed off. The CA and I discussed this during our 'threats' briefing since we were heavy, it was hot, and we would be performing a TOGA take off with the APU ON. It was my leg to fly. The start, taxi, and initial take off were routine. Prior to thrust reduction, we heard the ECAM chime and saw the Master Caution. I stated 'my aircraft' and called for autopilot 2. The CA advised ATC of troubleshooting a potential return to ZZZ. We were instructed to maintain 4,000 feet and fly heading 090. We cleaned up the aircraft on schedule, leveled off, and began the non-Normal methodology once we were stable. The ECAM still present was ENG2 EGT OVER LIMIT. This ECAM directed THR LVR 2 IDLE then ENG 2 MASTER OFF. I was assigned PF/Radios and we ran the ECAM via non-normal methodology. Once the engine was shut down, as expected, the ENG2 SHUTDOWN ECAM appeared. We started the non-normal methodology again. All checklists, normal and non-normal, overweight landing considerations, and briefings were complete. ATC vectored us around and was extremely helpful while we were troubleshooting and running checklists. Once we were ready to return to ZZZ we delivered the PAN-PAN REPORT and requested the full ILS to XXC in ZZZ. I maintained PF duties and the CA took the PM duties. We completed an uneventful single engine overweight landing and stopped on the runway. Once the [airport] response crews said the airplane looked good, we [advised ATC] and taxied to park. The fire trucks followed us to the gate.Aircraft malfunction, repeat gripe from 2 days prior. Bore scope and engine run appeared to be the sign off. I'm not sure that puts the aircraft in the same state that a heavy, hot take off does.Take aways/suggestions: ATC was outstanding during our event. Next, the QRH has a section for EGT 1/2 OVERLIMIT for IAE ONLY. We had CFMs. I believe there may be some benefit in looking at this specific malfunction and how our current procedures address it. If you follow the non-normal methodology, after FLYING THE AIRCRAFT, we identify the non-normal. We check if it is a quick action or ECAM exception. It's not. Once the duties are split, we go through the ECAM. This particular one directs you to shut the effected engine down. (We had the ECAM present until we accomplished the steps.) Once the engine is shut down, and you have cleaned up we do the follow up items and supplementals. When you get to the supplementals on this non normal (attached) it discusses referencing max pointer indications prior to either reducing the thrust lever or shutting the engine down. The problem is once you get to the supplemental, you have already shut the engine down if you followed the current procedure and strategy. Is there logic that keeps this ECAM on with CFMs if that temp of 970 degrees C is exceeded, or does the ECAM stay on even if only 915 degrees-950 degrees is reached? I believe this procedure as an ECAM EXCEPTION that allowed you to reference the max pointer prior to ECAM ACTION may make sense? It may also give the crew more discretion prior to shutting an engine down.
ASRS:1828655.s: The pilot flying and captain experienced an ENG2 EGT over limit on Aircraft X during a hot, heavy takeoff, forcing a single-engine overweight return to ZZZ. The crew attributes the recurrence to a potentially inadequate sign-off of the same issue two days prior and suggests procedural changes to allow engine temperature verification before shutdown.

ASRS:1828671.n: Dispatch received Supplemental Dry Ice request from ramp agent at XA12z. We made a note to send an ACARS to crew with the amendment of ' Dry Ice Supplemental Procedures in Effect'. However, the aircraft never showed 'initialized'. We noticed a block out time without an initialization, and realized that the aircraft was taxiing without having the dry ice amendment. Also noticed that several other flights were showing out of the gate without showing 'initialized'. We were not sure where on the airport property the flight was, so we called ZZZ Tower and had the crew call Dispatch. Crew called and we did the release amendment. Event was caused due to ACARS initialization never read over, so Dispatch did not know crew was on the aircraft yet.
ASRS:1828671.s: Dispatch failed to send a dry ice amendment to the crew because the aircraft never showed as initialized on ACARS. The flight taxied without the amendment until Dispatch contacted Tower to have the crew call for the release update.

ASRS:1828672.n: Aircraft X called on satcom at XA:09z located about XXXSM SE of ZZZ with a hydraulic 3 low and hydraulic 3 off issue. Flight requested priority handling and landed without issue on runway XXC and exited left. Cruise at FL380. Received a Level 1 #3 Hydraulic Elev annunciation. Looked up in QRH and it stated that the 3-2 NRMP would not work, and there were no other steps to take. Upon verification of the Hydraulic Synoptic, the Captain and I noticed Hyd Reservoir #3 was lower than the others, and dropping. At that time, it indicated 4.5 gallons. #1 was 5.9 gal, #2 was 5.7 gal. Within 5 min, the #3 reservoir was below 4 gal. We believed we had a hydraulic leak, although there was no annunciation. We referenced the QRH and selected Hyd - Manual, and turned off the pumps in #3. At that point, quantity had dropped to 0.1 gal. Within 2 minutes, the quantity displayed 12.0 gal. We [requested priority handling] with ZZZ Center, in anticipation of receiving a Hyd #3 Fail annunciation. We received vectors direct to ZZZ1, and started our descent. At approx 5,000 ft, in VMC conditions, we turned on the #3 pumps, and were able to get the aircraft fully configured without issue. We did receive the Hyd 3 Fail annunciation. The CA made a Flaps 35 landing on Runway XXC. We were able to taxi clear and taxi to our ramp entry spot where we shut down the engines and were towed in. Maintenance did not have a guess on what caused the loss of fluid in Hyd #3 system.
ASRS:1828672.s: The flight crew experienced a dropping Hydraulic #3 reservoir quantity at FL380, prompting a priority landing at ZZZ. After turning off pumps and later reactivating them at 5,000 ft, they landed safely on Runway XXC, though maintenance could not determine the cause of the fluid loss.

ASRS:1828673.n: Visual approaches to Runway XXR were in use at ZZZ at the time. Due to heavy traffic in the vicinity of the airport, and terrain to the southwest, ATC kept us on a vector that aligned us with a roughly 2 mile final approach to XXR. The airport was extremely difficult to obtain visually, and neither the FO nor myself had it in sight until about 4 miles out. We called the airport in sight, and were cleared for visual approach. At that time, I turned the aircraft to the right to align the aircraft for a downwind in a left hand traffic pattern, and descended the aircraft to 6,500 feet, the appropriate altitude for the 5 mile visual fix. Reaching 6,500 feet, we began to feel uneasy, as the terrain south of the airport forms a bowl, with terrain reaching 8,000 feet in places. Once at the 6,500 feet altitude, we could visually see that there wasn't any room to maneuver the aircraft in the valley to align it with the final approach course (we had about a 3 mile wide, terrain-free swath to work with). At about the same time, ATC issued us a low altitude warning, with the accompanying 'check altitude immediately' instruction. At that time, while on a heading corresponding with base leg, we executed a climb to 7,500 feet, and told tower we were aborting the approach. We overflew the airport and executed a right hand turn to set up for right traffic for XXR, a visual approach which was completed successfully. [Cause was] ATC's vector that led us into a valley not wide enough to maneuver the aircraft on approach. Poor charting of terrain on VFR maps in company publications. I'm filling out a separate safety concern report recommending an additional alert page on the company charts advising pilots of the difficulty of shooting a close-in visual approach to runway XXR from the West. ZZZ was conducting visual approaches to runways XXR and XXL at the time of the event. ZZZ Approach was descending us for arrival and told us to expect the visual approach for Runway XXR. At about 20 miles from the airport, we were told to proceed direct to the airport and report the field in sight for the visual. At this time we were also told to maintain 9,000 feet for terrain and traffic in the area. We did not obtain visual contact with the airport until about 5 miles away, at which point we informed ZZZ Approach and they cleared us for the visual and told us to contact the tower. At this point the approach controller has us on a vector to intercept approximately 2 mile final for Runway XXR. The Captain made a turn to the right and began a descent to traffic pattern altitude of 6,500 feet to maneuver the aircraft for a stable approach and landing. This turn brought us toward gradually rising terrain northeast of the airport. As we continued to maneuver the aircraft, it became apparent that there was not enough room to safely align with the runway. We initiated a climb and turned back toward the airport. At this time tower issued a low altitude warning and told us to 'check altitude immediately' (we were climbing through 7,000 feet at this time). We responded and said that we were climbing and turning back toward to the airport and that we would need to abort the approach and turn right to re-enter right traffic for XXR. A safe approach and landing was then completed without further incident.ZZZ Approach kept us high due to terrain and traffic and issued a tight vector for a visual approach that only allowed for a 2 mile final for the landing runway. Contributing factors included a busy GA traffic environment and inability to see the airport visually until about 5 miles away.A better way to conduct this approach when arriving from the west would be to join the RNAV approach from vectors or an initial approach fix (especially if this were to be conducted at night) or to vector the aircraft over the airport and down the valley to enter a right downwind for XXR.
ASRS:1828673.s: ATC vectored the crew for a visual approach to Runway XXR, leading them into a narrow valley with insufficient maneuvering room. The crew aborted the approach after receiving a low altitude warning, climbed to 7,500 feet, and successfully completed a right-hand traffic pattern.

ASRS:1828679.n: On approach, ATC called out a low altitude warning while we were turning to final. We leveled off in the turn and resumed descent once rolled out on final. We were above the minimum altitude of 500 feet for crossing the bridge.First time executing the approach, very busy.[We should] Practice charted visuals in the simulator.
ASRS:1828679.s: During a first-time approach, ATC issued a low altitude warning while the crew turned to final. The crew leveled off, then resumed descent above the 500-foot bridge crossing minimum, attributing the event to high workload and recommending simulator practice.

ASRS:1828694.n: On second start of the day after morning sortie, right engine oil temperature began to rise. At 109 degrees and climbing, PIC decided to secure engine. Oil temperature continued to rise to 115 degrees after shutdown. Submit to maintenance for a detailed investigation of malfunction.
ASRS:1828694.s: The PIC secured the right engine on the second sortie of the day after oil temperature rose to 109 degrees. Temperature continued climbing to 115 degrees post-shutdown, prompting a maintenance submission to investigate the malfunction.

ASRS:1828722.n: While practicing landings at ZZZ airfield. A landing gear strut cover detached in flight (plastic covering weight approximately 1lb.). We were in the pattern two separate times from XA22 local - XB00 local and XB50-XC22 local. The aircraft stayed with in 3.0 NM radius of the airfield and north of the centerline of ZZZ during its pattern operations. The aircraft is a [UAS].Neither the [visual observer] or crew witnessed the part departure. Discovery of the strut cover departed during flight was not noticed until shutdown and post landing inspection.
ASRS:1828722.s: During UAS landing practice at ZZZ airfield, a 1lb plastic landing gear strut cover detached in flight without being witnessed by the crew or visual observer. The part loss was only discovered during post-landing inspection after two pattern operations within 3.0 NM of the airfield.

ASRS:1828753.n: Pattern work at ZZZ. Normal landing, normal circumstances, no side loading or hard landings. Airplane veered right on landing, felt like a flat tire. Student, who was pilot flying applied full left rudder to correct but with little effect. Airplane exited the right side of the runway and the right main gear separated from the aircraft. I was able to shut the engine down and prevent engine damage or prop strikes.
ASRS:1828753.s: A student pilot flying at ZZZ experienced a right veer and right main gear separation during landing, suspecting a flat tire. Full left rudder had little effect, but the pilot shut down the engine to prevent further damage or prop strikes.

ASRS:1828775.n: Sector XX/XY combined at XY. I had just plugged in to receive position relief briefing. Before position relief briefing took place, Aircraft X broadcast on frequency 'I'm [requesting priority], lost pressure and initiating rapid descent from FL230 to 10,000.' I told supervisor there was [a priority aircraft] and jumped over to D-side to start coordinating with appropriate sectors. While R-side was talking to Aircraft X, I was able to complete point outs to Sector XZ and XA, but the aircraft descended so rapidly that I was unable to complete point outs to ZZZ [TRACON] X and Y departure sectors before aircraft flew through their airspace. We completed handoff to ZZZ [TRACON] Z sector.In addition, I didn't know it was a formation flight and it was the wing man that had lost pressure and rapidly descended to 10,000 prior the lead aircraft descending to 10,000. Because it was a standard formation flight, the wing man was squawking standby and descended before turning transponder back on. I never even saw a target for wing man's aircraft. I'm sure that aircraft descended through all affected sectors before coordination was completed.I think the most helpful thing is this situation would have been for Aircraft X lead aircraft to remain with emergency wing man in descent, so we would have had a target to track.Although we probably don't [have] staffing for it, some sim training on unusual situations and emergency could be helpful.R-side was trying to give wing man a squawk code so he could have a target to track. I'm not sure if it would be better to have wing man aircraft squawk [code] or to instruct lead aircraft to descend with wing man, who was in emergency descent, so not to place additional burden on pilot.
ASRS:1828775.s: An air traffic controller reported that a wingman in a formation flight lost pressure and initiated a rapid descent from FL230 to 10,000 while squawking standby, preventing radar tracking. The controller could not complete coordination with all affected sectors before the aircraft passed through, noting that keeping the lead aircraft with the emergency wingman would have improved tracking.

ASRS:1828803.n: This flight was an OE [Operating Experience] with a New Hire FO [First Officer], and double augmented crew. Normal briefings and departure preparations. Normal takeoff and climb out.I was on break at in the cabin with FO NAME (OE student). Approaching W040 at approximately XA:15 Z I was notified by one of the FAs [Flight Attendants] that I was needed on the Flight Deck. When I arrived there, FO NAME and NAME1 told me that the 'L HYD QTY' EICAS had appeared and that they were working the HYD QTY - L (C, R) (FM 2.130.4) checklist. At that time the left hydraulic quantity was at .48 and while we were watching it dropped to .47. In accordance with the checklist, we turned off the left hydraulic pumps.We then contacted and consulted with Dispatch and Maintenance Control and made an ELB entry. Dispatch advised that the weather and winds were forecast to be favorable for our arrival in ZZZ. Dispatch said that they would contact ZZZ and advise them of the situation. Maintenance Control advised that it was likely a slow leak and that the checklist offered the best advice for the situation. After the checklist and all coordination was complete, I returned to the cabin to continue my rest. I chose not to wake FO NAME2 and to allow him to continue his rest uninterrupted so that he would be alert as PF.About 30 minutes later at XB:08 a FA woke me again and said that I was needed on the Flight Deck again. When I arrived, I was advised that the R YAW DAMPER EICAS had appeared. We completed the YAW DAMPER - L (R) (FM2.90.46) and made another ELB entry. We researched and found that the hydraulic power source for the right yaw damper is the left hydraulic system that we had just depressurized. We concluded that they were likely related. We advised Dispatch and made another ELB entry. I returned to the cabin to complete my rest period.During the approach briefing we calculated the landing distance for a normal landing, and one for the loss of the left hydraulic system. We were concerned that when we turned the pumps back on during the approach that we might lose the left system quantity completely. We initially planned to configure early for the approach, but on reflection decided to configure normally and then turn the pumps back on when fully configured. If we lost the remaining quantity at that time, we were prepared to reconfigure for a flaps 20 landing. It was agreed that FO NAME2 would make the landing if the system quantity held and that I would make the landing if it did not.On approach we turned the pumps back on after we were fully configured for landing. The pressure came up on the system and quantity held for the rest of the flight. The landing was normal and uneventful. ZZZ had CFR available for our arrival and a tug if it was needed to help us clear the runway.The cabin crew were aware of the situation, but we advised them it would be a normal operation. We choose not to advise the passengers as we fully anticipated a normal landing.One concern arose during the event. During the calculation of the landing distance there was some confusion on which line to use on the chart. With a potential loss of the L HYD system it was unclear if we were to use the line for HYD SYS PRESS L ONLY or HYD SYS PRESS R and C. The title of the column says Aircraft Config/Condition and that does not clarify which row to use. To be safe we calculated both and found that we had ample runway in either case. But it brings up the question does the row titled HYD SYS PRESS L ONLY mean that you 'only' have the left system and the other two are failed, or does it mean that 'only' the left system has failed? After looking at the landing distances, I believe the right row was indeed HYD SYS PRESS L ONLY. But it might be worth a look at this chart for crews who are managing a more critical landing distance issue without the time we had to study it.All the crew did an exceptional job during this event. FOs NAME, NAME1, and NAME2 in particular were exceptional in their handling of the event.
ASRS:1828803.s: The augmented crew experienced a left hydraulic quantity drop and subsequent right yaw damper failure during cruise, likely caused by a slow leak. They managed the situation by turning off pumps, consulting maintenance, and executing a normal landing after confirming system stability on approach.

ASRS:1828820.n: During cruise we were getting a repeated issue where the control column would move slightly and cause the airplane to feel like it went through a bump of rough air. Then multiple times we had the screens flash momentarily and the auto throttle disconnected. Each time it would correct itself and everything worked normally. Eventually when this happened we got the L Gen Off light. We ran the QRH and the generator reset. Then it happened again but the QRH only allows one reset. Due to our APU being MELed we were then down to one generator. The QRH requires us to divert to the nearest suitable airport, so we [requested ATC assistance] and diverted to [a suitable alternate]. The descent and landing were normal on one generator.
ASRS:1828820.s: During cruise, the crew experienced control column movement, screen flashes, and auto-throttle disconnections caused by a Left Generator failure. With the APU MELed and the QRH limiting resets, the crew diverted to a suitable alternate and landed normally on one generator.

ASRS:1828832.n: Stadium visual 29 approach to EWR. 2.5 miles south of Meadowlands at 2,300 feet AGL. White plastic swing drone, coaltitude, went under right wingtip. No time for evasive action after sighting.
ASRS:1828832.s: A pilot on a visual approach to EWR at 2,300 feet AGL encountered a white plastic swing drone at coaltitude. The drone passed under the right wingtip, leaving no time for evasive action after it was sighted.

ASRS:1828895.n: During cruise at FL370 while deviating for thunderstorms in IMC conditions we encountered an airspeed unreliable condition. After performing memory items we ran the Airspeed Unreliable checklist. While going through the checklist we may have deviated from our assigned FL370 however we don't think we did. While running the checklist the event seemed to end. We continued through the entire checklist to make sure we were aware of all of the possible actions required if the event returned. This event occurred on the same aircraft about 3 weeks prior and maintenance addressed it at that time.I don't have any suggestions as we followed SOP and checklist usage. We don't think we had an altitude deviation but we aren't sure. During Airspeed Unreliable event at FL370 and IMC, CA (Captain) was pilot flying. Both CA and FO (First Officer) airspeed and altitude were unreliable for at least a minute or more, Airspeed Low and IAS Disagree alerts. Accomplished procedures, and hand flew based on Standby Flight Display. As best we could tell, stayed within +- 200 ft of FL370. Exiting IMC, indications returned to normal. ATC made no comment about altitude.Factors include equipment malfunction and icing. Equipment malfunctions unavoidable
ASRS:1828895.s: During cruise at FL370 in IMC, the crew encountered unreliable airspeed and altitude indications caused by equipment malfunction and icing. They followed checklists and hand-flew using the standby display, maintaining within 200 feet of FL370 until indications normalized upon exiting IMC.

ASRS:1828935.n: [We] encountered two wake turbulence events while on the downwind at 8,000 feet with Atlanta approach control. First Officer maintained control of the aircraft on both occurrences. After the second sudden right roll we observed the large aircraft we were in trail of and now was below our altitude. We realized the roll was likely not associated with a shear event from the cell nearby. We notified ATC. I would not classify either event as a severe wake turbulence event. There was no 'bank angle' aural. Perhaps ATC separation issue.
ASRS:1828935.s: The crew encountered two wake turbulence events while on downwind at 8,000 feet under Atlanta Approach control, causing sudden right rolls. The First Officer maintained control, and the reporter suspected an ATC separation issue after observing the preceding large aircraft below their altitude.

ASRS:1828939.n: Plane took off, normal call outs. Around 2,000 feet cabin started rapidly pressurizing. Crew leveled off and requested current heading and altitude, which was given by ATC. We maintained 3,000 feet and ran QRH and dumped the cabin. We returned to the departure airport with no other events. Maintenance flight should have been done before a repo to a live leg.
ASRS:1828939.s: The flight crew experienced rapid cabin pressurization at 2,000 feet after takeoff, prompting a level-off at 3,000 feet, QRH execution, and cabin dump. They returned to the departure airport, attributing the event to a missed maintenance flight prior to the revenue leg.

ASRS:1828950.n: While coming into XXX, getting close to ILS approach at 5;000ft, ATC has put us on a heading for vectors to final for Runway XXL, I started smelling burning smell, the FO smelled the same burning smell as well, at which point I told the FO to take the airplane and the radios, and called back to the flight attendants (FAs), I asked them if they smell anything and they both said they smell a burning smoke smell, I made sure with them that all the passengers were OK and they were ok as well as able to breath properly and see properly as well if there was any sign of smoke in the cabin which they said there was some in the aft of the cabin, I told them I will call back with further instructions and told the FO what the FAs told me, at which point I told him to [request expedited handling] for smoke in the cabin which I reached for the QRC which led to the [other procedures], and the QRH, which led us to further steps of [Precautionary] Depress, Cargo off, Recerc off, and pass signs on for below 10;000ft portion of the QRH. After I performed these steps which took about I took 1.5 to 2 minutes the smell disappeared, I called the FAs back and informed them we will be making an [expedited] landing, and performed the [preparation] items, they advised me the smell and the visible smoke is not there anymore, I also told them in that case we will most likely not need to evacuate after landing but I will call them upon landing with my decision. After that I took the airplane back from the FO and he continued his PM duties. After Landing I called the FAs again to re-verify there was no smoke or smell in the cabin, as well as all the passengers and both of them were OK and once assured there wasn't any smoke or smell or any issues with the passengers, and both FAs canceled the [expedited handling] and decided to continue to the gate. Descending through 15,000 feet in ZZZ, I suddenly smelled a very strong and potent smell in the cockpit and asked my Captain if he smelled the same thing. He said yes and then immediately called the Flight Attendants. The Aft FA informed us there was smoke in the cabin and they smell the same type of odor.
